Honestly this is about the fourth review I've made for the game, it's changed so frequently.  A little while ago the game was quite fun.  As you can see in the posted video there was a ton of action packed combat to contest these little pillars, once you got them all it would take down the enemies shield and you could chunk away at the core.  Game sizes were usually somewhere around 10 people per team, and it was fun.  But for some unfathomable reason that gamemode is gone now...  Teams have been cut down to 5 per team, and you capture the altars by sitting on them instead of shooting at the little chunks.  Sounds similar ya, and it is.  But here's the big difference.  The map feels so empty.  You're basically just wandering around hoping you don't bump into anyone because you're fighting them all alone.  Then you just sit there trying to capture the pad, sitting there, waiting, and waiting.  You don't even have that small excitement of shooting the little blocks away.  There's no more coordinated fighting, because everyone has to be so spread out.  No more having one guy tank with a healer on him while the flying guy takes pot shots and the artillery guy lays into them.  The game REALLY needs teams larger than 5 people.  But the way it's looking, that gamestyle is just gone.
My guess is that the devs are trying to save money by scaling back on their server size. And I completely understand that.  But in doing so they've really stripped the game of its excitement, and I just can't keep my review as a thumbs up.  It's just not fun with so few people in such large maps.

What to say... BUY IT!
Back in the day of the premiere of The Orange Box, I've bought the compilation only for the small, experimental game named "Portal". It revolved around using a gun that shoots small wormholes onto the walls. If you walk through one, you get out through the second.
Second installment is a logical masterpiece - not only it improved the gameplay in probably every way, but also came with unforgettable story revolving around AI gone rampant and a silent protagonist trying to "fight" her way out of the [eculiar situation she found herself in.
AND COOP. Co-Operation is the place where the game shines the brightest. Solving the chambers alone was awesome, but single player does not give that magical feeling of accomplishment than completing this game with a friend, utilizing unique mechanics as well as not two, but four portals.
AND PERPETUAL TESTING INITIATIVE! This game comes with small replay value... But why replay the campaign, when people have already posted THOUSANDS of custom-made maps into Steam Workshop? Open PTI menu, hit quickplay and tear through endless chambers that will not only test your mind, but your thumbs or wrists, depending on input device ;)
DEFINITELY A MUST-HAVE. Now I need a friend with whom we can tackle community co-op chambers :3

I want to reccomend this game. It has every ounce of potential to be amazing. However, espetially in light of the patch released I can't say I reccomend the game, and here's why.
There's absolutely no way to progress reasonably. It took me 11 hours straight (Of playing deathmatch) To get to level 6..... out of 100. Blocks are unlocked via levels and a lot of core aspects to making different kinds of robots aren't unlocked until significantly later. So essentially creativity is stunted severely until you've spent hundreds of hours playing their unballanced MOBA style game mode that makes the lack of any real level matchmaking frustratingly obvious. In deathmatch it was short, bloody, and if you got matched up against someone who just straight outgunned you, oh well, on to the next one where I might be on the other side of that coin.
Unfortunately this game is a prime example of trying to be something it isn't. You have minecraft type ideas behind a goofy creative shooter game that for some screwball reason tries to force hardcore ideas onto its players.

Portal is a masterpiece to me. The first one was pretty good, even though it was more a concept than anything, yet the Portal universe was so interesting. Portal 2 is now giving a lot, lot more of information and details about Aperture Science, the history of the company, Chell etc.. and this is really interesting! The game let you discover a lot more about how all these tests work, you're finally seeing the machine (well, beside GLaDOS of course).
The gameplay is the same as the first one portalgun-wise, but introduces a bunch of new mechanics. Turrets, our lovely turrets, are also back into the party. Puzzles are really cleverly-made, nothing is too difficult if you concentrate enough, though I felt I kinda cheated one or two rooms and somehow made it to the exit, without trying to.
This is of course a must-buy, it goes on sale regularly but is totally worth the full price. Not to mention the addition of a CO-OP mode with our two new friends Atlas and P-Body, each one of them controlled by you and one of your friend! Try to cooperate.. or mess around with your friend!

I love the idea of Robocraft.  I love that there is no limit to what you can create.  I love spending hours designing cool vehicles.  But I do not love the game itself.  Physics are practically nonexistant, so you'll find your bot rolling over or spinning out at the slightest movement, no matter how evenly balanced your craft may be.  Wheels are barely functional, and they are the only movement parts available when first starting out.  There is no tutorial, and the mechanics of both building and fighting are not the least bit intuitive.  New players will need to seek informatoin online to figure things out, but most information to be found is outdated due to the changes made to the game in the last few months.  Matchmaking is completely unbalanced, allowing higher level players to build simple bots with higer grade weapons, allowing them to slaughter lower level players.  Despite the limitless amount of customization, matches are generally dominated by the same 3 or 4 styles of craft.  Freejam is aware of these issues and many more, but they don't seem to be in any hurry to address them, other than constantly tweaking the weapons.  They're rushing to get more and more new content out, but are ignoring the bugs that are causing more and more players to leave.
In theory, this game should be amazing.  In practice, it has a long way to go.  I can't recommend it right now, but I'm hopeful that it will, eventually, be worth everyone's time.

I use to like robocraft, but I'm updating this review after I saw it from a while ago.
The games dead. Seriously.

After clocking up 135 hours and greatly enjoying it, my opinion has swayed over the past few months. Changes which break builds, tactics and so on and force you to learn, I expect but not to the extent and frequency to which updates have been released, infact, I enjoy it! The need to learn and develop new skills and builds is good, previous exploits fixed, broken builds, tactics, bugs and so on, fixed and balanced.
Now however, the motivation to go back has completely dwindled now as each update for a good while has reaped the same problems over and over. No longer do I hear about good matches, interesting builds or tactics but rather cheap builds which really shouldn't work at all like rectangles covered in boosters. I understand the game is early access and aspects of it can change drastically but over the past few months updates have been changing the game over and over in such a drastic and reckless manner and too frequently. It seems if people complain enough about how "Snipers are OP" and how they get slaughtered when an SMG gets close then an update will mess up the statistics of those builds, raising the power of other builds too much and just recycling issues instead of finding and maintaining a balance.
This game was fun, particularly when playing with a few people you knew, you could co-ordinate and compliment each others builds or make something special. Now, all that seems lost, I don't want to learn what works now since it just isn't enjoyable anymore and if I learned again, how long would it be before that knowledge is scrapped again?
Perhaps new players will have fun playing the game and learning and having fun in its current state, but if they keep changing it, I fear the cycle will repeat with longtime players and groups quiting and eventually this game may die out. There's still time to save it but I feel too many players have given up that it may never recover if large, calculated steps are taken to improve the game and content an to welcome veterans once again.
What I can still say for this game is its free to play model is excellent (Atleast the last time I played 25/07/15) there's no P2W, any part for your bot which costs real money is identical in stats to their regular counterpart or are purely cosmetic like a flag. There's a premium option which I believe awarded double RP and allowed for platoons of 3 or 4 players. Extra garage slots could be purchased for a reasonable price but you still had a handful if you didn't want to invest and premium bots were available which really just let you skip ahead in the tech tree and sometimes provided unique cosmetics. I never felt pushed or like I needed to spend money, I spent it because I enjoyed the game.
Perhaps in the future I may try this game once again but I don't have high hopes. If you play it then be aware of the issues some of us have pointed out in our reviews and be prepared to re-learn if you play long enough but for now, this game will gather dust in my library until I decide something better could use the room it currently lingers in.

Hello. My name is Jeff, I am 28 and I have been playing Robocraft for over a year and a half now.
In the next few paragraphs I will try to explain how and why Robocraft has gone from one of my all time favourite games, to no longer worthy of my time.
I will start by telling you more about me, and my account.
I have always been able to think outside of the box, and come up with great, new, original ideas. This gave me the ability to create, test, and perfect many bots that looked, and functioned like no one else's. I took great pride in spending MANY hours making these ground breaking bots. I enjoyed it so much I often offered to lend a hand to all of my fellow friends and community members. Thus - I have the account and passwords to 22 other accounts. Some of them have as much money and hours invested as mine, however none of which play any longer for the same reasons you are about to read.
I have more hours logged then most players.(928)
I probably have another 500+ hours logged on friends accounts.
I have more garage slots then most players. (30+)
Prior to the reduction of max CPU per tier I had all 30 garage slots full of max CPU builds (1511, -more details on this issue to come)
I HAD a bot for each Tier 1-4 and 2 bots for each tier 5-9. I kept a healer, and a DPS in every tier to allow me to help friends level up. (I used to premote this game heavily amognst friends)
I still have have some of the BEST T-10 max cpu builds possible. (16+)
Read that again. 16- T10 bots. All finely tuned and perfected for battle.
At one point I also had 2 max CPU Megabots - but tore them apart as the Dev team seemed to go in a different direction after releasing Megabots.
In other words.... They were a huge time and money sink with no real way to play them in any game mode without waiting 10-20 min to get into a 3 min game.
I have over 200,000,000 in-game credits.
I had every single part unlocked and some 150,000 T-10 tech points.....  I had many thousand Tech points in every tier until they did away with tech points at the same time they did away with tiers (more details to come)
None of this matters when you have changed the game to the point it is not enjoyable to play.
My advice - STAY AWAY!
-If you want a more details on why the devs are ruining this game - continue reading.
The #1 reason for me is a 3 step process. (represented by A,B,C)
-A. They put a Max CPU cap on all lower levels leading up to the old max of 1511.
T-1 500
T-2 600
T-3 700 etc. etc. etc.
They did this, because they claimed it was unfair to have a 1511 CPU bot in tiers lower then 10. My argument is the tiers were broken up by RoboRanking - not CPU.  So If I choose to be skimp on armor, and movement parts, to get a better gun, and play my bot to its strengths and weaknesses then that choice is on me.  The same give and take could be made with any combo of parts as long as you stayed inside the RoboRanking of the tier you wished to stay in. Each part added its respected value, meaning the better the item - the more RoboRanking it had. You could make a 1511 CPU bot with the same RoboRanking as a 900 CPU bot using different combination of parts.
At the same time they applied a max CPU cap per tier - they also made it impossible to add any guns HIGHER then the tier you were aiming to build in. In other words.... IF you took one white block, and added one T-7 SMG to it, your one white block is now a T-7. Same for any gun type, of any tier.
Not a big deal unless you already had 13-15 max cpu bots at lower levels that ranged from T1-T9. All of these bots I spent a GREAT deal of time making, and fine tuning. So suddenly all of these bots were T10. Obviously these bots were not able to compete with proper T10 builds.
-B. So I was forced to DELETE all of my T-1 through T-9 bots that I spent so much time working on. But I am not easily deterred, so I get started on rebuilding. I spend MANY MORE hours remaking lower tier bots inside the new ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t requirements only to have the VERY next update (2-3 weeks later)remove tiers completely.
Really?  Like REALLY, really?
If your whole plan was to remove the tiers entirely then why even release the update before it forcing all this nonsense on me? Why not release the updates together so I didnt just waste 3 weeks of my life??
To make them more "fair," (not sure how this process is fair to players like myself) is their official statement. "Balancing of the tiers."
-C. Now there is a broken match making system that attempts to put you in with other bots around the same rank as you. It fails horribly. They were trying to prevent people from stacking at the top of a tier to make it easier for the people at the bottom. Instead, they take you from wherever tier you are in and places you against people 2-3 tiers higher. Cause that's fair.
All they were trying to accomplish was water it down, so the young kids, and faint of heart, did not have a hissy fit when it came time to enter a new tier.
-Point of interest- It is supposed to be hard..... That is what leveling up, and grinding is all about. This is also how YOU, Devjam, make your money. By offering a solution to those who do not wish to grind.

Okay - So looking past that huge game breaker of tier removal...what else is wrong?
The new game mode?
You really think it is a good idea to give each team a shield around their base, that they can shoot OUT of but enemies can not shoot IN TO?
AND while doing that you want to buff snipers so they can 1 shot you?
The middle of the map became a no man's land.... People would literally just sit inside their base dome, camping, waiting for the enemy to leave the safety of their dome.... As soon as you leave your dome you get sent back to respawn. Said snipers are not playing the objective of the map. Just straight up camping. And - can you blame them? Thats on the Devs.
Robocraft is a PERFECT example of how devs kill early access games. They spend too much time trying to nerf this and nerf that so that all the little 12 year olds can get along. When are you going to build a game that time and effort is going to be a factor in your success?
The amount of time I spent fine tuning 1 bot until it was perfect is probably more time then most other people have played the game in total.... Only to have that 50-100 hours spent on 1 bot to be ruined by the next update, or exploited by a glitch. or even worse - reduce the max cpu per tier forcing players to remake their lower level bots - only to completely remove the tiers entirely... What a ♥♥♥♥ing slap in the face that was. No compensation for time lost.
- I can not even get a single Dev to respond to me anywhere, about anything. I have tried politely messaging them privately, publicly, on their personal pages, public pages, left forum posts, filled out reviews on the website..... ZERO response from anyone but noobs who have no idea WTF I am even talking about.
And why do you keep releasing "new content" when you can't even get the previous updates "new content" to work correctly.....
Talk about a joke....

I enjoyed it so much I often offered to lend a hand to all of my fellow friends and community members. Thus - I have the account and passwords to 22 other accounts. Some of them have as much money and hours invested as mine, however none of which play any longer for the same reasons you are about to read.
I have more hours logged then most players.(928)
I probably have another 500+ hours logged on friends accounts.
I have more garage slots then most players. (30+)
Prior to the reduction of max CPU per tier I had all 30 garage slots full of max CPU builds (1511, -more details on this issue to come)
I HAD a bot for each Tier 1-4 and 2 bots for each tier 5-9. I kept a healer, and a DPS in every tier to allow me to help friends level up. (I used to premote this game heavily amognst friends)
I still have have some of the BEST T-10 max cpu builds possible. (16+)
Read that again. 16- T10 bots. All finely tuned and perfected for battle.
At one point I also had 2 max CPU Megabots - but tore them apart as the Dev team seemed to go in a different direction after releasing Megabots.
In other words.... They were a huge time and money sink with no real way to play them in any game mode without waiting 10-20 min to get into a 3 min game.
I have over 200,000,000 in-game credits.
I had every single part unlocked and some 150,000 T-10 tech points.....  I had many thousand Tech points in every tier until they did away with tech points at the same time they did away with tiers (more details to come)
None of this matters when you have changed the game to the point it is not enjoyable to play.
My advice - STAY AWAY!
-If you want a more details on why the devs are ruining this game - continue reading.
The #1 reason for me is a 3 step process. (represented by A,B,C)
-A. They put a Max CPU cap on all lower levels leading up to the old max of 1511.
T-1 500
T-2 600
T-3 700 etc. etc. etc.
They did this, because they claimed it was unfair to have a 1511 CPU bot in tiers lower then 10. My argument is the tiers were broken up by RoboRanking - not CPU.  So If I choose to be skimp on armor, and movement parts, to get a better gun, and play my bot to its strengths and weaknesses then that choice is on me.  The same give and take could be made with any combo of parts as long as you stayed inside the RoboRanking of the tier you wished to stay in. Each part added its respected value, meaning the better the item - the more RoboRanking it had. You could make a 1511 CPU bot with the same RoboRanking as a 900 CPU bot using different combination of parts.
At the same time they applied a max CPU cap per tier - they also made it impossible to add any guns HIGHER then the tier you were aiming to build in. In other words.... IF you took one white block, and added one T-7 SMG to it, your one white block is now a T-7. Same for any gun type, of any tier.
Not a big deal unless you already had 13-15 max cpu bots at lower levels that ranged from T1-T9. All of these bots I spent a GREAT deal of time making, and fine tuning. So suddenly all of these bots were T10. Obviously these bots were not able to compete with proper T10 builds.
-B. So I was forced to DELETE all of my T-1 through T-9 bots that I spent so much time working on. But I am not easily deterred, so I get started on rebuilding. I spend MANY MORE hours remaking lower tier bots inside the new ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t requirements only to have the VERY next update (2-3 weeks later)remove tiers completely.
Really?  Like REALLY, really?
If your whole plan was to remove the tiers entirely then why even release the update before it forcing all this nonsense on me? Why not release the updates together so I didnt just waste 3 weeks of my life??
To make them more "fair," (not sure how this process is fair to players like myself) is their official statement. "Balancing of the tiers."
-C. Now there is a broken match making system that attempts to put you in with other bots around the same rank as you. It fails horribly. They were trying to prevent people from stacking at the top of a tier to make it easier for the people at the bottom. Instead, they take you from wherever tier you are in and places you against people 2-3 tiers higher. Cause that's fair.
All they were trying to accomplish was water it down, so the young kids, and faint of heart, did not have a hissy fit when it came time to enter a new tier.
-Point of interest- It is supposed to be hard..... That is what leveling up, and grinding is all about. This is also how YOU, Devjam, make your money. By offering a solution to those who do not wish to grind.

Okay - So looking past that huge game breaker of tier removal...what else is wrong?
The new game mode?
You really think it is a good idea to give each team a shield around their base, that they can shoot OUT of but enemies can not shoot IN TO?
AND while doing that you want to buff snipers so they can 1 shot you?
The middle of the map became a no man's land.... People would literally just sit inside their base dome, camping, waiting for the enemy to leave the safety of their dome.... As soon as you leave your dome you get sent back to respawn. Said snipers are not playing the objective of the map. Just straight up camping. And - can you blame them? Thats on the Devs.
Robocraft is a PERFECT example of how devs kill early access games. They spend too much time trying to nerf this and nerf that so that all the little 12 year olds can get along. When are you going to build a game that time and effort is going to be a factor in your success?
The amount of time I spent fine tuning 1 bot until it was perfect is probably more time then most other people have played the game in total.... Only to have that 50-100 hours spent on 1 bot to be ruined by the next update, or exploited by a glitch. or even worse - reduce the max cpu per tier forcing players to remake their lower level bots - only to completely remove the tiers entirely... A game about building your own vehlicle and using it to wage war against your foes.
You have various ways of movement, each with their own ups,downs and limitation.
The movements option you have avalible to you at most times are Wheels,Tracks,Walker legs (spider style),Hovers,propulsion jets,wings 'n rudders and Rotorblades.
Your allowed to use as many as you want in any combination as long as your vehlicle stays under the flop/crap on your vehlical limit (this limit raises with your level untill a a max at level 100)
The weapons you have availible are SMGs.Plasma (think motors from halo but faster), Railguns (snipers), Nano Disruptor  (Medigun that can hurt foes),Teslas (a 1 time use lightsaber sub weapon) and Lights (Its rarely used but lights for the enemy team can blind them from seeing the siloute of your ship which is very usefull for messing up snipers).
You can only use 1 weapon at a time along with as many tesla blades as you want as long as you stay under the limit.
There are also mountable sheilds in this game called electroplates which weight down your craft with the trade off of having bassically a force feild that can be recharged but also can be destroyed if hit enough when not charged (this saves you from being murdered by high damage weapons of teslas,rails and plasmas.
All these things are built into tiers that are suppose to be fairly matched against each other. Altough the matchmaking does not work in tiers anymore since the devs wanted to give the users more freedom with building their robot.
How the matchmaking system works NOW is that your robot is cumlitive off all its parts. All parts have a individual rating on them, this ratting is added up and you have your robo-rating. When sticked into match making, it adds up everyone's roborating on a certain team, averages it out, and then matches it with a team of equal rating.
This is system is great and all but you might be matched with an idoit who poorly design their bot and just has a high robo-rating due to the very varied tiers of the parts.
There is a building meta in this game but you can always♥♥♥♥♥♥around and make a reasonable bot in the shape of a doge head or something along the lines.

Now see, I'm in a difficult position. I want to recommend this game, because I've had a lot of fun playing it.
However, the key word there is HAD. Because there's been updates, and they've changed a lot...for the worse.
I mean okay, some stuff is good, like the new pieces, weapons et cetera, and the new maps. However, there's a lot of stuff I don't like either. So let's make a list.
1. LOCK THE ♥♥♥♥ING MOUSE
I do NOT want to be flying around mid-match and end up CLICKING ON THE CHAT WINDOW. This happened TWICE in one match. Bloody annoying. Also, being able to click the buttons at the top of the screen while in build mode? Yeah come on, this is just stupid.
2. TECH POINTS WERE GOOD
It meant that you could choose what you wanted to unlock, it gave you a reason to actually try to make a lower-tier robot, just to get those last few tech points to clean up the tree. I mean okay, the new tree, where it's based on level, s'kinda nice.
3. MATCHMAKING STATS TABLE
I guess this would be hard to add in, since the new matchmaking system is based on robot ranking or whatever, but I just liked being able to see how many were in each tier. How about show how many are in each robot ranking bracket? That'd be nice.
But yes, as said before, some stuff is good. The fact that you no longer have matches with over-tiered players is kinda nice, but to be honest? Wasn't that big of a deal. Uh...no, okay, more bad stuff.
4. KEYBOARD SHORTCUTS
I liked the old keyboard shortcuts for switching between Tech Tree (not really needed now), Shop and Building. But as far as I can tell, there's no direct shortcut to building. Small problem, but meh. On the subject...
5. OLD MENUS
I found navigating the old menus very easy. This new one is...a little confusing. I mean, "Drive" to choose which 'bot you want to use? Garage was much better. I dunno. The old one just seemed to...work better.
EDIT - Oh and holding left control to show mouse? Nope. Does not work.
So, I mean, this game has gotten worse in some important ways (PLEASE LOCK THE MOUSE) but has has improved in some areas. But at the end of the day...it's free. So why not give it a try? I found it fun. Perhaps you will too.

This is THE BEST f2p game available on steam.
Very in-depth building mechanics with empasis on physics, armour designs, and creativity.
Players are rewarded for doing good, and there is literally ZERO pay to win in this game. You can buy created full bots, but they are inadequate compared to a custom built bot created with in-game credits.
Bot design is EVERYTHING in this game. You must design, experiment, scrap, re-design, test countless times before you get something you like and enjoy playing. Some might consider this a con, but for me it is a HUGE plus. If you build a crappy bot, no matter how good you are you're going to be nothing more than a quick kill for the other team. Building skill is more important than player skill, but player skill does also play a big factor here. It IS possible to overtake a more powerful bot 1v1, but if so it would be entirely dependant on skill and your enemies lack of skill ;)
The game is free. DOWNLOAD IT, and give it a chance. This game has come a LONG way since launch and has damn near tripled its content.

I got this game a few months ago. I can't put it down, I started out intrigued, and then I got to hover blades.... I thought I found my ****, but then I made something that actually flew, not just hovered....
This game has most of everything I have really wanted to see/find in a game:
Creativity, pacing, community, and fair play.
Creativity:
This is the most obvious forte of the game if you've ever looked into it. If you haven't, worry not, I'll summarize here. This game allows to create whatever you want as a craft of war in the battle against others' crafts (not mentioned often is the fact you must have this obnoxious thing called a pilot supercomputer..... once you have that, you're set). There are limits of course, but as you progress through the game, those limits slowly wane, and you can craft a tool of war that is quite literally to your own style of fighting. For example, my first craft that was truly "mine" also happened to have hoverblades, which enabled it to hover; it was happenstance, but it also looks like a Manta, and uses plasma launchers (thus appropiately dubbed Plasmanta). My playstyle with it is flanking and ambushing. That's just one playstyle of many one can use with hovercrafts, or snipers, or tanks, or flyers, etc, the list goes on, and on, and on.
Pacing:
Depending on who you ask, this is a highly subjective subject, and for myself, I consider it highly regarded as a forte. When I refer to pacing, I mean both "grinding" and the gaming itself. I've played for a little over 24 hours, and I am at tier 5 with a second craft at tier IV (only because I want to level up while getting used to a new craft). I don't see an issue with this at all, even if the tier 10 grind comes around and becomes a week long experience, I'd expect a sort of exponential growth of the amount of grinding. That aside, the next thing is the more subjective point, which is the gaming itself.
Some people may not like to do 15-25 minutes of gameplay in one match. Okay, that's perfectly fine. This game does 15-25 minute matches perfectly. The easiest way to explain it would be that it's something of a cross between World of Tanks pace of gameplay and Call of Duty: fast (CoD), but not chaotic (WoT). There are times when the matches are really lopsided and the game ends in under only 15 minutes; but do note that I say "only," since that doesn't give much time for one to truly play the experience.
Community:  This one is a "biggie."
I come from the Wargaming crowd (ie, World of Tanks) if you have not caught on to that. There is more or less one of the most toxitic crowd I've been in, but also had some nice points and areas depending on where you ventured out. Here, while the games are somewhat quiet (too busy gaming, not enough time to type), it is obvious that most everyone knows what needs to be done, what is the objective, and somewhat  collectively gets together to accomplish the goal.
Fair Play:
It's free to play, so just about everyone, who hasn't played this game as of yet, will automatically think, "oh, must be pay to win." However, the only benefit paying gets you is a better finanical situation and a better reputation (for every premium user in game, everyone gets +5% boost to their earnings, including premium users), as well as cool looking gadget. How often is it that one hopes to themselves they see someone who is paying to play? Another thing is that this game basically forbids multi tiered battles; as in, tier 4s fight tier 4s, and tier 10s fight tier 10s. If you are being beaten out by another player, it's not because of an overwhelming advantage of strength, it's because they outplayed you. And that is a satisfying guarantee.
The only few bad things about this game I can point out is the way the tech tree is set up (where armor parts are individual, and electroreactive armor must be researched for both "right" and "left" platings... dumb, right?), as well as the absurdity of the SMG guns in the lower tiers. Most everytime anyone goes up against these wall of machine guns, they get blown away in a blink of an eye. It's annoying, but granted it does usually mean it can happen right back at them.
Loving this game so far, recommended it already to a lot of my friends, disappointed in the results (almost no one wished to try out the game). I would be willing to wipe my memory to be able to go through the first few tiers all over again, as they were actually enjoyable. If you made it this far, well, why are you still here? You're obviously interested, so go! Go see for yourself what an intense game this is, with such a vast potential for excellence and greatness!
Side Edit: I had written this review about a few weeks ago, before they got rid of the tier system and research grind in the way of just levels. I'm unsure how this really works, but so far, it seems like every other game I'm at the bottom, and at the next game, I'm at the top. So, I guess all I can say about that is to just play the way you want to.
Irrelevant Note: Graphics are ridiculosuly easy on the computer, just start from "fastest" in the settings, and go up and stop wherever comfortable.

Portal 2 is the follow on to the extremely successful first person original. The game retains all of the game play elements from Portal 1 and adds lots of new features such as bridges made from light beams, and splashing paint gel which accelerate your speed or make you jump higher.
In the single player campaign, you play as Chell. As with the original Portal, your character can take a small amount of damage before they die, thankfully like the original you don't take fall damage still. The aim of the story mode is to explorer the Aperture Science Lab, which is filled of complex puzzles that have a clear exit point, but there are also other parts of the game which are not so clear leaving the objects less clear.
The tutorial at the start of the game explains all of the game play elements very well and gets you well prepared for the on coming puzzles; and whenever there is a new element introduced, the game does a very good job of making you aware what it does without shoving a tutorial screen in your face every time.
Portal 2 is powered by the Source engine, like all of Valve's more recent releases (Half Life 2, Left 4 Dead, TF2), and it looks stunning. You will find it hard nowadays to find a game that looks as well polished as Portal 2, all of the colours, textures and visual effects are done perfectly.
Story-wise is the feature in Portal 1 that I thought it fell down on, however in Portal 2 they knocked it out of the park. It follows on from the story line set in the original and goes beyond the level of detail and complexity that you would expect. I needed to find out how it ended once I started playing, and the ending is just beautifully crafted.
The difficulty is like most puzzle games, if you are good at them, it will just come naturally. It definitely has a better difficulty curve when compared to the original, but even still at times I had to revert to a walkthrough to pass through some puzzles (shame on me eh?) but there is nothing here that can't be solved if you sit and think for a couple of minutes each time.
The single player story mode took me about seven hours to complete, this to me is a perfect length for a game of this type, the game ends at a high point and I was 100% satisfied with the outcome. There is also a co-op campaign included which will also add a good number of hours. On top of both of these, we also have Steam Worksho

This game continues the story of the original game in the (very) distant future. Story continues to be loosely woven into the Half Life universe, although the events of Half Life are now in the (very) distant past.
A few extra characters join the two main characters from the original game, and each one makes important contributions to the story. There are a lot of tests to solve, lots of history to explore, and plenty of pre-recorded messages to listen to. While the game has a serious tone, the dialogue is absolutely hilarious.
This is a much longer game than the original. There are a wide variety of different (but often familiar) environments that you must navigate to move the story along. Game play flows smoothly from one chapter to the next, and the experiences is extremely satisfying. There are some fun twists and surprises. All along the way the story, test chambers and other game environments are all very nicely knit together.
If you enjoyed the original Portal, you will love this sequel.
(This review is only for the single-player campaign. There are also multiplayer co-op courses that appear to be just as engaging and full of content as the main game: not just nice add-ons!)

Wait until it's out of early access.
I'm pretty annoyed due to random crashes and a horribly unintuitive UI (a teammate wants to surrender? Better cover up your map! Are you dead and want to see what's happening? Wait until you spawn to see the map because it's covered by a hint you've seen 20 times.)
Guns are pretty consistently being rebalanced, but nothing ever quite works. Something is always "OP", and right now that's rails and SMGs. Nanos are fun while Plasma bombs are a joke until you reach the end of the game.
Aside from that, it really needs a way to let players into active matches. "A player has disconnected from your battle" is common, and you can't be sure if it's because they just got fed up and quit, or if they crashed. And if you DO crash (which happens often enough), the game will treat you like you up and quit like a jerk.
The game will reduce your respawn in exchange for lost players, but this isn't actually game-changing for the team who lost a player. It lessens the blow, but it isn't going to win you fights. In fact, it likely just extends games that would otherwise end the misery of the weakened team sooner because it respawns you in your base, forcing you to defend or get farmed for easy score. There should be either an invulnerability period (a few seconds or until you shoot), or some sort of fountain where you cannot shoot from, but can be safe. This would also help prevent AFK players from feeding people who sit in your base and kill them. AFK players are just as big an issue as players who quit, or worse considering they can get farmed.
All in all, the game is great. The issues aren't.

Personally, I love the concept of this game, can't find fault with it at all.
HOWEVER, the game itself is a different matter.
Ever since the Epic Loot update, I feel this game has gone considerably downhill, and the recent BETA update was the final straw for me. I do understand that the game is still in development, but it's not exactly being developed for the better in my opinion. Let me explain why:
1) Apparently matchmaking in battles has become more evenly balanced, giving both teams an even chance of winning. I don't believe that for a second. Often the case is that the blue team will be full of random robots, and the red team will be filled with robots that completely outgun the blue team. Far too one-sided.
2) The game's currency has completely gone belly-up. Before the Epic Loot update, we had "Robopoints" (earned in-game) and "Galaxy Credits" (purchased with real money), which worked fine for everyone concerned. Now, we're stuck with a much worse currency called "Robits". You no longer get 50% of an item's worth when you sell it, instead you get 25%. Nearly all of the robots uploaded to the robot factory are WAY above anyone's price range because of this.
3) Another system introduced with the Epic Loot update was crates. The idea of them is that depending on the crate you get and the CPU level of your robot, you'll recieve a certain standard of items in said crate. However, this never seems to be the case, as it is left completely to chance, which means really low-level crates and CPU robots can often pick up really good items from time to time, and very high-level crates and CPU robots rarely get anything of any significant value. THIS NEEDS TO CHANGE, FREEJAM. It would be better if you were guaranteed a certain standard of items when you receive a crate (e.g. Rusted and Bronze crates should contain no more than items branded "Rare", and higher level crates such as Diamond and Protonium should guarantee at least one "Epic" item, with a significantly higher chance of receiving "Legendary" items).
4) There's no originality in designs anymore. EVERYONE (asides from myself and maybe a few other people) copies everyone else's ideas, removing the whole "creative" factor from the game. What's the point? Are people just too lazy to design their own? Is there one particular design that's so unfairly strong compared to other designs that everyone wants it just to thwart everyone else? Perhaps we will never know, but there needs to be more creativity in this game.
5) Finally, the biggest problem in my opinion is the fact that it seems you have to pay money to buy premium membership in order to solve all the above problems, which turns the game into yet another pay-to-play. I cannot overemphasize how much I HATE games like this. I am not going to pay [X] amount of money on a game that doesn't benefit me in real life in any way at all.
Overall, I think this game is extremely bad compared to what it once was in its early ALPHA form. Shame on you, Freejam, I honestly don't know how you managed to mess up something that was exceptionally great and everybody loved to play. This was once a brilliant free game, now it seems to have turned into another application that requires a wallet in-hand if you're going to get anywhere decent with it. Not something I'd recommend unless you're descended from Bill Gates and have literally NOTHING better to spend your money on.

Portal 2:
+ The story is a big improvement from the original Portal, which was vague and bareboned. There's more dialogue this time around which actually explains what's going on, along with the usual amusing banter.
+ The puzzles in Portal 2 are leaps and bounds ahead of the first Portal. They are more intricate, less predictable and require the use of multiple strategies in order to progress. They're also greater in number than the meagre 19 offered in Portal. Furthermore, Valve has created some new, interesting gameplay mechanics. The introduction of repulsion gel (which allows you to jump very high), propulsion gel (which gives you the ability to run extremely fast) and conversion gel (which alters any physical surface it touches to become portable), results in a varied, distinct gameplay experience.
+ The graphics are a step up from Portal, which is nice.
+ Co-op mode for those who enjoy playing with friends.
- Only 10-15 hours worth of content (singleplayer), which is quite short, especially when similar puzzle games like the Talos Principle have a solid 30 hours +
- Some elements of the puzzles in Portal 2 were made to be intentionally deceiving, at least in my view. The main culprits were parts of the environment (grates, pipes) obstructing my view of surfaces where I could fire portals. I could logically deduce a puzzle with ease, had I know such surfaces existed. Instead, I was left scratching my head for an hour, attempting to get through an unsolvable puzzle. Not my idea of fun.
- The story of Portal 2 is fine, but in contrast to other first person puzzle games like the Talos Principle, it becomes clear that it cannot measure up, to any degree. The Talos Principle combined a deep, meaningful and intriguing plot with important decision making, something Portal 2 doesn't do.
Overall Score: 7.5/10
Portal 2 is a pretty decent game and there's nothing intrinstically wrong with the puzzles or storyline, other than its longevity and perhaps its linearity. Only when you analyse it in comparison to other puzzle games like the Talos Principle, can you identify its weaknesses. Portal 2 can never meet the level of quality the Talos Principle delivers in its puzzles and its story (comparatively speaking) is lame.
Nevertheless, I do recommend Portal 2 for anyone who hasn't yet played it. A 95/100 Metacritic score is unwarranted, but it's still a cool adventure.
Purchasing on sale is a must.

When I finished the first game, I knew it would get a rightful place in my heart as one of my favorite games of all time. Portal brought a good story (ruled by a rather charismatic villain) and innovative mechanics -- and those are two elements that we see in many games, but there is hardly harmony between these two as there is in Portal series.
Portal 2 surprised me not only about visual improvement, but by expanding a story that I thought was complete and well done. This universe showed me that I did not know everything already, I still had much to learn and if you played Half-Life (especially the second one), you will plunge in this universe and will be very pleased by the divine surprises.
"Portal 2 being better than the first one" does not mean that the former game is bad or inferior in some way. It means exactly what I said: Portal 2 is better, and only that. I strongly advise you to play the first game and then the sequel, 'cause there are moments of history that will have much more meaning in that way.
In short, Portal is a piece of a cake, a cake stuffed with pleasant surprises. And we all love cakes, right?

When I finished the first game, I knew it would get a rightful place in my heart as one of my favorite games of all time. Portal brought a good story (ruled by a rather charismatic villain) and innovative mechanics -- and those are two elements that we see in many games, but there is hardly harmony between these two as there is in Portal series.
Portal 2 surprised me not only about visual improvement, but by expanding a story that I thought was complete and well done. This universe showed me that I did not know everything already, I still had much to learn and if you played Half-Life (especially the second one), you will plunge in this universe and will be very pleased by the divine surprises.
"Portal 2 being better than the first one" does not mean that the former game is bad or inferior in some way. It means exactly what I said: Portal 2 is better, and only that. I strongly advise you to play the first game and then the sequel, 'cause there are moments of history that will have much more meaning in that way.
In short, Portal is a piece of a cake, a cake stuffed with pleasant surprises. And we all love cakes, right?

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Overall this game is absolutely brilliant! XD It has everything you could ask for!
Creativity -Check - You assemble your bots exactly how you want, limited only by the parts you currently can purchase/unlock and your imagination. I've seen people make pixel art, 3-D models of real life things, or just plain mind-blowing bots! The possibilities are endless!
Explosions - Check - Nothing like seeing someone else's overpowered looking death machine on an opposing team blow apart into cubes when you've blasted them with plasma cannons or rail guns! :3
Action - Plenty - You'll never have a dull moment in battle. Perhaps you will in construction, but even then, the developers were nice enough to implement a few shortcuts to help that go faster. In battle, though, you are constantly having to keep your eyes peeled for anyone hiding to snipe you, whilst you charge at whatever your current target is.
Adventure - Eh... I guess it's a sci-fi kinda adventure, but if you just simply mean you'll never know what's gonna happen next, then definitely it's got adventure!
Plus, on top of all that, there's more than one battle mode, so you can fight to the death whilst capturing bases. Or strategize with your team to try and maintain certain capture points to deactivate the enemy's shield and destroy their protonium crystal power source. Or  join a group of friends (Or random folks if you're feeling really friendly) to fight against an entire enemy team in boss battle mode!
And with the developers constantly adding more/coming up with new ideas, it's only gonna get better! Course that being said, IT IS STILL IN DEVELOPMENT. There have been times I've been frustrated because the way they altered the game with an update made everything I'd worked towards pointless. However, once you adjust to the new update, redesign your bots a bit, and keep playing and testing to find what works, it still stays incredibly fun.
So don't get too discouraged if something drastic changes the gameplay on you and makes your bot malfunction. Simply take a deep breath, keep calm and redesign, you'll eventually get the hang of it. :3
So overall, would I reccomend this game?

Robocraft
a great game to play.
You can build robots Minecraft-style and fight with them. It's all about creativity and logic on how you design your bot. Now, a lot of players resort to copying builds they found on Robocraft Garage and anywhere else. It sucks.
There are many 3 modes to choose from: Team Deathmatch (also known as Classic or the original Robocraft game), Battle Arena (where it's pretty much like DOTA) and Challenge Mode (where your chances of death are 80%).
Team Deathmatch is the original game Robocraft was made for and it was awesome. No respawns, just some pretty quick matches. Battle Arena is annoying. Once you're stuck with suck-ish players, you have to live with them the whole battle. Challenge mode is where you get to fight a lot of lower ranking bots and they apparently kill you like a bunch of bees.
Before the Robocraft Unleashed update, there used to be Tiers in which your bot belonged to. That was way better than the current Robot Ranking-based matching where if your bot is taking 50% of the team's ranking you'll get paired off with lower quality bots.
The new UI is sleeker and cleaner and I love it. The elements in the Build section are well thought of and that's pretty much it.
I have the worst framerate during battles. My computer is well above the recommended requirements of Robocraft but I can only manage to pull off 20 - 29 fps. Back then, I could get 40+ fps in this game.
If you thought there aren't any more bugs, there will always be bugs.
They're always buffing and nerfing weapons, armors and shields (EPs). It gets pretty confusing.

I wrote the above review in August 2015, and have continued to follow the game.  They have recently done exactly what I said: changed everything around.  When I first got the game, there were tiers of play.  As I progressed, the lower-lever blocks and guns were still useful on the lower tiers.  I would play games of all the tiers because there were win bonuses for the first win with each bot.  It was very fair to play Tier 1 games because I was limited to the same technologies that the new players were.  It was very fun to progress through the game, and was fun to take smaller bots into lower-tier matches.
Now this is gone, and all of the lower-tier blocks and equipment are fairly useless.  I'm not even sure how they do matchmaking anymore, so I guess I'm just supposed to build the strongest bot with the least number of points and hit newbies in the head so I can get random parts.  It is nowhere near as fun as it was before.  This game makes me very sad.

Portal 2 is the preeminent puzzler, a first person game in which the player solves challenging puzzles, inhabits an interesting, off-kilter world and follows an engaging story line. Unlike its predecessor, Portal 2 has virtually infinite replayability, thanks to the addition of co-op and player-made maps to its single-player storyline. The graphics are good, the music is good, the humour (though rarely laugh-out-loud funny) is good and in-context within the game - overall: a flawless masterpiece. Whilst this game is a puzzler, it features immersive cinematic sequences and even one or two parts that 'feel' a bit like an fps - requiring quick thought and action.
Be warned, this game is quite challenging in places, so don't buy if you lack patience and don't get pleasure out of working through frustration and solving difficult problems yourself. For this reason, I would strongly urge you to try to resist using walkthroughs if you get stuck. I got stuck a couple of times and resisted; it made my single-player experience so much more enjoyable than it would otherwise have been.
After you complete single player, find a friend who plays (which shouldn't be too hard, given this game's popularity) and work through the co-op maps. They are fun and interesting (having two portal guns adds a whole new dynamic). Also have a go at making your own maps (total freedom) and playing through other people's. All in all it is the replayability that makes P2 so superior to even its brilliantly received prequel.

Despite Portal's incredible gameplay and incredible story, I would dare to argue Portal 2 is not just far better, but a mastery of what can be done with this concept. The fact that Valve usually don't make more than 2 of a franchise pretty much guarantees this is this is the last iteration Portal will see, so I am glad this game turned out as well as it did.
It is best to end with a bang.
First of all, the graphics had some touch-up from the last game, and the physics seem a bit more real-to-life(well, as real to life a game about portals can get). Second, the story of this game adds so many layers and questions upon what Portal had to offer, which keeps it just as interesting as its predecessor, if not more so. Finally, the inclusion of not only a level editor, but also a multiplayer mode and a much longer campaign make this game worth twice the price tag it's placed at. +Plenty of content this time around

+Lovable characters make a return, and the game introduces a great deal of new ones as well
+Level Editor with a bit of a learning curve, but is pretty easy to make basic stuff with
+New Multiplayer Mode
+Better graphics than the previous game
+Space Core. SPACE CORE. SPAAAAAACE CORE!
Cons:
-The fact that Space Core barely appeared :(

This game is fun for a while, but once you finally get to build something other than the basic types of bots the matching system becomes SERIOUSLY broken.  I realize the game is still in Alpha, but the very premise and hook of the game is the freedom to build unique weapons of war, and you simply cannot do that in this game and expect a rewarding experience.  You spend hours perfecting your bot only to be matched up against players with higher tiered weapons and armor, rendering your bot pretty useless in a match.  You literally have no idea what you will be up against every match as far as whether or not you will be outclassed or underclassed.  I have taken the exact same bot and would go 21-3 in one match only to go 0-13 the next match (no changes to my bot.)  That is a seriously broken matching system.  I may revist the game after another update, but right now the game has induced more rage in me than a video game has in a while.  Developers should listen to the many complaints along these lines or this game is dead in a few months.

ArtStyle в порядке. Обновленный взгляд из-порталы довольно бедными по сравнению с первой игрой, и только область игры, которые действительно выделялись визуально, что средняя часть игры я не буду, потому что спойлеры описать. Вы должны пойти в одного игрока принимать тот факт, что вы не играете портал, первый платформер-головоломка человек, но Portal 2, первый человек приключенческая игра.
Чтобы перейти с новой роли в качестве игры приключенческая игра, голос направление действуя потерять все подобие мягкой робота тона от первой игры. Стивен Мерчант имеет почти никакого искажения применительно к его голосу, и HK Сценарий Симмонса буквально ничего, но разовых шуток, которые предотвращают игрока из правильного подключения с ним. Эллен Маклейн в порядке, ничего фантастического, но она должна пройти через тот же сценарий ила в качестве остальной части броска. Сценарий просто отстой, слишком много blantant попытки шуток, не хватает вне порядка или черный юмор которая помогла протянуть игру свою неповторимую атмосферу. Так много элементов из Portal 1, повторно, что вы удивляетесь, почему клапан надоело.
Eta igra srazu ottalkivayet tekh, kto byli znakomy s pervym titulom, brosaya obnovlennuyu versiyu dvizhka Source v igre, kotoraya dayet chetkuyu razryv mezhdu, kak vy kontrolya i chto na samom dele na ekrane po sravneniyu s pervoy igroy.
ArtStyle v poryadke. Obnovlennyy vzglyad iz-portaly dovol'no bednymi po sravneniyu s pervoy igroy, i tol'ko oblast' igry, kotoryye deystvitel'no vydelyalis' vizual'no, chto srednyaya chast' igry ya ne budu, potomu chto spoylery opisat'. Ostal'naya chast' igry stradayet ot slishkom malo belogo prostranstva, s kotoroy, chtoby strelyat' portalov. Vy dolzhny poyti v odnogo igroka prinimat' tot fakt, chto vy ne igrayete portal, pervyy platformer-golovolomka chelovek, no Portal 2, pervyy chelovek priklyuchencheskaya igra.
Chtoby pereyti s novoy roli v kachestve igry priklyuchencheskaya igra, golos napravleniye deystvuya poteryat' vse podobiye myagkoy robota tona ot pervoy igry. Stiven Merchant imeyet pochti nikakogo iskazheniya primenitel'no k yego golosu, i HK Stsenariy Simmonsa bukval'no nichego, no razovykh shutok, kotoryye predotvrashchayut igroka iz pravil'nogo podklyucheniya s nim. Ellen Makleyn v poryadke, nichego fantasticheskogo, no ona dolzhna proyti cherez tot zhe stsenariy ila v kachestve ostal'noy chasti broska. Stsenariy prosto otstoy, slishkom mnogo blantant popytki shutok, ne khvatayet vne poryadka ili chernyy yumor kotoraya pomogla protyanut' igru svoyu nepovtorimuyu atmosferu. Tak mnogo elementov iz Portal 1, povtorno, chto vy udivlyayetes', pochemu klapan nadoyelo.

Despite Portal's incredible gameplay and incredible story, I would dare to argue Portal 2 is not just far better, but a mastery of what can be done with this concept. The fact that Valve usually don't make more than 2 of a franchise pretty much guarantees this is this is the last iteration Portal will see, so I am glad this game turned out as well as it did.
It is best to end with a bang.
First of all, the graphics had some touch-up from the last game, and the physics seem a bit more real-to-life(well, as real to life a game about portals can get). Second, the story of this game adds so many layers and questions upon what Portal had to offer, which keeps it just as interesting as its predecessor, if not more so. Finally, the inclusion of not only a level editor, but also a multiplayer mode and a much longer campaign make this game worth twice the price tag it's placed at. I would call it flawless(even the minute issue I had with the loadtimes was at least somewhat fixed).
Pros:
+Plenty of content this time around
+Interesting story which builds upon the plot of the original, leaving the player plenty of story questions to think about
+Lovable characters make a return, and the game introduces a great deal of new ones as well
+Level Editor with a bit of a learning curve, but is pretty easy to make basic stuff with
+New Multiplayer Mode
+Better graphics than the previous game
+Space Core. SPACE CORE. SPAAAAAACE CORE!
Cons:
-The fact that Space Core barely appeared :(

It's certainly changed from earlier versions. However, unlike most of everyone else, I like these changes.
The fighting is very well executed, with three main weapon types, and varying strengths of these weapon types, which are the laser, the artillery, and the railgun.
The laser is a basic, short range, fast shooting DPS outputter for all your CQB needs.
Artillery differs by having drop to your shots, which do much more individual damage combined with a low firing rate... unless you have 10 artillery pieces of the same type on your craft.
I haven't used the railguns much yet, but as far as I can tell, they're pretty much sniper rifles and everything that goes along with that assumption.
I only have two big complaints with Robocraft.
1: THE MATCHMAKING
Dear god, the matchmaking. It's terrible. Worse than War Thunder matchmaking. In game, they rate your craft in CPU, and at the very beginning you're craft shouldn't cost much more than 450 CPU. My first match, I was paired with people that had over 1,500 CPU... basically just under god-tier.
2: GAME-ENDING GLITCHES
This has only occurred to me twice at the time of writing, but the severity of these glitches means I can't let them go by unnoticed. I was trying to edit my tank the first time, and suddenly the game just locks up. No warnings, nothing wrong with my mouse or keyboard. The strangest thing is that the game wasn't "Not Responding", it was still active. I just couldn't do anything. The second time was very similiar, with the roles reversed. My mouse had free movement, and the entire game locked up.
An extra con! (Yay?)
The developers are pretty unresponsive to the people's demands. They haven't done anything about the matchmaking, and yet it's been like this for a long time, apparently.

Ask me for a review on this before Respawned and Overclocked update? (30/04/15) I would give this a positive review BUT AFTER Resspawned and Overclocked update....... That's a whole new side....
Here's why-
Before Respawned and Overclocked, this game inspired team work revolving heavy towards flanking, sticking as one big cluster of brute force because of the arena type mode. Once dead, you're gone. Once they introduced medics; it revolutionised the whole battle mechanic on whether a team would succeed or perish further reinforcing the team staying together. Moreover, when FJ released the team balance patch, the battles would last sooooo much longer and be even more adrenalin filled so you wouldn't be paired with 5 other rail walkers and be crushed by a whole team of smg tanks. As medic you would feel so valuable; one of my favourite memories...
Megabots arrive. Some of the player base decides this was a bad move (this was where the game started to get controversial) however, in my opinion, this was even better because now the T10's would stick by the Mega's siding them in one big turf war. Those were the good days of RC.
30th of April arrives. Respawned and Overclocked. The danger of dying now gone; stupid bots start appearing virtually killing the cleverly thought out designs using tri forcing ect. Team work is gone; no need to stick together. If you die, you can just respawn again. Don't even get me started on medics... Before Respawned and Overclocked, medics were the top priority on kill list. But now they're just replaced with respawn. Again, no fear of dying. Megabots are restricted to the old mode where hardly anyone played because of the shiny new Respawned and Overclocked. (The megabots were still fairly new yet all the work seemed to just be abandoned). Even though arena mode is still here, it feels as if it gets no love anymore.
Robocraft Unleashed touches down. The removals of tiers and tech trees are here. This resulted in a huge backlash from the community as many veterans felt that all their progress was for nothing as it took ages to grind up to each tier and save up for new parts to find that it's no longer the case. In addition, going up a tier made us feel amazing and satisfied giving us a sense of progression. I can see FJ wanted to enable full creativity as many wanted but it just won't work.
To some up-
Robocraft used to be one of my favourite games and WAS a fun and enjoyable game. Simple and easy to learn. However, as the updates passed, Robocraft got more and more complicated destroying the fun and simple factors or the arena game mode into a supposed 'moba' style game...
ps: if you read all of this; thanks for your time!

As a regular at the RC forums it is an issue that the base model of the game has gone through changes left and right but the last update works a lot better for user creation than before.
That being said, the matchmaking is a hit or miss as the players are ranked by their equipment and not necessarily if the equipment is in the right configuration. So will find yourself sternly shaking your head at the junkyard orgies people try and use as vehicles.
Even so the ability to unlock parts as you level up is worthwhile fun, as you get completley obliterated through many trials you will be constantly upgrading and moving parts to maximize defense and firepower will be rewarding. If say you don't like wheels there's many different types of  parts you can try from helicopter blades, tank treads, and even spiderlegs, there's more than I just listed but you can also combine the parts to invent new playstyles like Super-jumpers or the infamous Uber Warp Drive.
However a downside is that there's little to promote advanced building techniques unless by memo from another player or researching builds online. Techniques such as triforcing/damage redirection, hitbox utilization, and firing order are not discussed in-game. Damage redirection is specifically important for high end builds especially against rail guns which are the most crippling and low risk weapons to use, while the Aerorod parts compensate many new players can continue without knowing how to properly utilize them.
Despite this, this game is definetley worth giving a shot and personally I find  an aesthetic and effiecient build to be very rewarding. The learning curve in this game itself is enjoyable and the freedom of playstyle allows each player to have their own personal touch, those who love mastering game mechanics and those who love customization will enjoy qualities of this game.

All in all great game, but if you aren't aiming to be a pro... Don't even touch this game.

PROs:
You really can build what you want
Addictive if done right
The game is still in alpha, so you shouldn't expect much things pollished at all
CONs:
Devs can and WILL make mistakes, very, very often
The game in its current state is horrible when it comes to que time
The new ranking is extremely buggy
People WILL abuse the system
Verdict?
Optimism is key here people. The devs are learning. You can't just judge a game that's been in ALPHA its entire lifetime. Plus, the gaming community has been highly toxic lately, toxic as in sending death threats for years for a game that is now a lost cause for Valve (AKA Half Life 3). People can't appreciate for what this game is because it apparently doesn't live up to, "AHEM", standards anymore. Come on guys, 25 fps? THAT'S what you complain about? FreeJam has a narcissistic take on game design. If anybody complains, they seem willing to upheaval the entire game in order to satisfy the needs of those selfish few. This has worn out the trust of paying members such as myself, as it cannot be guarrenteed that when I log back on it will remotely be the same game, and if the robots I made suddenly have become outdated.
They do this because of their obsessive pursuit of what they call 'Free-to-Win'. They have pursued this to the point of being 'Pointless-to-Win'. They seem not to understand that for someone to win, someone else must lose. So, when someone complains that they were killed by an 'overpowered bot', it should be taken with a grain of salt because more likely than not the failure was on their behalf, not something the other player did unfairly. It is not the other player's responsibility to give up what they have worked on to achieve simply because the other person expects to succeed with no effort.
Currently, it is impossible in the game to determine whether or not your robot design will do well, since all methods of determining that have been removed. You'll be matched with robots that are 'close' to your design, which guarantees you'll either stomp another player completely with no fault of their own, or you'll be stomped by another player who's robot is a higher level than yours. There in no tiers anymore which force only robots of a certain level to compete with each other, thus guaranteeing a level of fairness.
The entire state of the game can be traced linearly, based on dev vs player feedback:
0. Base game classed robos into seperate tiers so that robos could be fairly matched with other robos. However, repairs were required after each match. While after each match the cudes that were destroyed were replaced, they were reduced to 'critical' status meaning the robo was weaker unless it was repaired.
1. Repairs used to require credits. Players might not get the credits necessary to repair their entire bot. Players complained about it, as their were stuck on T1 indefinitely unless they got absurdly good or paid up. The devs removed the repair costs. This, in my opinion, is the first and last time an update was considered 'good' almost unanimously by all players. (Since higher-tier players were lonely, and lower tiers were frustrated.)
2. Then weak players started clamouring for nerfs. The devs catered to these 'needs', but with little to no testing to see whether these claims of certain weapons being 'over-powered' were true. So, the power of plasma mortars and rail weapons, both skill-type weapons, were nerfed over time.
This caused experienced players to start 'over-tiering', in order to compensate for the lack of power in these weapons by simply having fewer bigger guns to engage softer lower-tier robots. Essentially, the problem with better players designing noob-crushing robos escalated, even though the nerfs were meant to stifle strong designs from crushing weak ones.
3. Then came moba updates. This made the over-tiering even worse, because kills=enhancements to firepower and speed, when such things should be LOCKED in order to stay fair when people can design 'the perfect robo'. This caused what I like to call the 'exponential rate of defeat', something Call of Duty does where it is nearly impossible to bring a game back from losing.
4. Weak players then attributed their failures to over-tiering (a problem they themselves created by complaining about how certain weapons were over-powered in the tiers where they belong, thus making them weaker and thus encouraging the behavior of taking these weapons down the tiers to get firepower back. Also, the moba elements did not help), and complained about that. The devs then forced weapons and movement blocks, BUT NOT ARMOUR, to only be allowed in tiers in or after the weapon was unlocked. A single T3 weapon could not be used to replace many T1 weapons, for example.
Did the noob stomping stop? No. But the noobs initially thought it did, because no longer were they being killed by over-tiered robos...but then appeared Gunbeds. With no other recourse to build their robo competitively, good designers built  wedges that allowed the maximum amount of guns to be able to fire at the greatest angles of attack. This took the form of arranging their guns like a battleship does, stacking rows of guns above one another and being careful to not allow them to block the fields of fire from other guns.
This killed creativity and competitiveness (since no longer could someone choose to sacrifice on element on their robo to buff another), and many people stopped playing the game, causing record lows. The combat had devolved into driving forward, encountering an enemy, shooting off all their guns before they shot off yours, and repeating the process with less and less survivability each encounter. Think of it like the 'Age of War' flashgame.
Additionally, new players could blaze through the tiers because having one gun of a higher tier immediately put a player in that tier, whether or not that robo actually stood a chance. This caused useless robos to flood the teams of higher tiers, frustrating the higher tier players who had earned their way up the tiers, only to lose because their teammates made extremely bad robos. It might be said that the 'anti-overtier update' was really a 'complete-undertier downdate'.
4. The frustrated higher-tier players then tried to have the devs make it so that it would be impossible for these under-tier bots to be in the higher tiers. The devs attempted to do this by requiring armour be at minimum one level below the tier the robo was trying to get into. It failed, however, because then noobs would simply use NO ARMOUR and throw two tracks together, add a seat and a gun, and call it good. The population still dropped.
5. Then dumb posts suggesting that tiers be removed altogether, since they were apparently 'the source of the problems', started cropping up. Desparate for the population to come back, the devs were up for anything and so did that. The 'Freedom Update' appeared, and simply gave every robo a number that could be matched to other similar numbers in matchmaking.
The population rose a tiny bit, and is now more of a line instead of constant mountains and valleys based on the time of day, but the update has only been out for so long. Right now, it is impossible to design a good OR bad bot because now its performance is determined by the matchmaking system. Design skills have no bearing on whether the match ends in your favor, since it could decide to match your robo with robos stronger than yours or match your robo with robos that are weaker than yours.
It is also possible to make a robo that the matchmaking system cannot figure out who to match you with, if the robo number is an outlier too different from bots above and below it. At least, that is my theory since while I don't have long matchmaking times with my tried and tested robo, but have increased times with anything new I've made, and people have claimed matchmaking times of over an hour.
Conclusion:
I belief that the matchmaking problems aren't necessarily because of a flaw with the algorithms, but perhaps because of a low population combined with the lack of robo grouping constants in a game that literally becomes a different game EVERY UPDATE, and not in a good way. The updates rarely add anything new, and simply reorganize everything that already exists to the point where any advice a long-time player might give to a new player is immediately outdated.
This obsessive pursuit of the 'Free-to-Win' game has taken away player agency in so many ways, it might as well be Call of Duty. A more accurate term for this game would be 'Free-to-Change', since now the plz nerf posts have become just as much a staple of Robocraft as it does any Activision or EA title.

Dustforce truly is a work of art. I don't mean that lightly. The way it's animated plus its music gives it that title in my book. I can find myself playing one level for an hour, maybe even hours at a time. The frustration of losing levels is filled with relaxation and calmness because of the ambient music. The way the levels are crafted is truly mindblowing. They had a system in which you had to perfect a level to earn a key, and you would use that key to earn more levels. In layman's terms, to earn more levels, you had to perfect current levels. They ditched that and added an XP system in which you gain more XP to earn a key the more levels you play and perfect. I'm very glad they added this system and was skeptical about buying it. But now that I did buy it, I do not regret it even for a second. One thing I really love about this game is how you don't have to unlock base levels. In a sense, this game is open world. That sense is that many levels are available to you, and you can choose whether you want to advance into more challenging levels, or stay where you're at. Another thing I absolutely enjoy about Dustforce is its expasive community. There are lots of Community Workshop maps for you to sharpen your skills on, and lots of people who can set a good example. I'm sure most of the people who get best times on all the levels have a Youtube channel, so you can probably catch them there. The community may or not be active, but it sure is good and friendly.
Overall, in terms of gameplay, music, artstyle, animation, and difficulty (it's not an easy game, but it's not that hard of a game either. It just depends on how much you want to play it), I rate this game:

Although the mechanics are the same as the first title with only a few additions, Portal 2 still feels like a completely different sort of game than the first Portal.
The first Portal was short lived and very focused. Although there were some secrets and deviations the formula for Portal remained only compartmentalized puzzle solving, in a very controlled environment.
Although this is still a puzzle game, it feels far less structured and controlled, allowing more room for experimentation and giving you less direction on how you are to complete certain objectives.
It's also far longer than the first game, and with a much bigger focus on story.
The story in the first Portal was excellent, and a big reason why it was so popular, but regardless, it wasn't the story that was driving the game forward, rather the sense of progression.
This game, however, is entirely story driven. Levels are introduced along with the charactes that direct you in those levels, and the atmosphere of each area is unique to the narrative of the characters who are with you in each section.
You want to complete puzzles in this game in order to learn more about the world, rather than you learning more about the world as you complete the puzzles.
While I love this change, many people might miss the hyper-focused nature of the first game.
If you're into the lore of the series Portal 2 is an absolutely wonderful game.
If you're more focused on the gameplay, Portal 2 is still a wonderful game, although you may be disappointed by the amount of "fluff" that's present this time around.
