The single-player story continues from the first game, but now the story is a lot richer. The characters are great. The story is mysterious and catching, and there are many humorous moments as well.
Of course there are a lot of puzzles to solve again. But now there are a lot of additions to the gameplay like gels or the gravity beams. Which makes the puzzles more challenging, but they are still doable.
There is also a co-op mode, so you can play with a friend. It has also a good storyline, and maybe it is a bit less serious than the single-player storyline. It is very enjoyable to play if you both are serious players, but also when you want to troll your friend. The puzzles are also nicely made for 2 players, you really need to cooperate and think together how to finish a level.
I think anyone can enjoy this game, even when it is a different genre than you usually play. If you are not so sure about it, I recommend to buy it on sale. I am sure that you won't be disappointed. I did the same and now it has grown to be one of my favourite games.
My rating for this game: 9/10.

Portal 2 is another masterpiece of puzzle FPS games Valve has ever forged out of their workshops, and this game remains to be fascinating and a reminder of how challenging things can be no matter how simple the direction this can give.
Starting off from the previous game, you awake as a girl on her mid-30s, confused as to what just happened and reminded that the facility you once destroyed reached conditions that doesn't reach the quotas of building inspectors from your local Department. Then of course you get to use a gun that blasts two kinds of portals, and
you dive in to the experience of the old, new and old and then new again before ending this all with a
As you'd expect, the gameplay is very simple, and that's exactly what everyone wanted it to be. The right kind of simplicity from a video game, while leaving a few more sparkles for us to walk into and look through the possibilities we can do with the portal gun in our hand.
You'll be introduced to the novice level type of puzzles before going to puzzles that requires more brain work than simply creating portals from your side to the other separated by the gaps that leads you to hours of falling. Companion cubes and other such remains, even the cute, feisty little turrets while introducing new elements to the puzzle that involves from pointing a laser device to unlock your way to salvation, light bridges that reminds you of most sci-fis out there, and other related physics stuff like gravitational bridges too. Oh, did I tell you that they have those jumping pads that makes the work easy? And yes! They have those gels that makes you jump higher, run faster, or give you a painful slip to your doom.
Environments and level designs are some of the best that Valve ever made. And while the new stuff is indeed a pleasant gift for those making their comeback here, vintage type of levels that reflects our early concepts of sci-fi becomes a refreshing moment of the past. Although some of them don't seem to get the appeal or rather an annoyance especially if they were puzzle levels, these sorts of discomforts fades away like you never noticed once you completed these levels and become satisified as a puzzle master.
And what this? A coop mode? Yes indeed folks, a coop mode. Inviting a friend ( or simply dragging them ) gives you a new experience of what Portal 2 can deliver to push in the interests of new challenges, which most of them requires more than just two portals and one brain! You gotta multiply them by two, and everything will be a piece of cake.
But if all of these don't seem to satisfy yourself and science itself, you can try the level editor! Yes, you don't need to go full complicated SDK making, making levels is simple as baking a cake and sharing it to the rest of your folks. You can make it alot more complicated, but overall challenging not only for yourself, but for everyone out there in the Steam Workshop! Yes, you can upload your levels, and that also means you can try out everyone's creations too! Solo or Co-op maps in the game will always satisfy your urges to complete the meaning of science itself, and portals too.
While this game already placed itself as the best puzzle game that involves physics and what not, I've already mentioned that some levels in the game are slightly repetitive. As for the difficulty,  every levels require the attention of your intelligence which is the point of this game, but the logic becomes unusually flawed by the time you reached the later levels of the game. Technical issues aren't present most of the times, but they still appear as a bit of a hinderance to anyone who's attempting to make a speedrun or just focusing on each level. The Coop levels shares the same issues in regards to both design and difficulty, but the latter two becomes predictable and doing all the puzzle now is a chore as you press on.
Well that's a long paragraph for some of the game's negatives but every games have their own pros and cons, and maybe I'm wrong with my experience on this game. But that doesn't mean I'm not gonna recommend this to everyone, because
It's a game worth both from it's value, gameplay and story. All for the sake of science they say!

If you liked Portal 1, you'll love Portal 2. Portal 2 is everything Portal 1 was times three: 3 times the number of rooms, 3 times the number of gadgets, and 3 times more fun wrapped into a storyline of 9 well-thought out chapters.
The game begins like Portal 1, but in a distant future where Aperture has become derelict and in disrepair. Chell is revived by the core named Wheatley, wonderfully voiced by Stephen Merchant. She is brought through a series of chambers that begins similar to Portal 1, but soon diverges into new challenges with new devices. She is then brought through a history of crude alpha, beta, and gamma test chambers that originate from Aperture's beginnings in the 1950's through the 1980's, introducing us to three new devices: boucing, accelerating, and portaling paint. She is then led through a series of newly created chambers that make use of the new paints, as well a new launcher, light walls, and levitators.
Whereas you could spend a day solving Portal 1, you could become absorbed for a week solving Portal 2. Like Portal 1, Portal 2 will keep you engrossed in the gameplay and wanting more... a completely enjoyable experience.

I have played this game, both as regular FTW (love the change from FTP, good job devs :D)  player and as paying member, and have enjoyed it immensely.
You don't need to buy anything to win, you actually get bonuses (within a match) from all members that are paying.
IE Payee's get 100% experience and $ reward from each match ending than non-payers, but the non-payers get a 5% bonus to their match experience and $ payout for every Paying mermber that's in the match.
Some matches, if all are payers, reaches 210% exp and currency for that match for each player.
That's pretty COOL!
Membership does get an extra bay for building another Bot  (you start with 3) and it stays even if your membership expires. That's really cool.
This game IS NOT about soaking you for $$ to do anything or to have a chance in matches.
PAYER PERKS?
Payers get to host 4 player platoons instead of the basic 3 platoon when joining a match. This includes the BOSS BATTLES that ALL PLAYER can start playing at TIER 8. You may be "dragged into one" as your "match" while lvl 4-6
BOSS Battles are, in a nutshell, you (and any platoon members) against the entire opposite team, which is made up from 8 lvl 4 players (VS 1  Tier 8 bot for example) to 8 level 6's (VS 1 Tier 10 bot for example).
It's fairly well matched up, the low level team usually wins (with good exp payouts) unless the BOSS is good and has a well-built Bot (and having a few friends along never hurts, especially a healer).
NO battle is EVER the same, although it could definitely use a couple more map options as it's limited to like 4 maps ATM.
WHAT?? Blown up in battle??
Meh, back to the hanger and re-que to go again without waiting for vehicles to become "available" like in some other MMO's I wont' mention right WoT :P
GOT SOME RADICAL DESIGN? BRING IT!!
Just remember, this IS A TEAM EFFORT GAME. If you build crap YOUR TEAM will SUFFER (and might not like you too much, lol).
SO, MAKE SURE TO ALWAYS TEST YOUR BOTS before taking them out into battle!
TO THE DEVs; I think allowing friends into your "testing" (for practice, et al) would be the ultimate cool, although that's not an option ATM,  I hope that's a consideration soon!
OVERALL a great MMO with great potential for growth (new ranks, maps, new weapons/block types) and just plain fun for all ages.

So from my experience from this game is this pretty good on multiple counts.
For one thing it lets you build practically anything you want as long as you have the cubes and CPU necessary. You can get cubes by spending RP and you can get RP depending on your performance in the Mechwarrior-esque matches. CPU is gained by leveling up and with more CPU of course, you get more freedom in building your vehicle.
Matches usually run about 2-5 minutes long so you can usually get the RP you need fairly quickly. Now there is something else called Tiers. The more blocks you use the higher your Tier Gauge will rise. Of course using blocks or parts of higher tiers makes that tier gauge rise quicker. The point of the gauge is to match you up with people of similar tiers so you won't have a guy with a giant vehicle on one team with his remaining teammates while the other team doesn't.
Now there are physics involved with your vehicle. If you don't have your balancing right then you just might start flipping around everywhere and end up doing nothing but get shot at.
Now what's wrong with the game? For me personally it's lack of modes for now. I hope they add more modes in at a later point in time since for now it's just a capture the base on a single life. Also my main issue with the game is that they limit some of the more interesting parts to really high tiers like T6 and up and it can take you a while to get there as you NEED to be able to be in a certain tier to get tech points for that tier unless you want to spend real money converting those specific tier points to Uber Points which is universal. Now performance wise it runs pretty well on my mid range system though it scares me everytime I launch it since it locks up my video for about two minutes while it loads but the audio in the background like a skype call will continue playing. I know it's not an issue with my GPU as it only ever does it with this game.
So I do recommend this game right now if you have the paitience to get to the higher tiers to build whatever it is you want.

You are a test subject called Chell in an underground testing facility called Aperture Science. Since the last game “Portal” after you killed GLaDOS (Genetic Lifeform and Disk Operating System) Aperture Science has been filled with vines, weeds, dirt and other junk. At the start you meet a personality core called Wheatley, you both want to escape from the collapsing Aperture Science. After awhile you and Wheatley have to go through GLaDOS’s Chamber, where she is broken and deactivated. But you and Wheatley pull some… well a lot… well all the switches turning GLaDOS back on, she grabs you and sends you through test chamber, after test chamber, after test chamber
The Characters in Portal 2 are memorable, with fantastic voice acting making you love the characters (even if they are against you). The Characters make you feel emotion, like feeling sorry for them and getting angry at them etc. The Characters have great and interesting character progression, and interesting backstories. The characters can make you laugh with funny humor (mainly Cave Johnson).
The models and textures in Portal 2 and improved a lot, the personality cores looks have been changed, now they look more realistic. The textures around the test chambers aren’t that white anymore, now looking brown because a lot of time has pasted since the last time you were in the these test chambers. The textures overall look pretty realistic, giving more life to Portal 2. The models are also very well made. GLaDOS has also gotten a makeover, making here able to express emotion not just through here words, but now here eyes.
The Portal 2 music is very atmospheric, making you feel boxed in and alone. The music in Portal 2 is noticeable different in style to the original Portal.
There are plenty of Easter eggs and secrets to find in Portal 2, and the return of the Doug Rattmann dens.
In conclusion Portal 2 is a fantastic sequel to Portal. It has a great story, characters, textures and models. The ending is interesting and good, and has great puzzles to solve and different environments. I would say this is my favorite game I’ve played so far.

Robocraft...........I can only say that it is among the single most fun mmo I have ever played. I have played alot of mmo's and they all suffer from the same thing.....Best Builds. A build or a set of builds that can beat all others in pvp and pve.
Robocraft does not have this. Some builds are better then others in one thing and crappy in another. It is very much up to the player to decide how they want to play and while you can grab a tutorial or buy a bot (the pay to get bots are usually really crappy and serve mostly as a fun cosmetic thing rather than a viable build to play) there is trillions of ways to build a bot. I am almost in tier 10 myself and i have seen planes with wheels or cruisers that can hover. Tanks with legs and so much more.
While there aren't many play modes each battle is different. One battle you will get utterly crushed and the next the timer click to 0 because you were too evenly matched and got a long battle. The variations in bots and tactics make it very fun. The devs are polite kind and helpful. Ususally offering a day of free premium every once in awhile. If the servers crash they work tirelessly to get them back up. They care about the players and seem pretty determined to avoid a pay 2 win model.
But don't take my word for it, go in there and play fr yourself.......be warned though you will probably get addicted to it.

So, its about time I edited this review.
I used to love Robocraft, and part of me still really wants to. It was such a good game with unique takes and a huge potential. It was a fun, free for all team deathmatch game with custom building and wacky weapons.
But then, it all started to change with "MARKS VISION". The game was increasingly becoming more MOBA-esque at one point, and then it became more user friendly. By that, I mean it is now entirely possible to play the game without ever,
EVER
building a robot. And ONE THIRD OF THE SLOGAN IS STILL "BUILD". The developer team has progressively made the game so new-player oriented over time, that nearly all aspects of the game have suffered. Weapons are inconsistent, and never feel satisfying to use. Ones that do often become too "powerful" and are nerfed to the mundane levels of other weapons. Perhaps one of the first in a terrible line of decisions was the idea to make the primary income source of the game based on RNG Crates. No personalized rewards beyond "maybe I can get the chance to get a slightly better item."
But you dont even need that, now its actually possible to get a fully fledged meta-build robot from the global factory for free, no payment, no incentive to get creative and do things yourself.
Between the split development mindsets of competitiveness and user friendliness, to the series of unfortunate events, to straight up copying the concepts of other games (Wi n dowmaker module anyone?), I still really want to say I enjoy this game. It used to be so good, but...
It's just gone downhill. If you read the recent reviews instead of all time, you should see it.

This has led to a very positive community that is willing to help you out in designing robots, playing them effecively, and clarifying game systems. Oh my, where do I start? For an Alpha game that is completely free-to-play, this is the best-of-the-best.
Essentially, the game is what you think -- you build a robot craft, and then take it out into battle and see how it fares among other player-created robots.
The physics part is what truly makes this game awesome. If you place too much weight on one side, it'll flip, or be more prone to flip. If you don't put enough tires, it won't move right. If you don't place the hoverboard things in the right way, you'll find your craft flipping, spinning, and failing.
While the game is prone to crashing, not giving points, etc. it is totally worth the time you're willing to invest in it. I can honestly say this is the best game I've played thusfar.
Pros:
Awesome gameplay.
Excellent (form = function) robot creation.
Smooth game without hiccups and without lag (I've never experienced any lag in a battle).
Cons:
It needs more construction items in order to allow every craft to be 100% unique.
It could use a slight tweak in graphics (the graphics are really good, but they aren't "great")
Thrusters need to have a much bigger impact on speed (apparently they used to but were nerfed recently)
The cons aren't really cons, honestly, and it's still Alpha so this game is just going to get way better. I have no doubts that this game will blow up into one of the best games ever created. That is almost a certainty.
Honestly, you can spend 2 minutes and make a functional vehicle, or you can spend an hour tweaking it, prettying it up, and making it totally your own.
It's f2p and is very small in size -- just download it and check it out. . . seriously.

February 08, 2015
Robocraft is a really fun game to start. You can think up absurd or cool designs for vehicles and then battle them against the designs of others. It's great fun to play as a race car, a plane, a giant dinosaur, a tank, a mecha, a flying saucer or anything else you can dream up. You can make your robot drive, walk, hover or fly. And it can shoot lasers, balls of plasma, rail shot, nano/repair beams or just ram them with blades!
But, as fun as it is, it has some serious problems. The first is that almost half the parts available are gated behind many hours of play. This means that you have to commit to playing this for 40+ hours to gain access to things like wings, legs and ramming blades. Another problem is the moderation, both the team and automatic. The mods are rarely seen to enforce the rules and there ARE no automatic, in-game systems to discourage poor behavior. EasyAntiCheat is a shoddy and disreputable piece of software that has been shown to be intrusive to privacy.
Now, the above problems could easily be changed by the time this game leaves Early Access. If the above was fixed, the game would easily score a 70/100 and would only rise from there as more content is released. However, there is one blindingly unethical practice that bars me from ever recommending it.
That is the degree of Pay-to-Win that this game possesses. There is a premium time option, where buying premium time increases the income of players by twofold or more. There are also many things to buy in Robocraft and very few are purely cosmetic. ALL parts can be purchased with real world currency, you can even purchase whole robots. In fact, purchasing whole robots gives players the benefit of extra 'CPU', which is the in-game limit of how many parts can be placed and is increased per level. A greater level of CPU significantly widens the tactical choices of players, giving them a hard edge over players of similar level and tier. Now, players must play to gain an in-game currency to unlock new tiers of parts, but you can pay real world currency to upgrade the in-game currency to a form that can unlock parts at all tiers.
This is an unethical PvP game, stacked in favor of those who pay real money. However, I will say that anyone who finds the premise of the game interesting should give this game a shot. If you play the game and have fun with it, I beg of you to refrain from giving Freejam your monetary patronage. Please do not support a developer who does not provide fair and balanced play between paying and non-paying players.
As this is an Early Access review, it may become obsolete. To those playing this game after it has been released as a full product, please research this game. I have outlined the present problems with this game, but I cannot speak for the future and I am unlikely to return to this review.

TL;DR Version - World of Tanks + Legos = Ridiculous amounts of fun.
========
I must ask you this, intrepid player of games:
Did you like Legos as a kid?  Did you like creating ridiculous battle machines with them and then duking it out with your sibling(s)' and friends' similar offbeat creations?
Then this is your game.
You start out with some pretty basic parts; but very quickly branch your way out into a pretty sizable tech tree letting you build everything from tanks with massive railguns to dune buggies with laser machineguns to land battleships with plasma cannons or even aircraft with healing beams, if that suits your fancy.  (And those are merely a few common combinations, not limitations on how one can build).
Now, this game is not flawless, being in Early Access - fliers can be hard to build and the weapon types could probably use some fine tuning balance-wise... but in terms of raw fun... it's kind of hard to beat; and I have high hopes that going forward it'll just get bigger and better.
So yeah - as of right now Feb 8th 2015, I can give Robocraft my full endorsement.
Oh, and a tip for anyone who's read the entire review:
If you get overwhelmed and can't figure out what to build, try building a tank and, as much as possible, stickin to real life tank design principles.  (IE:  Heaviest armor to the front, then sides, then rear, then top , low profile, that kind of thing)  - It's surprisingly effective even in a game like this; and from that good starting point you can build up experience (both the game currency kind and the 'you learning how to play' kind) before you worry about going for the more outlandish designs.
Though obviously if you want to experiment, go for it - this is THE game for it.
Just... please make sure your design will actually fly/drive/hover etc in the Practice room before queuing for a match.  You're no good to us upside down in the starting area.

This game is pretty sweet!
Essentially you just start off with a blank canvas and you build your craft with cubes and add some basic weapons to it. As you get kills, destory bits off other crafts and obviously win some matches you get RP (Robot Points) to spend and some tech points in which you use on upgrading your cubes and weapons and the RP points allows you to purchase those new items you unlocked.
So you upgrade your craft, go higher levels (tiers) and constantly spend time building and just testing out your craft. You can build pretty much anything and surprisingly it all seems to fit quite well, without feeling unbalanced and frustrating. You can build drones, bombers, repairers, plasma/rail cannns/smg's/nano rays, and the options go on! Obviously you can't buy a massive shiny rail cannon and meet up with people who just installed.
You see a lot of crazy designs, like complete and utter silly ones and even stupid ones that you know will just fail the moment someone shoots at it and if you're really unlucky, some show up not even being able to control properly, but that's rare - though sometimes funny. And personally this is why I've enjoyed this game. It feels fresh and not your usual tank or craft game.
Being a free game of course there's real money to spend in-game, but that buys you "Galaxy points" which is in-game currency that basically boils down to RP points just simply multiplied. So if you grind a few games and get 10000 RP which is exactly the price of say a weapon you want, with galaxy cash, you can buy that and purchase whatever you want without grinding. Essentially you're paying for time spent.. If you just want to enjoy playing the game, getting the points and upgrading as you go, then it's completely fine as that's what you're here for.
Unlike some free games, where you can join a match and get owned, go back to the shopping menu, buy a bunch of new flashy items and come back and be on par with the exact same person, with this you gear restricts you to certain tiers so no pay-to-win, just pay to speed up time at the cost of I guess some experience in playing. I haven't felt like I'm playing against people who just out-purchased me, though I have seen some screenshots with insane RP/GS so yeah.
Some games just simply shouldn't be free (or so it seems as sometimes it's just poor decision making), but this seems like it was designed to be free.. There seems to be absolutely no benefit in having multiple accounts, other than I guess if you can't get enough of the game and even then it seems counter productive to split your efforts/energy into seperate accounts. Nor can you trade anything so you're practically and objectively just playing for fun.
There's no specific rating system where in other games you end up in matches with just people obessed with ranking up or gaining some sort of imaginary points. Maybe that sounds like a 'con' rather than a 'pro', and a game worth playing when there's not really a competitive end-game, but personally it turns out to be good for me, at least.
It seems to still be in alpha development stage and honestly it feels more close to being almost released.. So either these guys, (which are from the UK) have some pretty high standards or they have a lot more planned.

Not too sure what to write here so heres a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

This game is such an amazing improvement on Valve's Portal, that it actually makes the original look nowhere near as good in comparison.

Do you like Minecraft? How about World of Tanks? A quick Multiplayer matchmaking system and a Free-to-Win gaming experience? If you answered yes to any of these questions, download this game, get an account, and roll out!
Building is fun, and requires a fair bit of thinking and tinkering to get going, and you'll only start with basic wheels. but as you go, you'll get into hover blades and treads, airplane wings and even walker legs.
The game is addicting, and anybody who does pay for bits and pieces won't overpower those who don't. All players have equal access to each part and a tiering system helps balance out the different parts. You won't be starting out by getting destroyed by someone with the strongest gun in the game because a Tier 10 weapon can't physically exist in a Tier 1 game.
Let's break this down a bit.
Things I Like
-FREE!
-Matchmaking is super quick most of the time.
-Matches are super short, and once you're destroyed, you can leave without penalty. Or, y'know, stay and watch the remaining carnage. You get your exp, money, and tech points either way.
-Building is fun.
-Players who pay don't have any real advantage over those who don't in terms of power.
-Progression system is great
-Players who "down tier" or use higher tier equipment in lower tier games give you an idea of what to look forward to. Don't worry though, in most cases down tiering places really strict limits on how dangerous their craft can be. For example, aerofoils (wings) are unlocked in the fifth tier, but players can make limited small flying vehicles as low as tier 3, but they sacrifice much armor and firepower to do this
-Players who pay give bonuses to everyone. For every paying player in a match, every players' rewards are increased by 5%
Things I don't like
-4 person party size is restricted to players who are premium, and the host of the party has to be the premium one.
-Spedometer and Altimeter are blocks that are placed on your craft, not HUD elements, and are also items you must pay to have.
-Pickles on my cheeseburger. I ran out of negatives for this game.
Seriously, its a free game, isn't super hardware-intensive, and its fun. Give it a download, play it for an hour (or 70, at the time of writing). Game's so addicting it rocketed to my 5th most-played game within a week of downloading, and is endagering Dungeon Defenders' spot on my activity board.

-The game has been changing very fast. Its quite impressive. I have removed parts that are no longer relevant I beleive. It was heavily flawed in some aspects, but I havn't played the game in a time and there has been several large updates so those flaws may no longer be relevant. The games alot of fun as its virtual lego fighting vehicles. Definetly one of the best free games on steam.
Building your robot to do just battle against other players who are on a level playing field where only your wit about yourself in the fight or your engineering prowess at base can give you an advantage is an extremely attractive design. We all played with legos as kids and imagined this (or atleast thats what boys do). It translates reasonably well into a game aswell but its not quite all there. Its extremely frustrating at times to the point where you just Alt-F4 and ask what were they thinking? I hope a in the coming months when this game is released the devs will open their eyes to what can only be described as bad designs.
Building your robot is very fun. Designing something to go out and kill the red guys and making it do it better than the red guys is a truly entertaining venture. You have many types of blocks to choose and a few sets of each type of block/item to strap to your vehicle. Unlocking new items and choosing what to build is extremely gratifying especially when you find something that really holds its own.
Its not pay to win, but its pay to skip hours of grinding and skipping many games lost because you don't have good enough spec gear. So in a way it is pay to win and pay to skip. Honestly I couldn't advocate spending money on this game though until some designs are sorted out like balancing and physics.

But what it excels as is in the design choices and variations of vehicles you can make. This is what makes this game good when its good but it dousn't help it from being bad when its bad. Its free to play so its worth a download to try it out and Im sure most users will like it for a time and maybe even get hooked. Its a great idea to actually put out a game like this. I'm giving this game a recommendation, but with a HUGE caveat, so I'm hoping the developers do read these reviews.
Robocraft is a very fun game, however, there is a major imbalance in the weapons. Particularly the Railgun. The Railgun is the sniper rifle of Robocraft, and it can reach clear across the entire map. There are players who are very skilled with it, and others who use aimbots despite the "very poor and ineffective" anti-cheat software that's installed with the game.
The Railguns are extremely powerful. In most cases they're a one-shot, one-kill weapon regardless who tier armor you're using. You enter a match, see a red beam target your robot, and suddenly more than 50% of your hit points are gone. The power and range of these weapons is making Robocraft nearly unplayable in the higher tier matches, and even in the lower tier matches.
Some players are building robots that are just the pilot seat, a helium canister, a block, and their weapon. They can't move, all they can do is float upward to the top of the map, and sit there sniping at people from extreme range. I've seen one player sitting in the same spot the entire match vaporize the entire opposing team. There are unlockable addons that are supposed to be countermeasures to the railgun but they don't work. The guns are just too powerful. I learned the devs recently buffed them, making them far too strong. Its extremely frustrating to work on a robot for several hours, get into a match, and then get ripped to pieces by some guy on the opposite side of the map who can only see your name from that distance. Until this is fixed I've stopped playing, and that makes me very angry because I really liked this game.
If the developers are reading this, please do something about this.
If you choose to play this game, be prepared to face serious frustration.

Portal 2, Portal 2...where do I begin? Well, a friend of mine, of whom is a big fan of this game, suggested it to me. Not being a big videogamer, I was hesitant and opted to watch a 2 hour playthrough of it on YouTube, just to see if it was my kind of thing. This game is AMAZING. It's very easy to see why it has so many positive reviews. Admittedly, buying this game was the sole reason I joined Steam in the first place. Though I promise not to spoil any of the plot for anyone reading this before having played the game.
The one thing I tend to look for it any videogame is a good plot. For me, it's what keeps me playing. And heck does this game deliver in that sense. I admit, I've never played the first Portal, as I did some research and found that there wasn't much plot other than 'do the tests, kill GLaDOS'. However, its' sequel has a really interesting ongoing plot. Even when you're doing GLaDOS' tests, Wheatley will often pop out of the panels with an encouraging "Just hold on for a few more tests, then we'll break out of here!" Though I have to admit, I've never had a videogame plot give me so many feels before. When it gets to the point when you feel sympathy for the antagonist before you're about to destroy them, you know it's a quality game.
However, every plot needs good characters, and Portal 2 had a surplus of those. As is the same for the first game, Ellen McLain voices GLaDOS, the cynical, sarcastic and very sadistic AI that is obsessed with testing. I know they obviously used a lot of autotuning to make GLaDOS sound like a machine, but I still think Ellen McLain's monotonous voice carries the character very well. Now that GLaDOS has some history with Chell (mainly of Chell 'killing' her), it is absolutely hilarious hearing that AI hold a grudge. Some of those lines are just brilliant.
"Oh, it's YOU. How have you been? I've been a bit busy being dead. You know, after you MURDERED ME."
The AI's attempt to insult Chell during testing also has me cracking up.
The second main character in this game is, of course, Wheatley. Steven Merchant does Wheatley's character such justice. Wheatley is your lovable, kind of moronic, sidekick in the game. It's worth it during gameplay to just stop what you are doing to listen to his quality lines. He isn't completely useless, though. Often, Wheatley will help you navigate through the Aperature Science facility. After all, the place is massive, so getting lost could be quite easy without him as your guide. The fact that he also has a built-in torch inside of his optic is also very useful.
"Aaah! Oh. Oh, they told me, that if I ever turned this thing on, I would DIE. They told me that about everything! I don't know why they bothered giving me these things if they didn't want me to use them!"
The last of the main characters in this game, is of course, Chell. She is the character you play in the game. I really like her because, despite the fact that she is in fact female (which I've seen is pretty rare in videogames nowadays, especially females that aren't sexualised in someway, which Chell is NOT, thankfully), she is also totally mute. She can't-or won't-speak at all in the game, but still manages to totally kick robot butt.
There are other characters in this game, but they are only present through various voice recordings throughout the old Aperture Science Testing Facility. These characters are Cave Johnson, the (rather arrogant) creator of Aperature Science, and Caroline, his (overly enthusiastic) assisant. Both characters, though they don't play very big roles as they are, help the player get an insight to what Aperature Science used to be like before everything went downhill and GLaDOS went rogue.
Another thing that I find useful in a good videogame is a quality soundtrack. I have to admit, during gameplay, there really isn't that much of it, other than to create ambience during the 'epic' parts of plot or during the boss battle. Otherwise, I find the testing areas pretty quiet and found myself popping in my headphones during those parts. The credits song was amazing, though. Just like the first game's credit song, it was sung by Ellen McLain as GLaDOS and is sung (rather sarcastically in parts) to, presumably, Chell. It's called 'Want You Gone' and I tend to listen to it a lot due to it's greatness. XD
There is also another ending song, sung by the Turrets at the very end. It is an Opera-style song sung in what I assume to be Italian. It does sound great, though.
And finally, we get to the gameplay itself. I don't really have any complaints when playing it, myself. (Just as a side note, I'm not referring to the Co-op part of the game, as I've only ever played the single player game.) Sure, the tests can get a bit repetitive, but the plot usually furthers before you can get fed up with it. The tests, thankfully, are never too mind numbingly difficult. Sure, they are really challenging and it may take you a while to figure them out, but all of them are do-able, even for a gaming newbie like me. And, let's be honest, ripping holes into reality was never going to be boring.
Overall, I 100% reccommend this to anybody, veteran gamer or otherwise. It was highly enjoyable and is guarenteed to be replayed again and again. I know I'm going to be replaying as soon as I finish writing this review. :)

If I had to give Portal 2 a score between 1-100, then it would be 999999>
This game has got a lot of funny moments and a good plot that tells you the story, without spoiling too much. Maybe the biggest spoiler in the game was a turret.
For the music; almost perfect, but sometimes a bit too electric. I liked the fact that the music changed with your actions, your location and plot. I don't see that often in games (if they already have music that fits). I.E; it intensifies when you're defeating the boss and it changes when you use the blue gel or if you kill a turret.
The gels are an amazing addition that really adds a new element to the game. Now you don't have only need to think with portals, but also with speed, fysics and bouncyness.
And when you're in co-op modus, you have to think with portals twice as much as in singleplayer.
Don't forget about the perpetual testing initiative! Since Portal have got an end, and after palying the game more times, you know how to solve the puzzles. But in Portal 2, you can use the maps of the community. And if you want to, you can make your own (like I did).
The detaillness of the maps where amazing. You can spilt Portal 2 in 6 parts and every part has got its own properties. For instance, when you're playing in the underground, you see that everything is falling apart due to a lack of maintenance. You also hear that. The soundscape fits amazingly well!
Shortly;
If you're hesistating, buy it. Portal 2 is worth it. It's even more worth it when it's on sale.

Portal 2, Portal 2...where do I begin? Well, a friend of mine, of whom is a big fan of this game, suggested it to me. Not being a big videogamer, I was hesitant and opted to watch a 2 hour playthrough of it on YouTube, just to see if it was my kind of thing. This game is AMAZING. It's very easy to see why it has so many positive reviews. Admittedly, buying this game was the sole reason I joined Steam in the first place. Though I promise not to spoil any of the plot for anyone reading this before having played the game.
The one thing I tend to look for it any videogame is a good plot. For me, it's what keeps me playing. And heck does this game deliver in that sense. I admit, I've never played the first Portal, as I did some research and found that there wasn't much plot other than 'do the tests, kill GLaDOS'. However, its' sequel has a really interesting ongoing plot. Even when you're doing GLaDOS' tests, Wheatley will often pop out of the panels with an encouraging "Just hold on for a few more tests, then we'll break out of here!" Though I have to admit, I've never had a videogame plot give me so many feels before. When it gets to the point when you feel sympathy for the antagonist before you're about to destroy them, you know it's a quality game.
However, every plot needs good characters, and Portal 2 had a surplus of those. As is the same for the first game, Ellen McLain voices GLaDOS, the cynical, sarcastic and very sadistic AI that is obsessed with testing. I know they obviously used a lot of autotuning to make GLaDOS sound like a machine, but I still think Ellen McLain's monotonous voice carries the character very well. Now that GLaDOS has some history with Chell (mainly of Chell 'killing' her), it is absolutely hilarious hearing that AI hold a grudge. Some of those lines are just brilliant.
"Oh, it's YOU. How have you been? I've been a bit busy being dead. You know, after you MURDERED ME."
The AI's attempt to insult Chell during testing also has me cracking up.
The second main character in this game is, of course, Wheatley. Steven Merchant does Wheatley's character such justice. Wheatley is your lovable, kind of moronic, sidekick in the game. It's worth it during gameplay to just stop what you are doing to listen to his quality lines. He isn't completely useless, though. Often, Wheatley will help you navigate through the Aperature Science facility. After all, the place is massive, so getting lost could be quite easy without him as your guide. The fact that he also has a built-in torch inside of his optic is also very useful.
"Aaah! Oh. Oh, they told me, that if I ever turned this thing on, I would DIE. They told me that about everything! I don't know why they bothered giving me these things if they didn't want me to use them!"
The last of the main characters in this game, is of course, Chell. She is the character you play in the game. I really like her because, despite the fact that she is in fact female (which I've seen is pretty rare in videogames nowadays, especially females that aren't sexualised in someway, which Chell is NOT, thankfully), she is also totally mute. She can't-or won't-speak at all in the game, but still manages to totally kick robot butt.
There are other characters in this game, but they are only present through various voice recordings throughout the old Aperture Science Testing Facility. These characters are Cave Johnson, the (rather arrogant) creator of Aperature Science, and Caroline, his (overly enthusiastic) assisant. Both characters, though they don't play very big roles as they are, help the player get an insight to what Aperature Science used to be like before everything went downhill and GLaDOS went rogue.
Another thing that I find useful in a good videogame is a quality soundtrack. I have to admit, during gameplay, there really isn't that much of it, other than to create ambience during the 'epic' parts of plot or during the boss battle. Otherwise, I find the testing areas pretty quiet and found myself popping in my headphones during those parts. The credits song was amazing, though. Just like the first game's credit song, it was sung by Ellen McLain as GLaDOS and is sung (rather sarcastically in parts) to, presumably, Chell. It's called 'Want You Gone' and I tend to listen to it a lot due to it's greatness. XD
There is also another ending song, sung by the Turrets at the very end. It is an Opera-style song sung in what I assume to be Italian. It does sound great, though.
And finally, we get to the gameplay itself. I don't really have any complaints when playing it, myself. (Just as a side note, I'm not referring to the Co-op part of the game, as I've only ever played the single player game.) Sure, the tests can get a bit repetitive, but the plot usually furthers before you can get fed up with it. The tests, thankfully, are never too mind numbingly difficult. Sure, they are really challenging and it may take you a while to figure them out, but all of them are do-able, even for a gaming newbie like me. And, let's be honest, ripping holes into reality was never going to be boring.
Overall, I 100% reccommend this to anybody, veteran gamer or otherwise. It was highly enjoyable and is guarenteed to be replayed again and again. I know I'm going to be replaying as soon as I finish writing this review. :)

If I had to give Portal 2 a score between 1-100, then it would be 999999>
This game has got a lot of funny moments and a good plot that tells you the story, without spoiling too much. Maybe the biggest spoiler in the game was a turret.
For the music; almost perfect, but sometimes a bit too electric. I liked the fact that the music changed with your actions, your location and plot. I don't see that often in games (if they already have music that fits). I.E; it intensifies when you're defeating the boss and it changes when you use the blue gel or if you kill a turret.
The gels are an amazing addition that really adds a new element to the game. Now you don't have only need to think with portals, but also with speed, fysics and bouncyness.
And when you're in co-op modus, you have to think with portals twice as much as in singleplayer.
Don't forget about the perpetual testing initiative! Since Portal have got an end, and after palying the game more times, you know how to solve the puzzles. But in Portal 2, you can use the maps of the community. And if you want to, you can make your own (like I did).
The detaillness of the maps where amazing. You can spilt Portal 2 in 6 parts and every part has got its own properties. For instance, when you're playing in the underground, you see that everything is falling apart due to a lack of maintenance. You also hear that. The soundscape fits amazingly well!
Shortly;
If you're hesistating, buy it. Portal 2 is worth it. It's even more worth it when it's on sale.

This could've been a good game if it weren't for the abysmal matchmaking, pairing people with tier 2 equipment against those with tier 4. Various guns have obvious balance issues (Plasma cannon and rail cannon can both 1-shot kill), and progression is severely dampened by the pittance they give us to unlock (and actually buy) new blocks. This is one of those games where people will say "it gets better once you hit the level cap", or in this case, the tier cap. But grinding your way through this abysmal game is not worth reaching end-game, no matter how cool the videos may make it seem. Your early game will be boring and you will die. A lot. To people with better equipment. Did I mention that you can buy parts for real world cash? The only thing keeping this from being a proper P2W is the fact that you can't throw cash at the research. Oh wait, you CAN! You can buy high-tier robots if you don't fancy playing the game, immediately skipping all the pre-requisite PLAYING and unlocking all the research for blocks included on the robot. Why should I actually play this game when I can throw money at the screen to get a beefy ship? Why should I grind 5000 points in order to buy a new turret when, guess what, you can throw MORE money at the screen, and just buy the turret. This is a sad attempt at profiting from the lazy, ruining the game for those that actually want to play. Did I mention the matchmaking? Oh yes, I did. Getting smashed by guys with tier 4 weapons in a tier 2 match isn't very comforting or inspiring. It certainly doesn't make me want to keep playing.

I first played this many months ago and decided to give it a try tonight, only to find they have added "EasyAntiCheat" as a requirement. While I get that client side anti-cheat software can be useful and seems to have been needed based on forum posts, I have considerable privacy concerns based on what EAC is requesting it be allowed to do on my computer.
The software itself has full access to screenshot, keylog and google searches have shown the results are publicly available for all to see. The only limiting factor is their word that it only operates while the game is running. While I'm sure there is other anti-cheat software running on my computer (ie steam), the data it returns to any third party servers has never been Google searchable.
I recommend the developers for Robocraft force a migration of their users to Steam and use Steam's built in anti-cheat instead of using a third party app developer who obviously has zero clue on how to secure data being returned to their servers. There's no excuse for that to be Google searchable.

Never have I seen such a massive 180 degree turn. While. The objective-based gameplay was removed, and the teir system was changed to a better point based system, making playing together significantly more difficult.
I cannot recommend this game in it's current state.
-----------------------------------------
Robocraft is a constantly evolving game over time. Mechanics change, and new features are added.
They've gone with a system where, depending on your performance, you gain crates which have components in it. This seems like a pretty good idea, as you can score a high tier object, and are then faced with the challenge of finding a way of putting it on your bot, or you can sell it for robits, and forge the item you want.
They've brought back objective based gameplay as well, yet with the addition of multiple-weapon types for certain robots, robot designs have all devolved into a samey design that overrules all. Legs, and a few weapons. The defined roles that existed before are no more. Bombers don't exist. Medics are beyond useless, as the nano-beams no longer damage enemies, and robots self-repair after 10 seconds. (It's impossible to out-heal most weapons.)
A lot of my issues have been resolved, but the design aspect of robots, as well as the combat, for me, has goten nothing but more stale. I'll likely forget about the game, and it's content until friends suggest I try it again. They've resolved some things, but other issues crop up that generally take away what was considered fun. Either that, or rose-tinted glasses cause undu bias. It's up to you to decide.

While singleplayer is a simple and straightforward sequel to Portal, the second installment has a good replay value of its own as it features a variety of extra content, such as a co-op player campaign, plenty of user-generated puzzles as it allows the player some creative freedom in making their own challenges via the ingame puzzlemaker, and there are at least two available story-driven campaign addons on Steam. Portal 2 carries forth the the core likable elements from the predecessor in a charning, quirky sequel.
Portal 2 is a sci-fi physics FPS-puzzle game taking place in a chronologically-ambiguous position in the Half-Life universe. Following the events unfolded in Portal, the sequel brings the faces old and new to the player between the continuity of the experiment courses. It has an entertaining cooperative mode to enjoy with a friend, and user-generated content from the "Perpetual Testing Initiative" that brings the inner mad scientist of the user to life with the ingame Puzzlemaker.
Taking the place of the test subject "Chell" once more, the player accompanies her journey through the now-ruined Aperture Science facilities, meeting an old enemy and new faces along the way while solving the various puzzle challenges through the Enrichment Center's remains. The game also features some exploration of the past of Aperture Science, solving some possible loose ends and letting them know about the past of the lab complex. A dark humor-packed character development is noticeable between the messages left behind, and the new quirky characters introduced into the game.The co-op mode also reveals some details of Aperture through the portal experiment course between the two players.
The singleplayer mode is considerably similar to the first game's mechanics, though with a number of twists. New testing elements and various new puzzle-solving techniques make the player think, move and portal their way through the tests with trial and error, either involving the classic testing elements such as moving platforms, turrets and acid pits, or new elements such as lasers and redirection cubes, crusher plates, catapult plates, among others.
Without some cooperation the players won't advance in this mode. (Literally. You really can't even get past the level selection if the players don't cooperate and play in such manner.) More advanced puzzle techniques such as timing and advanced portal placement are introduced with a fair amount of trust being in the hands of the partner player. The incompetence (or mischievousness) of either of the parts might end in hilarious failure results.
Using an upgraded Source Engine, the game is able to render great-looking environments at relatively low performance cost. Highly detailed testing environments, from the ruins of Old Aperture to the production lines of the upper facilities, you'll see yourself stopping for a few moments to admire the scenery on the areas with more visible attention to detail.
The soundtrack of Portal 2 and its iconic eeriness, generally accompanied by the 'robotic' sounds inserted into the music tracks make Mike Morasky's work fit perfectly into the game.
The sound effects of the game, not unlike the soundtrack, are highly detailed. From the slight noises of the testing elements to the rampaging avalanche brought by things like crusher plates in the game, every sound aspect has a high level of detail.
The voice acting is priceless, the character dialogue (or, in most part, monologue) is now fitting to each character's personalities and role. Including names such as J. K. Simmons, Stephen Merchant and Ellen McLain, Portal 2's VA cast is noteworthy in that regard.
Aperture Science's Perpetual Testing Initiative -better known as the Ingame Puzzlemaker- is a tool both simple and intuictive to use. Simple controls and a range of elements available, the player can build test chambers to his heart's content with the tool. You can even export your maps to edit with the Portal 2 SDK, for further detailings like custom assets and elements.
Portal 2 is worth picking up if you're a fan of puzzle games, sci-fi or some quirky humor. The co-op mode warrants some hours of fun with friends, and the puzzlemaker and user-generated content will assure you some extra replay value.

Used to be a great game till it became a pay to win garbage

Tier 1
It's a bit of a slope once you begin playing, use a promo-code for premium to power yourself to T3 before it expires. Beginning a game and flipping on your back right away, enjoy seeing friends and enemies stuck as half-crippled all over the battlefield if they forget to place a 'flipper' on their car. Or seeing just how many guns you can fit on your build. It's a lot of fun and hilarious to see.
Tier 3
This is where the real fun begins, competing on the leaderboards against your friends who you so love to hate if they surpass your high-score. (>w0) Snipers, mortars, smg's. The real guns go out and you see yourself driving happily down a road till half your tank explodes with a well-placed snipershot. You also get thrown with 10 others against a monster tank (Also called Tier 8)
Tier 6
You've gone up a few levels and get to build bigger tanks when suddenly there are planes everywhere, that's right. You can get wings and rudders to bombard all those puny ants down there till one of your wings get clipped and you crash down as a silly little heap. Heal-guns are thrown into the mix, people keeping that one guy alive you've been preying on the entire time. You flank enemies, cripple them, act like hot stuff and hoping they won't shoot back at you.
Tier 8
Now you are the big dog, getting access to boss-battles as the boss. See yourself get mutilated as 11 little monsters surround you from everywhere, shooting off your guns so they can drive circles around you in a mocking manner. How awesome you feel one-shotting each and every single one of them like the badass that you are. You begin gtting scared of the game as more and more pro-players begin shooting you down like the greenest grass, advanced team-play and horrifying tanks that send shivers up your spine.
Tier 10
After months of endless grinding and getting 6 mere tier-10 blocks out of your 100.000,- cash while your tank consists of 700 carefully placed blocks that are excrusiatingly hard to replace one-by-one, you finally made it to Tier 10, where you find the most advanced and most redicoulus gameplay. Players either making sickly dangerous tanks or players that make their tanks into sculptures so that you at one point or another see a creeper, a pokemon or a huise (including windows, lawn, pool and mailbox) casually drive into battle.
Tier Mega
It's still tier 10, but the parts cost stupidly much more than they should, which means that you are the♥♥♥♥♥♥on the block when you manage to put them on your tank. You kill all you see, get killed by all you see sporting the same gear and you feel like the king of the world once you do a bossbattle and hose down those poor Tier-5's with a barrage of lasers.
This is where the big boys play and only the big boys survive.
Robocraft: An awesome game where every battle either makes or breaks your day.
Edit: At least, it used to be, till they removed this tier-system, added a crate-loot system, removed the techtree, locked 70% of the most used colors behind a pay-wall and ruined the balance of the game.
Robocraft used to be amazing, it's worthless now. Yet another title fallen into the pits of Pay-to-Win.

There are awesome moments when something clicks in a puzzle and it is terrific when that happens and you finish a very hard puzzle. It is awesomely priced when you see how much work was put into the game to perfect it and make it as awesome as it is. I am very impressed. As for those who may be worrying there is not enough content I still have co-op mode to do as well as an infinite amount of community test chambers. It is easy to see why this is the top rated game on steam. Probably the only con this game has is it can be a bit hard at times, I myself never needed a guide but I can easily see how others might and there were parts where I very nearly broke down and looked at a guide but I figured it out right at that moment. I think that is all I have to say, and I highly reccomend trying this game, it is worth it.

Edit: Be advised that my review now is reflective of "classic mode" as there as been a new mode added, i'll update once i feel confident with my experiences of it.
I guess i will update this review later on, but after putting in that many hours, im feeling confident for an initial review.
Robocraft makes you craft your own robot (duh) and face in a teambased deathmatch. Alternativly a team can win by capturing the enemies base. As you fight in matches you get Tech points for your current tier, and slowly gain more capacity to actually equip the things you unlock with your tech points. Once you have enough parts (or enough valueable parts) on your robot it falls into a new tier and you earn tech points for this tier. So there is a constant progression in the game.
Pros
The combat is reasonable fun.
A good amount of weapon types. Sadly they cant be combined (cause balance?).
Building is quite nice and allows for very unique ideas being realized.
Boss Battle combat is a cool idea, where one high tier player faces many low tier players.
Fair free to play model which only allows for faster progress, but wont give you an unfair advantage during a match. Nor is there any exclusive content concerning gameplay.
Good map sice and design, misses some more details though.
Cons
More intersting weapon types and equipments are locked behind the tier system. Allowing advanced players to build a lower tier vehicle with better parts. They are smaller but and more dureable, therefore a problem. For example its rather common that people build a very small flying robot with a one shot kill (high tier) railgun.
As there is no fluent ranking system, based on energy used or tier parts used, but instead a strict tier based system in place you always are the weakest robot in a match once you enter a new tier.
The game uses Easy-AntiCheat, a software that logs stuff from your computer, more on that below.
Building takes a long time, and could need a minecraft-styled hotbar. As well as a floodfill funciton which allows replacing a certain blocktype with others. As you have to replace every single armor block on your robot every time you get better armor blocks. Hours of replacing...
Tech points aquired for a low tier cant be converted in higher tiers if no real money is spent.
EAC-Controversity
Many users had and have doubts about which information is actually sent away to this third party company. According to developers no screenshots are taken (as EAC does in CS:Go) and only the process of the game is overwatch by the software.

This sadly does not clarify if the password you use in robocraft is sent as well, so if you are a carefull person you might not wanna use your standard password.
I think the game is worth a recommendation if you want a game you can casually go in and have a nice shootout with others. But it clearly has some problems, and it wont do for a game you play for hours every day.

Portal 2: A serious review.
So if the opening line of this review caught your attention, it might be that you're like me. You wanted to read some reviews before buying this game and you quickly got fed up with most of the 'most helpful' reviews giving absolutely no real information about what the game is like. Instead, you get the feeling that anybody who's played this game has sustained permanent brain damage. To not go on any longer, here are 5 reasons why I think Portal 2 is one of the best games I've ever played.
1. Graphics: The game is beautiful! Portal (1) looked great and it was released in 2007. Portal 2 looks 10x better! The game doesn't use too many resources so an average gaming PC or laptop will run it at max settings without a problem.
2. Physics: One of the greatest elements of this game is the amazing physics. You will have great fun discovering how to use the portals and other tools supplied to navigate and solve the well thought out puzzles. The game requires you to use forward momentum, perfect timing and fast thinking (amongst many other things) to complete puzzles. There is never a dull moment.
3. Pacing: The developers has again achieved a perfect sweet spot between making the puzzles challenging but not impossible. The game starts out with a few simple puzzles that really help you understand the basics of the game and how you can best use the portals and other tools to your advantage. After that the game gradually ramps up the difficulty keeping the game challenging and fun. With some patience and perseverance you can play through this whole game without having to consult a single walkthrough.
4. Dark Humor: Portal 2 returns with more characters than Portal 1 and the scripts are again absolutely hilarious. The game treats you as what you are a test subject and the machines are as you would expect them to be, cold and calculating in carrying out their agenda. However, I have to admit that GLaDOS was funnier in Portal 1.
5. Story & Uniqueness: This game continues the surprisingly compelling story of Portal 1. I didn't think a puzzle game would have any decent kind of story but boy, was I wrong! Portal 2 is in a class of its own as an fps puzzle game that offers many hours of fun, challenging puzzles and great, hilarious scripts. My only regret is taking so long to finally play it.
P.S: these 5 points apply to both Portal (1) and Portal 2. I highly recommend you play Portal (1) first because it helps you paint a more complete picture of the full story and there are plenty of references to Portal (1) in Portal 2, including some steps in solving puzzles.
Thanks for reading. Do yourself a favor and buy this game!

First, I'd like to make one thing clear:
For all people panicking around EAC, the official disclaimer is here:

---
The game is fun to play both in creating your own tank, plane, rolling fotress, giraffe,... (yes, I've seen tank in shape of giraffe) and fun in battle seeing your creation being disassembled part-by-part by enemy gunfire.
Even though I would recommend this game after all, I start with one (only) thing that surprised (and dissapointed) me.
- Game is based hugely on action (skill), teamplay. and how well can you design you vehicle. You have several types of parts, wheels, thrusters, radars, shields, guns. Several types of guns, SMG, plasma (AoE), Railgun ("sniper")... BUT you are limited to ONE type of wapon per vehicle.
So you can only go all SMG, OR all plasma, etc. which greatly limits customization potential of game. WHY would one do this in game based on customization?!
The arguments are that, to keep game team-based, the absence of all-in-one solutions is essential, so by wapon choice the vehicles are divided into classes.
(I strongly disagree with that. Since the possibilities will be same for all the players, the teamplay always beats all-in-one solutions, and also, even with possibility of universality, the specialised vehicles, will always have more significant strenghts in trade for their weaknesses, and universal ones will not have any significant strenghts.
I get that it would be really hard to balance, and if classification would be preserved, it would be rather tentative.)
After all this my complaining and whining, what I see good in the game?
Everything else! :D
+ It's not P2W, only allows some cosmetics, and faster progress, but even if you progress faster, you are matched with people based on tank tech level, and it's overall strenght. (So premium players get to fight against stronger people faster.)
+ Destructive model of tanks, destroyed cube-by-cube, most fun is fighting with, like, barely moving half of what used to by your vehicle.
+ Graphics, simple, not too resource demanding, yet pretty.
Tl;dr
Con:
- only one weapon on tak at the some time
Pro:
+ graphics/performance
+ customization
+ fun
+ NOT P2W

Portal 2: A serious review.
So if the opening line of this review caught your attention, it might be that you're like me. You wanted to read some reviews before buying this game and you quickly got fed up with most of the 'most helpful' reviews giving absolutely no real information about what the game is like. Instead, you get the feeling that anybody who's played this game has sustained permanent brain damage. To not go on any longer, here are 5 reasons why I think Portal 2 is one of the best games I've ever played.
1. Graphics: The game is beautiful! Portal (1) looked great and it was released in 2007. Portal 2 looks 10x better! The game doesn't use too many resources so an average gaming PC or laptop will run it at max settings without a problem.
2. Physics: One of the greatest elements of this game is the amazing physics. You will have great fun discovering how to use the portals and other tools supplied to navigate and solve the well thought out puzzles. The game requires you to use forward momentum, perfect timing and fast thinking (amongst many other things) to complete puzzles. There is never a dull moment.
3. Pacing: The developers has again achieved a perfect sweet spot between making the puzzles challenging but not impossible. The game starts out with a few simple puzzles that really help you understand the basics of the game and how you can best use the portals and other tools to your advantage. After that the game gradually ramps up the difficulty keeping the game challenging and fun. With some patience and perseverance you can play through this whole game without having to consult a single walkthrough.
4. Dark Humor: Portal 2 returns with more characters than Portal 1 and the scripts are again absolutely hilarious. The game treats you as what you are a test subject and the machines are as you would expect them to be, cold and calculating in carrying out their agenda. However, I have to admit that GLaDOS was funnier in Portal 1.
5. Story & Uniqueness: This game continues the surprisingly compelling story of Portal 1. I didn't think a puzzle game would have any decent kind of story but boy, was I wrong! Portal 2 is in a class of its own as an fps puzzle game that offers many hours of fun, challenging puzzles and great, hilarious scripts. My only regret is taking so long to finally play it.
P.S: these 5 points apply to both Portal (1) and Portal 2. I highly recommend you play Portal (1) first because it helps you paint a more complete picture of the full story and there are plenty of references to Portal (1) in Portal 2, including some steps in solving puzzles.
Thanks for reading. Do yourself a favor and buy this game!

Well, this was quite a drastic change from the first Portal. Not in a bad way like Hitman: Absolution (which i reviewed in a bit too much of detail). This could be one of the best sequels for a game, I've played, though it really didn't start as a serious project and since bloomed into something that's pretty damn great.
If you're not familiar, this was really just a lone physics game that valve aquired and then turned into Portal. So where to go from a shot game about puzzles with physics? Start with: new puzzles (obviously), also make a well made story with atmosphere and humor the game was originally known for, include a mysterious deeper lore for previous fans, add new ways to solve puzzles, have friends co-op on a seperate part of the game with even more puzzles, then finaly as Cave Johnson would probably add "Market the crap out of it".

So i am here to say they did it all, and they did it right. It's hard for me to say anything bad, not even sure there is anything inherently bad about this game. Maybe how mainsteam the game has become? Not really. Lack of puzzels after game? No they fixed that. Maybe the lack of answers from the lore? Hopefully in time it will all be answered. But overall in gameplay, visuals, and story, this one is a keeper.

Robocraft, a game of freedom and learning from the powerful. Playing like a cross between World of Tanks and War Thunder, Robocraft is a "Build your own" style of the World of Tanks PvP system, two teams of 15 fight to see who is the last man standing or who can capture the enemy base. Varity goes as far as you can imagine, if you can dream it and you think it can fight, you can create it. Overall its just a more casual game but still has the anger that can stem from the other titles mentioned such as getting one shot across the map. luckly this game is somewhat forgiving as all parts have their own HP with the chair being indestructable, though if the block the chairs is on is destroyed, your knocked out. Weapons are broken down (at the time) to: SMGs - Fast shooting and highly accurate when tap-fired though low damage per shot, Plasma Cannons - AOE explosive weapon with drop and a decent charge time, Rail Guns - The snipers of this game with a long charge time and high damage, Nano-Beams - Healing tools that do tons of damage at close range and new Plasma blades - Melee weapons for those who want to get in nice and close. Progression can be pretty slow when grinding out a teir post 3. Overall matches can be quick and you dont have to wait for one game to end before using your creation again. Note that planes can be hard to make as balance is an issue when design them, so always test in the solo arena first.

Seriously, where do I start with this game? Well...to put it simply, IT'S F-ING AMAZING!!!!
If you like the original, buy it.
If you like GREAT stories, buy it.
If you want a good co-op game to spend days and days playing with a friend, buy it.
It's a great sequel and continues the story from the first game. The story is really well done, it has it's highs, it's lows, it's funny parts and its sad parts. It's really well written, and it's one of my favourite stories in a game, of all time. Also it's pretty lengthy, I spent about 23 hours doing the story alone.
Ontop of the amazing single player campaign, there is also a co-op campaign in which you and your friend (or a random stranger if you can't find a friend) can spend hours completing. It's not as long as the single player campaign, but it's good for about 5-6 hours...maybe.
Then there are loads of amazing fan made maps. They are some amazing ones that are single player and some that are co-op, and these add hundreds and hundreds of hours ontop of this amazing game.
To put it simply, if you don't own this game - you're missing out.
Oh...and I almost forgot to mention the content creator. It's great for creating basic single player and/or co-operative test chambers that are half decent. There are some (test chambers) that have clearly been made using better editing software, but the content creator is great for you to express your creative vision with the world.

The game starts pretty much like you expect it. You do some puzzles, race towards GlaDOS, and even have a funny side kick (great voice acting by Stephen Merchant). After the first couple of chapters however, the game and story completely pull the rug from under you. Like the first Portal, the story and characters are a highlight in this game.
The best part of this game is it's pacing. It never bores, never makes you do the same kind of puzzles for too long, and throws some new mechanics at you every hour.
Concluding, an amazing follow-up to an already amazing game! And I haven't even played the co-op campaign yet!

Great game - it delivers exactly what it promises, and what it promises is good.
Basically, you build your own robot, piece by piece, from scratch - and then you take it to battle to crush other people's robots.
For movement, you have wheels, tracks, legs, skis, thrusters, wings, and a kind of a baloon. You can combine those any which way. At one point, I had a walker with wings, who could fly propelled by thrusters. He also had wheels for when the legs got shot away.
For defense, you have raw armor (cubes) and shields (that can absorb a bit of damage and recharge automatically).
For attack, you have basic lasers, artillery, sniper, heal, and melee. Those are all mutually exclusive - you can only use one type of gun.
There are various utlity and vanity items like radars and nameplates.
There are two types of games - team vs team, and boss battles (one high level players vs an army of low level players). There are also 5-6 maps. If there is one thing the game needs in its current stage of development, it's more game-modes and maps.
Robocraft's graphics are decent, and the purchases system is NOT pay-to-win. Essentially, there are 10 levels of robots, and the robots of each level only fight between themselves. In effect, donating to the developers allows you to progress between the levels twice as quickly. It took me ~40 hours to get to level 10 (as a "supporter" of the game).
Robocraft is a great game, one of the best I've ever played. I'd say it's already a classic. Hopefully, with another year or two of development it will blossom into a game for the ages.

I can see this game going far into the future, with more and more players entering the land of robots and historical battles.
I didn't need to play more than an hour in this game to see just how beautiful it looked. The controls are very easy to get used too, and the internet connection required to play this game is subtle - sometimes a mass of internet is required over some parts of online battles.
Like any other game I love, this game requires your imagination to build tremendous robots to aid your team's battle.
As well, this game already acts as a fully functioning, and safe game, with security to prevent hackers from joining and ruining your fun, and rendering and effects in this game are positively accurate and remarkable. As far as I've seen, no glitches, no crashes, or shutdowns. This surely might be one of the best functioning games on Steam currently.
The terrain is very well made, and the concept is very easy to get used too. Tiers, parts, and the Tech Tree aid the player to advance into the leaderboards of this fun, thrilling game.
If I could say anything bad about this game, it would be the internet usage. Unless you are certain that you have plenty of internet to use without running out within the month, you're good to go - Otherwise, you can watch your internet slowly get wasted within a minute.
This game requires a lot of internet, and if you don't have the amount needed, think twice and reconsider.
I would reccomend this game to those of you who are familiar with basic controls and functioning, and those of you who have a smooth processor and video card. Unless you're looking to make your slow computer catch fire, then go ahead, nothing's stopping you!
Overall, it's a great game, especially if it's still in early access. If you expect more from these great creators, you'll be stunned to see what they can come up with.

Like lots of people say, Minecraft + World of Tanks. Don't let the blocky look fool you though, there are some pretty amazing things you can build (you will also see, and probably kill, really ugly ones too).  There are little to no restrictions on F2p people, compared to subs, you make less money and you get one less group slot...but believe me that doesn't take away from the fun. With 4 different types of weapons ( + one defensive weapon) and about 5-7 different ways of moving (wheels, tank tracks, hover blades, etc) you can build almost anything. They did, however, put a limit, each part adds cpu, and that increases with each level you gain. With each level and Tier (your vehicles current rank) you get more and more complex vehicles. They even give out free sub days quite often, with promo codes. The game is fun by yourself, but better with a group. Also, being an early access game there are very few bugs at all, any that happen are usually server problems, which they usually repay with a free sub code. I would rate this a healthy 8/10.
