O.k., I feel this game needs a two part review:
1) The game play. Some of THE BEST I've seen in gaming. Period. This is a game that requires skill, but in a different way than most. Anybody can build your most rudementary bot, but the best will come on top. It requires you to be great at building and understanding how the blocks work in tandem with each other, and how they will respond to dynamic destruction. Bery smooth, fast paced, bot-fueled action, you can't go wrong with this game.
2) It's Free to Play model. F2P games inherrently have some flaw in their system. Even Tf2, even LoL, every f2p game has something annnoying about it's system. This game does a pretty good job with it though. If anything, the only time I've been tempted into throwing down a fre dollars is in the later levels, as those can require quite a bit of grinding to get past. However, this game is NOT pay to win. It has many systems im place so no matter how much money you spend, you will be put against those who have just as good bots. So, for a free to play game, it doesn't screw you over massivly.
All in all, you should give it a go. Don't like the gameplay? Delete it and move on. But I can guarentee that most will enjoy this indie title.

Robocraft, if you couldn’t guess, is a game about building robots, using these robots to kill other robots and earning currency to build more elaborate and deadly robots so that you can kill other robots more effectively. Robots feature heavily in Robocraft.
Let’s start with a major downside, just to get it out of the way: Robocraft is essentially a pyramid scheme with pretty much every pay-to-win element you could imagine (apparently only recently) tacked on. Tired of getting blasted out of existence by players on the other side of the map? ‘Pay £5 and you can get access to all the high-level weaponry and start blasting too!’ That being said, it is completely free to play if you don’t mind slogging your way through the various combat tiers – swings and heavily armed, mechanised roundabouts, I guess.
Robocraft - 1
Not pictured: heavily armed roundabout.

Despite (or perhaps because of) its simple premise, Robocraft manages to be surprisingly addictive and encountering anyone particularly overpowered is, from my experience at least, relatively rare – they’re likely to get moved up to a higher combat ‘tier’ than you anyway and be matched with other, equally overpowered players. At the start, the game puts you in your spacegarage and provides you with a selection of building blocks (cubes, ramps, etc.), some wheels, some basic weaponry and that’s it – you’ve got all the tools to build a basic, and very flimsy, robot. As you earn currency and tech-points from competing in multiplayer matches, you can unlock more advanced weapons, wheels, jet engines, hoverpads and armoured blocks. Other gadgets you’ll gain access to include radar, radar jammers, shields and various other bits and pieces that allow you to tweak your robot to suit your style of gameplay. When sticking on weapons or wheels (or jet engines), yellow lines will pop up showing you the component’s movement arcs, and how much thrust, if any, it is capable of generating, etc. – this is a nice feature as it allows for some fine-tuning of your robot’s design – you can’t shoot through yourself, so it’s good to know whether or not a weapon turret will have it’s line-of-sight blocked by another part of your vehicle. The actual building of a vehicle is easy: select a block type from your inventory (or buy more from the Cube Depot), place it with a left click of the mouse, right click to remove the block you’re pointing at, and press R to rotate a block before placing it – just remember to stick a pilot’s seat on somewhere.* Build a tank, build a gunship, build a floating rail-gun-platform-thing, build a ridiculous cube coated in guns, whatever – if you can make it out of cubes and ramps, you can weaponise it, take it into combat and roll it off a cliff and sit helplessly while the enemy approaches. I’ve seen all shapes and sizes (said the actress to the bishop…) of death-machines, from lumbering panzer-esque tanks, to attempts at deathstar-style spheres to tiny 4 or 5 block creations armed with (hugely overpowered) rail-guns, to the inevitable 50ft tall penisbots.
*Yeah, a slight break in the game’s logic here; you would assume that you’re building a robot vehicle, but actually you’re building a vehicle for your robot to drive. I understand the point behind needing a ‘pilot’ block of some kind, but they could have done something less likely to make my OCD senses twitch.
Robocraft - 2
Pictured: The cubes, ramps, machine guns and swirly yellow lines that go into making a gunship.

Once you’ve built your mechanical (and potentially phallic) monstrosity the only thing left to do is head out to battle. Multiplayer battles involve roughly 20 robots (10 per team, at Tier 4 anyway; the numbers seem to decrease as you climb in ranking) placed at either end of the map. The objectives are simple: either capture the enemy base (called a CPU Core) by parking on top of it or kill everyone on the other team. As yet there are no other game-modes (apart from a seemingly pointless ‘practice mode’). What makes Robocraft unusual is that it’s a multiplayer game with no respawns – there is only violent, explosive death, or hilarious robotic maiming. It’s not unusual to find your entire team in various stages of disablement, with players left completely immobile or unable to control their movement properly or to have players left fully mobile but without any weapons. I sat in spectator mode halfway through one recent match and flicked through my damaged teammates’ perspectives: there was the guy with the helicopter-thing who was unable to do anything but fly, very rapidly, in a tight clockwise circle; the guy with the intimidating looking tank had rolled off a cliff and was stuck upside down behind a rock – relatively safe, but useless; one guy had taken a couple of heavy hits from a plasma launcher, and his vehicle was reduced to nothing more than the pilot’s seat and two armoured blocks – he sat patiently (or whatever the robot equivalent is) and awaited his demise. Our one mobile player had lost all his weapons and half his vehicle in a previous engagement and was creeping toward the enemy base in a vain attempt to capture it. As he did so, a heavily armed enemy robot appeared over the brow of a hill, ‘Run!’ I screamed impotently at my screen, the enemy took aim, fired, and I was immediately transferred back to the perspective of my other teammate and his upside down tank; shortly afterwards I was transferred again, this time back to the guy who had nothing but a pilot’s chair and then again to the crazy spinning helicopter guy as my team, my band of limping gazelles, my parapalegic robo-brethren, were picked off one by one.
Seeing bits get ripped out of your robot is actually surprisingly satisfying; it makes you feel battle-hardened – arriving at the enemy base with a missing wheel or (as is possible) a missing 90-odd-percent of your vehicle sends a silent signal to your teammates, its the closest equivalent to a really cool scar that I’ve come across in a game. If you’ve lost your weapons, but can still move then you’re not quite out of the game; you can sneak over to the enemy base and help capture it. For all the fact that Robocraft is a ridiculous game, I can’t help but find this unusual element of realism refreshing; it’s pretty rare in an era of “crouch to regen’ health” multiplayer games to have to think about how to survive in an extremely weakened state.
The graphics do the job, but it’s clear where the developers have left bits out because its only in Early Access. As I mentioned earlier, the game’s physics can also be a little unpredictable, leading to fair amount of flipping onto one side and potentially leaving you stranded if you didn’t include a self-righting mechanism; this problem is particularly noticeable for hovering vehicles. Whilst you won’t take damage from hitting the scenery, or even falling off a cliff (which will happen a lot), air vehicles seem to have an annoying habit of flipping upside down if you go down a ramp too steeply.* Whilst this won’t kill or even damage you, it will reverse your movement controls and potentially cut off the line-of-sight of your weapons, leaving you a bit useless. It can at least, usually, be solved by finding another ramp to fall off.
Other than some balancing issues (plasma launchers and rail-guns are hugely overpowered in comparison to machine guns, for example), polishing and tweaking, Robocraft is very playable, with a learning curve that depends almost entirely on how badly you design your robot. In fact, its currently so popular that the developers had to implement a queuing system to prevent the servers from being overwhelmed – thankfully, it clears pretty rapidly.

Seeing bits get ripped out of your robot is actually surprisingly satisfying; it makes you feel battle-hardened – arriving at the enemy base with a missing wheel or (as is possible) a missing 90-odd-percent of your vehicle sends a silent signal to your teammates, its the closest equivalent to a really cool scar that I’ve come across in a game. If you’ve lost your weapons, but can still move then you’re not quite out of the game; you can sneak over to the enemy base and help capture it. For all the fact that Robocraft is a ridiculous game, I can’t help but find this unusual element of realism refreshing; it’s pretty rare in an era of “crouch to regen’ health” multiplayer games to have to think about how to survive in an extremely weakened state.
The graphics do the job, but it’s clear where the developers have left bits out because its only in Early Access. As I mentioned earlier, the game’s physics can also be a little unpredictable, leading to fair amount of flipping onto one side and potentially leaving you stranded if you didn’t include a self-righting mechanism; this problem is particularly noticeable for hovering vehicles. Whilst you won’t take damage from hitting the scenery, or even falling off a cliff (which will happen a lot), air vehicles seem to have an annoying habit of flipping upside down if you go down a ramp too steeply.* Whilst this won’t kill or even damage you, it will reverse your movement controls and potentially cut off the line-of-sight of your weapons, leaving you a bit useless. It can at least, usually, be solved by finding another ramp to fall off.
Other than some balancing issues (plasma launchers and rail-guns are hugely overpowered in comparison to machine guns, for example), polishing and tweaking, Robocraft is very playable, with a learning curve that depends almost entirely on how badly you design your robot. In fact, its currently so popular that the developers had to implement a queuing system to prevent the servers from being overwhelmed – thankfully, it clears pretty rapidly.

Devoid of context, Portal 2 is a narrative-and-exploration-driven physics puzzle game played like an FPS.  You shoot portals to try to find your way out of various locked rooms or death traps, and, as the slogan suggests, encourages you to Think With Portals.  Purely as a puzzle game, it's a little on the short side, but it adds to this with exploration.
Sadly, compared to the low-budget original, Valve got it into their heads that we really wanted something visually impressive in this game.  While good for the exploration angle, it also means that they spent so much time and effort on giant caverns that it takes away from the actual ability to use portals to solve puzzles.  You spend about half the game walking along catwalks just trundling forward looking for the single tiny spot that might accept a portal so you can move on.  They're lifeless (but pretty) set pieces, rather than jungle gyms that encourage trials of physics puzzles and the creative application of the wonderful little tool you're here to enjoy.
There's more in this game than the original, but it still feels like you spend more of the time more constrained.  The physics puzzles really come into their own when they give you a huge, open field, plenty of deadly obastacles or bottomless pits, and just tell you to go for it, with hundreds of wrong moves, and potentially even having more than one solution than to have a hallway where there's exactly two places where portals can be placed.
Late in the game, however, there's a chance to play with a white gel that you can actually "carry with you" from one puzzle room to the next, expanding where you can portal, and actually making it feel like you've broken out of those restraints... too bad it's so late in the game...
Co-op is also good fun, if potentially a little more frustrating (especially depending upon how you get along with your partner), and also a bit short.  With just vanilla, it's possible to blow through it in just a couple hours, and replaying puzzles is of dubious additional entertainment value.
Fortunately, there's modding encouraged in this game.  There might be some things you really enjoy, but the typical problem of 90% of what's in the Steam workshop being worthless tends to apply, as well.

It's an already very good polished Early-Access game with active developers and few bugs. It has loads of content when it comes to building your robots, not so much when it comes to playing (there are currently two game modes and five maps). The F2P model is very fair: You can pay for "Premium" which increases your rewards so you can progress faster, but gives you no advantages during the game whatsoever. Also you get a bonus for each "Premium" member playing with you, which makes you like them (in some other games premium-members are hated). You can also buy cosmetic items and pre-build robots with real money, nothing you really need in order to enjoy the game.
It's good and free. Go get it!
The trailer gives you a good look at what you can expect from Robocraft. It has basically two parts:
. The content here is already pretty decent for an Alpha state game, you can choose between different types of movement (e.g. wheels, legs, skis, caterpillar tracks, wings and thrusters) all of which are combinable and have their own purpose and special application area (besides skis maybe).
In addition, there are currently
: SMG (basic machine gun, high DPS); Plasma launcher (bombarding gun with high splash damage and medium recharge time); Rail cannon (sniper riffle, very high damage and long recharge time); Nano disrupter (healing gun which can also do damage, close range). Contrary to means of movement you can also attach one type of weapon to one robot. Additionaly, to those 4 weapon classes there are so-called Tesla Blades which can be independently attached to a robot and deal damage to enemies when touching them.
There are also several extensions one can use to make his robot more competative (e.g. Scanners, Radar Jammers and Radar Receivers).
. Robots are divided into 10 different Tiers depending on their strength and fire power. When playing the classic Team-Deathmatch mode one will only play with robots about your rating (neglecting Platoons). These games are usually 10-vs-10 and in order to win your team has to either wipe out the enemy team or capture their home base. Destroying enemy bots works a little bit different in Robocraft than it does in a lot of other games. You do not have a life bar with HP that reduce when you get hit until they get to 0 and you are dead. It's more like every individual part of your robot has its own health bar, you only destroy what you actually hit. This gives direct combat a strategic element, you can decide to focus on your enemies guns to make him helpless, or demobalize him. Parts of a robot which are no longer connected to the cockpit are automatically destroyed, so you should try to target important weak points. A robot is completly destroyed when it has lost the block that his cockpit was attached to. This allows for fast kills (sometimes even one-hits) if the cockpit is exposed.
The other game mode is called boss-battle. It features an assymetric fight were a small group of higher tier robots (1-4 players) fight against a huge group of lower tier robots (about 15).
. Honestly, the developers are anxious to allow a good gaming experience even in its current Alpha state. As for bugs the game is already very polished. There are some issues with people not being able to start the game at all because of their antivirus software not liking Roboshield (a third party anti-cheat software they use), but for most of them exist fixes in the game forums. Also, sometimes their servers are overloaded and you will have to wait in order to get into a game.
However, the developers are very motivated to resolve issues. E.g. there was a big server problem before Christmas and the developers spend their holydays fixing it. They also give away free days of Premium as an apology.
Robocraft is, with its current policy
. You can pay for "Premium". Being a premium member pretty much doubles everything you get, so it helps progressing very fast through the tiers. However, for each Premium-member in a game, all other also get 5% bonus from their rewards. This means that Premium members have no advantage in a game whatsoever, and also that Premium members are liked and welcome. Apart from Premium, one can also spend real money to buy cosmetic items (masks or badges with flags on them) and pre-build robots (-> nothing one does actually give you an advantage). In some other F2P games you can pay real money for items like "15% more damage" or other unfair advantages and are therefore condemned by other players. The system Robocraft uses is very appealing and should be industry standard.

Online battles are capture the flag style with no respawns, and matchmaking is split into tiers depending on how good the parts for your robot are. Creating your robot is very easy (like a mix between Minecraft's creative mode and Halo's forge), and finding a match takes no time at all. Handles pretty well on lower end computers. Overall, very fun. Highly recommended.

Portal 2 was easily one of the most enjoyable games I have ever played.
Pros:
+The gameplay is smooth and fast, I had no lag issues whatsoever. Also, the controls are very basic.
+The music played can change your mood in an instant. Some of it can be very creepy and adds a lot of suspense to the game.
+The graphics are beautiful and really enhance the quality of the game.
+The puzzles are challenging and require thought and attention to detail, though there were a couple puzzles that I actually had to look up how to solve because of their difficulty.
+The storyline of the game is very immersive and really keeps you on your toes, especially after a couple of plot twists.
+The characters are funny and lovable, and though there aren't many, you get to know each and every one. (My personal favorite is Rick the Adventure Sphere, you'll meet him at the end...he's hilarious)
+The level creator/editor is easy to use, very innovative, and is open to everyone. Also, once you've created a chamber you can submit it to the public for others to try.
+Building on my last point, you can play test chambers built by others and there are always new ones being submitted, causing the game to continually have new, playable content added.
+The co-op is easy to find and use, even for beginners. There is no complicated server set up or anything of that sort.
+There is a challenge mode available for those of you willing to try. I haven't attempted it yet, so I cannot give you my opinion on it.
+The ending of the game is easily one of the best endings in game history.
Cons:
-When choosing a chapter to start at (after you finish the game), there is no insight to what goes on in that chapter or where you start at. This is especially difficult when you are trying to replay a certain point.
-When you are loading a save, you don't really know where you were/start at. It just says the chapter # and name and the date/time you saved. I have so many different saves, so this confused me quite a bit.
Overall rating: 9.5/10, exceptional
Note:The plot can be kind of difficult to grasp at first if you didn't play the first game, but I feel you get enough of a backround to understand what is going on. I would recommend playing the first game before beginning this one, unlike me.

Robocraft used to be my favorite free game on Steam. Creative, fun gameplay.
Now though, if you want to play Robocraft, you have to install a piece of third party software called "EasyAntiCheat" to play. EAC is flagged by most antivirus software, and for good reason - it is blatantly spyware that compromises users' privacy.
I am deeply disappointed at the developers' decision to carelessly disregard their users' privacy, and will not play Robocraft or any other FreeJam game again until I am allowed to play without downloading intrusive third party software. Sadly, I cannot recommend this otherwise excellent game to anyone who cares about their privacy.

TL;DR: Game is fun. Game is balanced. New content all the time. Its like Lego + World of Tanks except cool.
To summarize Robocraft: there are 2-3 main aspects of the gameplay in Robocraft.
Firstly, you need to build your vehicle(s) which is done in a 3D grid system with all main chassis components being 1x1x1 cubes and then attaching necessary weapons and movement devices.
Secondly, you play! You get match made into a match against players of roughly the same tech level as you, with no compensation for player skill. Controls are standard for a driving game, and there is a variety of asymmetric maps with different sets of terrain that favor different vehicles and different tactics. The map is chosen randomly, your best chance is to design something that works well on ALL maps as opposed to one in particuilar.
Third and finally, you unlock and purchase (using F2P or P2P currency) more parts. Due to the need to unlock new parts and upgrade your bot to proceed to unlock more new parts, it can be prohibitively expensive to get everything, and you may need to focus, and after a while you'll find it takes a while to get to the next tier. Although this isn't necessarily part of the gameplay it's nonetheless a very big part of the game, and it directly dictates how you play the game. After all, you can't make an airplane or a walker if you don't get the parts.
Reasons Why It Works
Large variety of parts and a large number of effective ways to build your robot ensure lots of variety, and attentive developers as well as the release of new content keeps the metagame flowing so it never gets too stale.
Gameplay tiers are defined by robot ranking. Each component directly adds its robot ranking to your total. Robot ranking, the maximum robot ranking per tier, and in general the health pool of each block and damage of each weapon increase exponentially with each tier.
What this means is that within a tier, you're allowed to use a fairly large amount of  components from within that tier, but only a few from higher tiers, otherwise you end up pushing yourself into the next tier. Similarly you can use a very large amount of components from lower tiers, although this is often undesirable. This prevents you from getting completely smashed by someone who has better components than you.
Problems
There are a few balance sweet spots and plenty of times you will go up against robots that are UNFAIRLY strong, and in some cases will have no real way to deal with them, other than to radically change your robot, and sometimes you will be forced to conform in order to win.
Nerfs are sometimes given out rather heavy handedly which has overreaching effects due to the variety of ways components can be used. Ultimately these nerfs are for the good of the game but sometimes that means cool, unique and creative bot designs become completely unviable because a more competitie use of the parts required them to be nerfed. For instance headlights, as seemingly harmless and functionally cosmetic component had a significant limit put on the number you can use because their overuse was detrimental to players on older computers and this was being used for a competitive advantage.
The difficulty and time involved in creating a functioning, viable and fun robot is too much for some people, which results in them simply copying the most common design, leading to games being flooded with 3 types of bots when there are theoretically ENDLESS bots that can be made, and I fear as the community gets larger this "follow the leader" approach will only become more and more pronounced.
Ultimately though I find the game very fun inspite of all that as to me, it's simply an excuse to vary my bot design and strive harder to craft something that can break the meta.

This game is a masterpiece. It's story and puzzles are out of the park. If you only buy one game, ever, it should be this.
Story:
This game takes place in a run-down version of the aperture labs seen in the first game. But, unlike it's predecessor, you are helped along by a sphere named wheatley. As you try to escape, you end up waking GLaDoS, the antagonist from the first game, and you are thrown back into full testing. It's now up to you alone to escape.
This game's story is very deep and intricate, with nods to the Borealis in some easter eggs, and even the direct mention of black mesa. It has characters with immensly deep and suprisingly dark backstories, and is a game I contemplate still to this day.
Puzzles:
The puzzles are much more difficult than the first game, and less hand-holding than before. It introduces some nice new testing elements, as well as makes new use of the old ones. The puzzles never end, either, thanks to the "Perpetual Testing Initiative" (Level editor + Custom levels on the workshop). The co-op puzzles double the fun, and difficulty, resulting in a massive need for teamwork.
Graphics:
The game is suprisingly beautiful, for running on a game engine from the turn of the century. It's lighting and shadows outmatch other popular games, and they don't kill your system. My computer can run this game at medium settings, and my graphics card is an Intel Integrated Graphics HD 4000 (Planning on building a PC soon, using a laptop). It's still a good looking game, and will probably hold up for a while.
Audio:
This game's music is always there, whether ambiently in the background, or boosting your pulse as you run through broken halls, death on your tail. The music is actually availiable free on their website, 3 full albums with all of the music included in the game.
Multiplayer:
This game's co-op is brilliant, with customization of the two robots "Atlas" and "P-Body". Using the ping system to coordinate, you don't even need a microphone to communicate with someone random you meet. It even has a bit of story to the game, with the last level group revealing a large secret. The custom levels recentley updated to allow multiplayer, so this dosen't end for a while.
In conclusion, the game has a ton of nice features, content, and is really worth the $20 USD, if you are a first time player. I'm planning on getting a few more copies when it goes on sale to hand out to my friends that don't already own it, and play through with them. I love this game, and it's what got me back into PC gaming.

Portal 2 is inovative, refreshing, challenging and downright brilliant. It's a blast to play, and between the puzzles that did my head in so much I needed to restart to get a new viewpoint and the awesome feeling of owning a coop test chamber, there is no other game I could recommend more. If you don't have Portal 2, it's a must have for any gamer. The clever gameplay and the witty characters will keep you entertained, and once you've completed the single player story, jump onto the steam workshop and download more maps others have made! What's more, Portal 2's coop system is amazing, allowing communication through the game in an instant with clear commands on keys for those without a mic to talk to their partner on the other end of the net. I rate Portal 2 a (9/10).
(I know I said there's no other game I would recommend more highly, but that was for this genre).
Thanks valve! Another great game.
P.S. If anyone is unsure of whether to buy Portal 2 or not, I recommend downloading the free "Portal: The First Slice" game from the store.

This game is a masterpiece. It's story and puzzles are out of the park. If you only buy one game, ever, it should be this.
Story:
This game takes place in a run-down version of the aperture labs seen in the first game. But, unlike it's predecessor, you are helped along by a sphere named wheatley. As you try to escape, you end up waking GLaDoS, the antagonist from the first game, and you are thrown back into full testing. It's now up to you alone to escape.
This game's story is very deep and intricate, with nods to the Borealis in some easter eggs, and even the direct mention of black mesa. It has characters with immensly deep and suprisingly dark backstories, and is a game I contemplate still to this day.
Puzzles:
The puzzles are much more difficult than the first game, and less hand-holding than before. It introduces some nice new testing elements, as well as makes new use of the old ones. The puzzles never end, either, thanks to the "Perpetual Testing Initiative" (Level editor + Custom levels on the workshop). The co-op puzzles double the fun, and difficulty, resulting in a massive need for teamwork.
Graphics:
The game is suprisingly beautiful, for running on a game engine from the turn of the century. It's lighting and shadows outmatch other popular games, and they don't kill your system. My computer can run this game at medium settings, and my graphics card is an Intel Integrated Graphics HD 4000 (Planning on building a PC soon, using a laptop). It's still a good looking game, and will probably hold up for a while.
Audio:
This game's music is always there, whether ambiently in the background, or boosting your pulse as you run through broken halls, death on your tail. The music is actually availiable free on their website, 3 full albums with all of the music included in the game.
Multiplayer:
This game's co-op is brilliant, with customization of the two robots "Atlas" and "P-Body". Using the ping system to coordinate, you don't even need a microphone to communicate with someone random you meet. It even has a bit of story to the game, with the last level group revealing a large secret. The custom levels recentley updated to allow multiplayer, so this dosen't end for a while.
In conclusion, the game has a ton of nice features, content, and is really worth the $20 USD, if you are a first time player. I'm planning on getting a few more copies when it goes on sale to hand out to my friends that don't already own it, and play through with them. I love this game, and it's what got me back into gaming.

Portal 2 takes the concepts from one and expands upon them tremendously. The original was more of an extended demo, which could be completed in a single sitting. The second one, while still short, is much more dense with content. The story and world are more fully realized, the puzzles perfectly build off of one another, and the humor comes back in full force. The new mechanics feel like a necessary evolution, and they all work rather well. In truth, my only complaints regarding this game are the engine and the eleventh hour pacing. The engine is starting to show its age in that loading screens are entirely too frequent, and it really breaks up the gameplay. As for the so-called pacing at the eleventh hour, I'm not referring to story. The story pacing stays on point throughout. However, the last few puzzles introduce 2 new mechanics that I feel got rushed in and out of the game. You only use them in a handful of puzzles before being whisked away to the finale. Furthermore, I don't feel as if there was any puzzle that took every mechanic I had learned so far and sythesized it into the perfect puzzle to test myself in. Oh well. The game is still VERY fun, and I think it's an experience that everyone needs to have.

Loved building LEGO vehicles in your childhood (and probably love it still)? Ever wished you could actually fly/drive/crawl/hover/slide/float your built vehicle into battle against other vehicles built by other players? Enjoy theorycrafting and building the best next thing? Or, maybe, just want to dive head-first into the battle without thinking of stats/consequences? Love showing off your lovely/hilarious/wtf designs? If you have answered yes to at least one of the above questions, then you should definitely give Robocraft a spin! Heck, even if you don't enjoy anything of the above, try it still, it's free, who knows, maybe you'll find something in it for you!
Robocraft is a blend of LEGO vs Space Engineers vs World of Tanks vs War Thunder, taking best of each and none (or few) of the worse. You craft your robot out of lego-style building blocks and then head off to battle other people's robots in a capture-the-base-or-kill-'em-all style of battle. This game features a selection of various weapons, propulsion, armoring items, and you will definitely find your own combination in there, whether you enjoy bombing others from high in the sky, sniping from afar, supporting and repairing your teammates, or just melting faces in an all-out close quarters brawl.
Would I recommend Robocraft? Hell, yeah! See you in game!

Original Jan 2015 review
So Robocraft is fairly unique in that its a multiplayer PVP FPS match style game, but it uses "robots" which are 100% fully designed, created, piloted by you. You start with meager resources and a BUNCH of free, low level building "blocks" - things like different shaped armor pieces, guns, turrets, rockets, wheels, etc.  You upgrade their strengths and abilities through a tech tree, which spends a different currency than actually buying blocks.  This is the tiering system - you can only buy the tier youre in (and under), and SOME of the next tier - As you win battles and gain levels and build bigger ships, your tier increases, thus progressing you up the hierarchy - bigger bots, better opponents, better rewards.  The game seems to be full -featured and not at all buggy - i believe i only crashed once.
The crafting and creativity component itself is what makes the game.  Experimenting with building fast light gunner buggies, massive plasma launching tanks, Hovering snipers?, what about high flying drone bomber? The limit is your imagination... and of course your currency.  :)
30 hours into Robocraft over about a week, I found myself really enjoying the game!  I have to admit that the grind to get the next tier tech points got a bit tiresome, but i've never played an RPG / Progressive game without the Grind, so no points deducted, just a note - you will grind.  That said, you need the currency the grind gives you anyway to experiment and upgrade all those blocks!
Now it must be noted that this is a F2P game, which usually means there are in-game purchases available, and of course there are.  I have not invested money into the game yet - something i would typically do after 50-60 hours of game play and really know what im getting for my money - and also support the devs.  I see myself doing that very soon.

I understand this game is still in beta, but it still has a long way to go, yet. The gameplay idea is brilliant, I can see the potential in it, but it is too pay-to-win-esc if that makes sense. Instead of fighting your way to the top, like players like me, who are trying to save money, the game is kind of a losing battle after Teir #1. A lot of other players either buy their way to the top, buy better weapons only, and win their way to the top, or spend all of their upgrade points on weapons and, again, win their way to the top. And players like me, who play fair-and-square, have to muck around in the lower levels, because the pay-to-win jerks make sure we don't upgrade as fast as them. And in half of all the matches I HAVE played, half of the enemy team puppy-guards their capture point, then send the other half to smash down what little resistance the opposing team has. The Build-Your-Own-Robot idea is a good one, don't get me wrong, but another thing people like to do is just buy the most powerful armor blocks, turn their robot into a pyramid-shaped tank, mount as many guns as possible, and charge in using the artillary guns, which are one-hit-kills. That pretty much sums up every Robocraft battle that has ever happened and probably ever WILL happen. This game has potential, but that's in the far future. For now, I give it 4/10. If you like wasting money on crushing hard-workers, or you like to get extremely furious at  pay-to-win jerks, then this game is DEFINITELY for you.

I've played right through to Tier 10. I've experienced the ups and the downs this game has to offer and know enough about the game to make a solid assessment. While it was founded on great potential, Robocraft has really has lost a lot of it's original charm.
The developers have gone back on things they said they'd never do, taken directions that detract from the games unique style that set it apart and added/changed some content that is questionable to the relevance of the game. I stopped playing a few updates ago but more recent updates have included earth, as they said they wouldn't do. They have added a power system, as they said they wouldn't do. They have taken away specific class roles allowing the attachment of multiple weapons. They have removed the pilot seat and unfortunately in my opinion, taken away a lot of the elements of this game which really made you think about the design of robots and how you would protect vital sections.
Not to say it's all bad, the game is still a solid platform. It is very much geared to either a very young audience and caters mainly to those who shout the loudest. I can't say this game excites me with prospects for it's future as I see no clearly defined direction. Much of what they say may or may not be taken for turth.
So relucantly I have changed my opinion, there are better games out there which offer more challenge and stability than robocraft currently does. I do not recommend this as a worthwhile game to invest in.

Were you one of those kids who, instead of kids who, now-a-days. play with iPhones, actually played with LEGOS, made ships and picture waging war against other ships? Well then this is the game for you!
The game, due to recent changes, is now pretty balanced, most considered it to be a P2W game, now it's pretty balanced, each major update they release codes with free premium, you, being one, gives 5% extra money to other players, so picture 20 people with premium (About both full teams with premium) gives, players without premium 100% bonus, and with premium 200%! All prices for GC, currency in which, as you may have guessed, acquire with real money, which can allow you to buy robots from the shop, cosmetics (Aka Flags, Dev badges, pieces of masks to make a full one, trails and name tags all for your bot) or even cubes and hardware you'd have to waste RP on.
You start off with 3 garages, one with a fully built bot for you to use, modify, and another for you to create from scratch, be creative! As you grow, from Tier 1 up to Tier 10, the games grow more strategic and intense, instead of going solo with over 20 guns on your bot and wrecking people, now you must stick to your teammates and medics to survive, going in rambo into 5 or more enemies will be your doom.
As you battle per tier, you gain Tech points, in which you use to unlock new blocks/hardware/movement class parts for your bot, then of course, you buy them off the Cube Depot, You tier up your bot by replacing it's old T1 blocks into T2, hardware as well, as you grow in Tier, so does your hardware, your guns an dmeans of transport, meaning you'll have to reshape your own creation, make it bigger, more intimidating!
Physics have been heavily modified in previous patches and complains about it seemed to vanish, no longer do you have one wheel and roll in mid air, nor do fliers still fly without half it's wings! Strategy is simple and easy to follow, stay with allies to create a much bigger force, and recently with Boss Battles, staying together is the key to destroying the boss, so is the Boss or Bosses strategy, remain together, work as a team for both your survival.
The community is mixed, you can both find friendly, awesome people to platoon with, helpful who gives you advise or helps you with your bot when you got a question or two, or more childish new players who spam random stuff or curse like hell and don't give a crap, of course you can relly on Mods to keep the chat clean!

This game was made well. It knows what it is and sticks to that, It doesnt pretend to be a big fancy action game and it plays on that. This games fun comes from the crazy customisation of your tanks or ships or just about whatever you want to build.
The combat isnt amazing its mostly just holding left click but that hilarious breakdowns of opponents robots can be worth 10 mins of driving around. The guns on your robots are made to destroy and that they do well. With a few bullets you can knock off opponents wheels, guns, satelites leaving them defenceless, One shot to their character or avatar inside the robot and they are out for good.
Now the customisation follows various skill or unlock trees. As you play you will get amounts of the two currencys which are used to buy the parts and unlock the parts. You can follow a few different paths on the unlock trees the three main paths/branchs being
1- Movement - Focuses on new movement items such as jets, hot air ballons and wheels
2- Armour - Focuses on new  blocks to craft your robots out of.
3- Weapons - Focuses on new tiers of the same gun or new guns all together.
The fourth minor tree is based around tech such as satelites and an item that un-flips your robot.
One issue is that a lot of these things will take some time to reach along the skill trees so be prepared for some grinding.
Overall if your looking for some free to play fun with some friends  I definitely recommend this game.

Robocraft
This game was made well. It knows what it is and sticks to that, It doesnt pretend to be a big fancy action game and it plays on that. This games fun comes from the crazy customisation of your tanks or ships or just about whatever you want to build.
The combat isnt amazing its mostly just holding left click but that hilarious breakdowns of opponents robots can be worth 10 mins of driving around. The guns on your robots are made to destroy and that they do well. With a few bullets you can knock off opponents wheels, guns, satelites leaving them defenceless, One shot to their character or avatar inside the robot and they are out for good.
Now the customisation follows various skill or unlock trees. As you play you will get amounts of the two currencys which are used to buy the parts and unlock the parts. You can follow a few different paths on the unlock trees the three main paths/branchs being
1- Movement - Focuses on new movement items such as jets, hot air ballons and wheels
2- Armour - Focuses on new  blocks to craft your robots out of.
3- Weapons - Focuses on new tiers of the same gun or new guns all together.
The fourth minor tree is based around tech such as satelites and an item that un-flips your robot.
One issue is that a lot of these things will take some time to reach along the skill trees so be prepared for some grinding.
Overall if your looking for some free to play fun with some friends  I definitely recommend this game.

Not too sure what to write here so heres a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

Robocraft is an excelent game that mixed the sandbox, make-your-own elements of games like Maxis's Spore and Mojang's Minecraft with fast paced, third person shooter elements and Tank game elements, like World of Tanks. With five weapon classes (Subatomic Machinegunner, Plasma Bomber, Rail Sniper, Anti-Air Gunner and Nanotech Medic), seven vehicle classes (Cruiser, Plane, Hover, Helicopter, Sled, Mech and Walker), and 5 gamemodes (Singleplayer, Team Deathmatch, The Pit, Battle Arena and Challenge Mode), gameplay is never bland. Go solo or lead a platoon of up to 3 more players into battle against an oposing team.
Can't think of a good robot to build? Want to pimp your ride even better? Want to support the developers? Got some spare cash on hand? No problem! In addition to the Robot Points earned from regular play, you also can buy the alternative, Galaxy Cash. This special Galaxy Cash (or GC) can be used for a variety of things. You can choose from a variety of premade vehicles in the game's community-driven Robo-Store, as well as a large number of holoflags,vapor trails, a name plate, masks, headlamps, and windshield glass. GC is also used as an alternative to Robot Points (RP for short).
Still not satisfied with simple currency? Instead of GC, invest some money in a few days of Premium! Premium accounts not only have their RP winnings after each match doubled, but also multiply the winnings of every user that was in your match by an additional 5% - this stacks with multiple premium players, too! On top of that, premium also give you access to a variety of additional colors to paint your robot - more than the normal White, Grey, Baby Blue and Orange.
Of course, if you don't have any spare bucks, that's perfectly fine as well. The game is 101% playable without spending a single penny. Not only can you easily climb the Robot Ranking ranks, but you can still make som wicked looking robots with what you're given for free. Not to mention, Freejam sometimes drops special codes that do stuff like give you free premium, GC or cubes for free!
What are you waiting for? Clear up some C drive space and install this early access masterpiece!

In the end of the day, after all of my struggles with life, I take a good look at the moon, and I remember this game.
I remember all of the puzzles, all of the dialogue, all of the sounds, and the characters.
I remember completing this game during a very difficult time of my life, where I didn't understand a disease that was affecting my loved one, and after reading upon some more of the lore, I somehow understood it, and I felt less lost with life.
I thought I lost myself, I thoguht I lost the only person that mattered to me, but after playing this simple game, I felt alive once again, and I knew that I need to fight another day, not just for myself, but for the people that fought for me.
It may sound REALLY cheesy, but this game saved me. It made me laugh, cry, get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off on some puzzles that I couldn't solve, and then happy again after I solved it.

Try it, if money is an issue, get it on sale. Buy the two pack and give this to a friend you know is struggling with life, it will make them happy, just like this game did to me.

Robocraft is a multiplayer shooting game, wherein the main draw is that you can build your robot basically however you like, within limitations. You start off with basic weapons and cubes to build with (it's nothing too complicated. Think legos, with automatic wiring), and go about shooting other people's robots with your lasers. The game is won when either all enemies have been killed (there's no respawn, as of the time I played), or the base is captured.
It's alright. If I had to pay for the game, I maaaay have been less likely to recommend it. Is it worth your time? If it sounds interesting in the least, then yea. Give it a try. As for long term staying power...it could use a little work. Balance, and the buying of new parts, was a little confusing to me.  And, it can be a little frustrating being shot apart quickly. It's a game that requires a sense of cover and tactics to stay alive.
But who can be mad about it when you see some of the silly creations? Birgirpall has a video on it, and I think one of my favorites was a LOL car. It was shaped with LOL, and after debilitating an enemy to the point it couldn't move or shoot, he sorta rolled in front of it a little for some fun. I really don't think I could be mad if I saw that lit up LOL taunting me, it's just too silly.
In short, I live it a duplex, and Robocraft is a good game.

The game itself is great though. You can do the whole game from tier 1 to 10 without IAP. You can build a flying♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥with tank treads, or a hovering♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or build a whole body with a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥for a gun, or just make a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥shape on top of your vehicle. The possibilites are endless, however in endgame you have to use intelligent designs, which really limits how well you can craft the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
The leveling of levels is the usual grind. Get kills to get money and levels, get newer weapons to fight harder enemies, etc. You get more "CPU" to add more stuff the more levels you have. The interesting part to me is there is a separate Tier system that is based on the value of your craft, so you can have a piece of crap on wheels with a tier 5 gun and fight noobs and hope you dont get hit, or you can be a noob in a mega tank thing with crappy guns and be in the same tier as the former. Overall its very well balanced, except for wheels which seem to give you an unusually high amount of tier rating for what they return.
You can make your armor out of shields, which recharge after taking hits, or just raw blocks, which dont recharge but cost less CPU. You can get repaired by medics, sniped by railguns, bombed by planes, and rammed by♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥with plasma blades on them.
By far the coolest aspect is that your vehicle changes how it functions as you fight, because blocks get blasted off of your craft. You might lose a wheel or 5 and barely be able to move. You might get all your guns blasted off. You might end up as just a chair strapped to a rocket thruster. How you build your craft to deal with these things is extremely important, as important as not sucking.

Saying the game is pay-to-win is a copout. The big 'grind' in this game is getting to new tiers, but you get to new tiers by playing the game! You don't have to complete some mundane quests or anything like that, it's all playing the game which is already really fun. So calling it a grind at all doesn't do it any justice.
Nothing you buy with money can't be earned, aside from cosmetic items that have no stat bonuses (the armor on the pieces is a fraction of a T1 Armor block). There are purchaseable pre-built ships that, any player with half a brain would realize those don't affect people until tier 10, which by then you could have earned the necessary pieces to build these crafts yourself. It's not like the devs buffed them so people were forced to buy them, they are made with pieces that EVERYONE can unlock.
No doubt in my mind that the game is good, despite the occasional little bug and sometimes the server going down unexpectadly, but it's in Alpha and already feels very complete. I wouldn't say there's much of a balance issue, you can play each vehicle type a different way to take advantage of enemy vehicles, and vice versa. It's all about strategy and making sure you know what you're doing.
All-in-all. Anyone with a measely couple of hours played saying it's pay to win, doesn't really know what the game is like.

Building upon the greatness of the first game, Portal 2 is a great adventure that will challenge you even more than before. It starts off slowly, re-familiarising you with the mechanics of the first game amongst the ruins of the Aperture Science facility, going through test chambers you played in the first game (albeit, a lot more dilapidated now). But soon, the game changes once again and you have to face more challenging test chambers, with a little help (but not much) from the core that woke you up and wants to help you escape, Wheatley (voiced by the brilliant Stephen Merchant). About halfway through though, the game changes entirely, widening the scope of everything entirely. You have to get to grips with some totally new mechanics, and you learn a lot more about the history of Aperture and GLaDOS along the way. CAUTION: ADDICTIVE GAME
Robocraft is good. No, I'll say more: it's super good. To me, it's a combo of killer features.
It's a challenge to your engineering skills. Before going into battle, you'll need to construct your war machine yourself. Make it efficient and reliable, or your end will be swift and merciless. Run tests. Try different variants. Look for balance. Play with center of mass and other physical characteristics. Find a way to place a lot of firepower on a limited space. Devise sturdy armor. Whatever.
It's a challenge to your tactical skills. You can choose the role and way of playing that fits you most of all - or create your own. Rush and assault. Go tanky. Follow and heal. Sneak and snipe. Fly and bomb. Go under the radar and ambush. Use the terrain for your benefit, to find escape routes or to attack the enemy from direction they do not expect to be threatening. Distract the opponents so that they have to split their forces.
It's a challenge to your superhero skills. The game offers a wide and rich selection of stupid players who make one-shot constructions, go for the middle of the map to get shot from every possible direction, run into the whole enemy force alone, or find other ways to get themselves killed in the first 30 seconds of a battle. Then it's time for you to courageously resist half a dozen of hardly scratched opponents.
It's a challenge to your testing skills. This is an alpha version at the moment of writing, so it contains an amount of bugs. Hunt the bugs and report them to make the game better. You shouldn't be scared off, though: the game is basically stable, and its general quality is better than that of some post-release games I dealt with. It also gives you that special feeling of involvement: you're right into the development process, new major updates arrive every month or so, the developers communicate with their playerbase in a most active manner.
Last but not least, it's not only free to play but also free to win. Donations are accepted, but they only help you to progress faster. In a battle, you'll find no difference between a paying and a not paying player.

This is a very interesting game i've yet to see any other like it. You can make a robot any shape you want limited only by the blocks you use, which you can buy from the ingame store. Currency is earned by doing damage to other players robots. Right now the main gamemode is capture the enemy base. Each battle only can last up to 5 minutes. You got to stand on the enemy point until you own the base then you win, or if you destroy all enemy players you also win. There'd 4 type's of guns, Machine Guns, Cannons, Railguns, and Nanotech Beams which heal allied players. Machine guns are 100% accurate if you fire one shot at a time, fire faster the more you have on your robot. Cannons do massive damage, have a quick reload time, and really good at close or long range. Railguns are like snipers, they're only 100% accurate when you're holding still, and they have a long reload time, which isnt increased by the amount of railguns, so more railguns is more shots before reloading, they do massive damage. There are 7 ways of getting around, thrusters, wheels, tank treads, walker legs, wings, helium balloons, and hover blades. The physics in this game is decently done to the point where you have to make sure your robot is balanced when you're using thrusters, or anything that involves flying, try to make it as even as possible. When you robot is not even in flight, you can tell by how difficult it is to drive. More weight can making being even not mean as much when you're using helium and thrusters, but when using wings, or lightweight robot designs, being even matters the most. All ground methods of moving seem to be stabilized by adding more weight, being even doesn't matter as much. Anyway this is a great game, and I recommend downloading it and playing it, its free, its a quick download, and its quite a bit of fun.

Despite this game being a free-to-play and in its alpha stage in development, FreeJam has done well building and maturing Robocraft. I recently found this game by accident a couple months ago, and ever since I've been hooked. Building with blocks, choosing a method of transportation (flying, wheels, tank threads, hover blades, or walker legs), and adding weapons (healing guns, SMGs, plasma mortar, and sniper guns), there are endless combinations for the kinds of vehicles you can build and play with in this game.
Recently, other games of the similar type have popped up on the Internet, but Robocraft is the original and it is still going strong. Best of all, it's free!
Now the game is not perfect, however, but with active developers and a strong community, fixes come out quickly with small updates every couple days. And even though I like the tiered system this game offers, I have a personal gripe with over-tiering, the use of high-tier weapons on lower-tiered matches. Overall though, this is one of my favorites, and it would be a disservice to yourself to not check it out.

I would recommend this game due to the fact that it is a fun game to play, however there are some big problems with it. First, with each patch they seem to "fix" a way of making a bot. a while ago, it was possible to make a rail-cannon that floated, a lot of people complained, and it got changed. The problem is, there was no problem with them. The only problem will them is that people seem to refuse to put armour on their bot.
Secondly, currently, there is only 4 maps. 2 ice maps, 2 normal maps. What I feel is needed, is a map editor. If they added a map editor, it would allow many, many maps to be create, tested, and have feedback on them without them lifting a finger.
Thirdly, the devs never seem to give even little fixes if the community wants it. There is currently a "Easter egg" where you can exit the ship, however once you do it you're stuck outside the ship until you re-login to the game.  From being a programmer I know how stupidly easy it is to add a button that you can press to reset your position, it's three lines of code in most languages.
Despite all these disadvantages, I do like this game. Unlike similar games such as World of Tanks, it does not take years to get to the highest tier (tier 10); I managed to get the tier 10 in about 80 hours with about 30 hours being premium (double money). Robocraft devs seem to give out a free premium code every month or so. For this reason, I do not play this game very much due the fact that I am now expecting a free day's premium, and just play it when there is free premium.
When it comes to balance of the game I feel this game is nicely balanced from the weapons perspective. however, with the new tank tracks using wheels is pointless tier 3 and up. this is due to the fact that tracks work fine when there are only 2 left, meaning putting 4 on your tank makes you very hard to stop. tracks also have multiple connection points which is a nice feature.
when It comes to the pace of the game, I feel that it is just getting slower and slower. they have nerfed the speed you get from boosters, and they are going to remove the ability to make super speedy bots (called hyper-drives). I think that it would be really nice to see some game mechanics added that allows smaller bots with lots of boosters to go so fast that they are very hard to hit, and have massive bots go slow enough for it to feel like a disadvantage while driving a big bot. Another note to make about the speed of bots is that when, for example, you get the next tier of wheels, it only goes up by a few Km/h, the difference of tier 1 bots (that are meant to be weak and under-whelming) and tier 10 bots (massive or tiny bots that should have a huge vaitity and be really fun to play with and against) is 20 Km/h, more and stronger armour, and more damage on guns. While they have tried to help this by adding more things you can play with in the tech tree, I feel that there should be items that just don't have high-tier equivalents. this would force different play styles at different levels. This would have to be done carefully, but I think it would work.

(TL;DR at bottom)
Okay, I think that I have played this game for a long enough time for me to write a review about it, and this one will be going in depth:
The concept of RoboCraft is to make a vehicle that is piloted in a way that falls into one of the following categories:
Wheels / Car
Wings / Plane
Hover propelled / Hoverboard
*New* Treads / Tank
In combination of one of the following types of weapons:
Machine Gun - Good Damage / Great rate of fire / Low Range / Medium Accuracy / Great up close / no reload, but heat bar instead
Plasma Cannon - Works more like a mortar - High Damage / Medium fire rate/reload speed / Far range (Not the best up close, see MG)
Laser / Beam Rifle - Basically a sniper - Very High Damage / Slowest fire rate/reload speed / farthest range
*New* Bumper Lasers - Haven't had any skill in this yet, it is a T8+ weapon, basically it allows you to ram opponents, melee weapon
Put any one (or several if you are good at it) type of transportation with one type of weapon and make a robot to your liking, with different armor cubes, dont forget that radar dish and jammer so you can pick up your enemy and he can't pick you up. Also add shields so that they take damage and not your robot.
If you have ever played World of Tanks, Then you will know how the battlefield plays out. Get to base and take control of it or destroy the enemy team. While you play even if you don't kill anyone, you can still be a spotter and spot the enemy so your teammates can see that said enemy and take him down. It becomes a very interesting game when you get a robot that works for your play style and you take down enemies with ease.
Tiers of robots happen by getting better stuff unlocked on the tech tree and using those items on your robot which then brings your bot up in tier ranking, from T1 all the way up to T10.
There are some minor problems with the game that although most can easily be fixed, can still cause small hiccups in gameplay:
1. You have to survive battle to get victory reward - This means that even if your team meets the victory conditions, either by taking the base or wiping everyone out, if you did not survive, you get defeated, although it is easy to survive if you stay out of danger and don't charge into battle, it still sucks to have to survive all the way to get any sort of reward.
2. Rewards for defeat are very minimal - This makes sense but if i just finished a battle and we are defeated you will only get very little gold. this at least is fixed by a drop out system after being destroyed like WOT, so if you die early on, you only played for a few minutes. Battles also only last up to 10 mins tops
3. Leveling up takes far too long - After a certain point, character leveling is a chore to do, your robot is only as big as your imagination and the amount of "pFlops" that you have available to you, these "pFlops" are used as a sort of block limit, each type of block. weapon, defensive, etc. item takes up different amounts of these, and the higher tiered items take up more than the tier before them, once you reach the limit on each robot, you can't build on that robot anymore and to increase that limit, you need to level up, the way you level up is by going into battles and doing stuff in them, whether it is taking down enemies or taking sectors of the base, but as you get higher in level, the much more you have to do. MUCH MORE! As I write this am level 24 and that was just reached about last week, and i only got about 1/3 through after several hours of playtime.
4. The higher tier unlocks can take forever to get -  Okay so around T5+ it will take a lot more Robopoints to unlock things on the tech tree, at T6 it takes around 40 points to unlock one item, the only way to get these points is, you guessed it, killing enemies and taking control of the opponents base. So it becomes more of a grind to get the points that you need to unlock that one item you want / need to finish up your winged shield devil to take down your enemies.
I would say that some weapons should be nerfed/powered more but with the way the weapons work, I think it is a perfect balance, sure the rail cannon can take you down in one hit, but it is a sniper weapon, how many snipers usually take more than one shot on a critical area to kill someone?
The developers are always updating this game with bigger and better things suggested by the community, so if you don't like something about the game, just tell them that "Hey, this should be changed." that is how all of these updates came to be.
TL;DR The game is great, very well done mechanics / weapons.  Battles are quickly done, turn the game on for about 15 mins and you can get about 4-5 battles done. The Developers are always fixing / updating this game. Although the game encounters a few problems that you may scratch your head on and wonder "How did they miss that?" It is still a great F2P game. If you like the creativity of minecraft and you like the battlefield / play style of World of Tanks, then seriously try this game out. Simple controls that you can now customize. You have nothing to lose on this game, Seriously, what other game gives you the freedom to make almost any type of vehicle you want and shoot and destroy other vehicles that some other person made with their creative mind. You may even see some vehicles that will give you ideas on your next build.
All-in-all: Try out this game, no risk in playing, just go in with a creative mind each time you play.

The freedom to build your own vehicle and have every block count is a very cool and unique concept. The only real suggestion I have is to make parts count for each vehicle rather than across all vehicles. This would make it much easier to experiment with different types of vehicles without spending too much money or tearing apart a design you already like. Also, perhaps a small single player mode that gives players a good starting point and something to do offline would be a nice addition. None of this is really necessary of course, but it'd be really cool to have more freedom in building. Of course, I'd also recommend increasing the prices of blocks a little to compensate for such a change.
Another thing I'd recommend is adding a permanent premium membership option. I don't particularly like it when games make you renew your ownership of the game. It always makes the company seem greedy, whether it's actually out of greed or not. However, I will admit that while premium members definitely get benefits, you can do anything the same with a free account if you put extra effort into it, which I respect. Still, I get that you want to make money (who doesn't?), but I don't feel this is the right way to do it.
Despite the changes I strongly recommend, this game is no doubt enjoyable, and I still would recommend it to anyone.

I really had to question whether or not I would reccomend this game. The plot is the worst idea ever thought up, put on paper, and released on Steam, so that was a little dissapointing. In case you don't know, the first portal game had you roaming around alone in enclosed rooms listening to a creepy voice that sounds like the described video mode on your television. When I first played this game, there was alot of suspense leading up to the final boss, and it would have been nice to see something like that done in here. Don't tell me they had to use the exact same characters from the first game, because they certainly didn't have any trouble creating a million new characters to explain apeture science's backassed backstory. It's not like you are ever isolated, either. You see GLaDOS 2 minutes into the game, and it looks like a cartoon character. After that, there's this giant eyeball which follows you around, then a talking potatoe that is attached to your portal gun. Still, the point of a story in a video game is to explain the gameplay, and Portal 2's plot does a good job of explaining why all this stuff wasn't here before for the most part. AND THERE IS A LEVEL CREATOR! ACTUAL CHALLENGING PUZZLES! AND YOU CAN MAKE YOUR OWN! I wish I could comment on the co-op, but I never got to play much of it because I'm the only person I know that still plays Portal 2. Just the thought of there being co-op destroys the whole isolation theme of the first game. My last complaint is the music. WTF IS WITH THE TECHNO MUSIC?! You can probably see why I don't want to reccomend this game, but the gameplay is good. Ok, the gameplay is like Portal 1 crossed with TAG: Thw Power of Paint, but there are alot more levels, which was the one problem with Portal 1. I reccomend this game to anyone who wants more of the original Portal. If that is you, make sure you have the entire Portal, Unreal, and Myst soundtracks ready to play over the actual music. If you are looking for something better than Portal 1, stay away.

Portal 2 is (mainly) a puzzle game which gets you 'thinking with portals',
that basically means it's a game which will suck up a lot of your time if you do not know what you are doing in it.
Singleplayer has a interesting storyline which leads off from the start of portal 1, or Portal, and you get woken up by a funny robot called 'wheatly' who has some laugh out loud dialogue. Anyway, the puzzles in the game can be difficult from time to time if you are completely new to the franchise. But a player who isn't new to the franchise shouldn't have to much of a problem navigating the puzzles. Oh by the way, some of the speed-run times on this game are insane.
If singleplayer wasn't enough, you have multiplayer too. This multiplayer involves you and a buddy navigating through completely unique testing chambers exclusive to this co-op mode. These testing chambers can be difficult if you don't have communication or your buddy is being un-cooprative. These testing chambers aren't difficult if you know what your doing but novice players could find it a challenge. Multiplayer also h a feature where you can play the game on the PC and your buddy can play on a console and you can still join each other providing that you are on each other's steam friends list.
To conclude,
Portal 2 has a solid singleplayer as well as multiplayer and you have access to a constant stream of new content due to the modding community is producing new, challenging test chambers for you to 'test' in.

Throughout the single-player campaign I was constantly surprised how clever you could use this "simple" formula of two portals, and I admit, I had to look one or two times in a walkthrough - still, it's manageable for others like me who don't solve puzzles often and I really liked the feeling of accompishment after solving a puzzle and the reward of getting a new piece of the story (told in an unusually silly and amusing way; "lemonades").
And the coop-campaign: I don't know any other game where you solve puzzles this way. Really, it's a lot of fun and shouldn't be missed out either (if you have someone to play with). It was also one of the first games on Steam with Splitscreen support. Although it's made only for two players only, I'm pretty sure that it also would be funny with three or four people locally, when everyone's trying to figure a puzzle out together and the gamepads get handed around.
Lastly, there's the Workshop integration, and boy oh boy, are there a lot of puzzles. There are very complex ones with custom terrain and more simpler ones, created with the later released simpler editor, and there's an endless supply of new ones. I acctually recommend trying the simpler editor out yourself, just to see how hard it is to come up with puzzles.
Anyways, this is a game that everyone should play, even if it's not your genre. Because this is one of those defining games others will draw inspirations from and have to be measured by for years to come.

I love this game, and if you haven't, it's definitely worth a shot!

Anyone who is a fan of puzzle games will definately want to give portal a go, and not regret any second they spent playing it.
This game has a lot going for it; beautiful visuals, a range of puzzles varying in difficulty, excitement, humor, confusion and much, much more. Valve definately knew what they were doing when they put this together. The story behind Aperture is intriguing, it makes you want to find out more about Cave Johnson and Caroline. It is not boring in the slightest either, sure some puzzles may test your skills to a point of searching for a walkthrough, and it is so easy to lose your way whilst exploring outside the test chambers. But once you realise what you are supposed to do you get a sense of pride when you finaly solve the puzzles, and the dialogue from Cave, GLaDOS and Wheatley is great. Talented voice actors reading a large amount of humorous lines, leads to an enjoyable experience to go along with the gameplay.
Plus messing around with the portal gun is always fun, especially  when you get stuck - why not earn the 'terminal velocity' achievement whilst you work out how you're going to get that energy pellet to the receptacle.
The addition of the gels makes the game that much more unique, its great to try and place blue repulsion gel on every surface and bounce around like a bouncy ball.
The battle at the end is really not that difficult, slightly more difficult that the one at the end of Portal however the most dificult thing about it is finishing within the time limit.

Take everything you love about Portal, then times it by five. This game has so many good aspects to it, it's hard to know where to start.
Sound? Witty dialouge, excellent voice work, a really cool soundtrack, and even something as simple as the sounds that the portal gun makes sound awesome!
Gameplay? Addictive.
Story? Really good. There are some parts to the story where I genuinely felt threatened and isolated.
Graphics? Nothing to complain about.
Although Portal 2 is undoubtedly one of the best games I've played in a while, there are two errors that I find with it:
#1 There are parts in the game where you have to use the "zoom" key to find almost unfindable portable surfaces. I thought this gameplay mechanic was rather silly and annoying.
#2 There are parts in the game where the events that happen don't make much sense, and you wonder why you have to do certain things or why you're in certain places.
Overall this game is one of the best games of our generation, and it's loads of fun. It's good aspects overwhelmingly outweighs my tiny nit-picked errors.

ORIGINAL REVIEW
I'm changing my 'Yes' recommendation to a 'NO'. Allow me to explain why.
It's been an incredibly long time since I've played Robocraft. I wound up leaving due to the absolute garbage that the developers insisted on calling 'updates'. I won't even try to explain how acidic the community has become, either. It was a total fustercluck, and the number of players who consistently chose to take advantage of glitches, use builds that rendered them nearly indestructable, and the complete lack of teamwork made things so unbearable that I wound up dropping the game entirely from my library long ago.
When I first start playing, the game was FUN. I would sit and play for HOURS at a time, racking up points, designing bots, testing out new builds, and ENJOYING my time with the game.
Then came the balancing updates. I began to find myself on teams filled with poorly built bots, either focusing entirely on DPS, or build for trolling and insta-kills. I would sit there and seath at the staggering amount of time (little, by the way) my team would be alive, before being overrun by the enemy. There were also bots CLEARLY over-tiered to ensure that they would get more kills and more damage dealt, leading to more points recieved for the ONE bot.
I kept playing though, hoping the devs would notice of the issues. However, nothing happened. Until the Megabots came into play. Then things became infuriatingly difficult to do. Boss Battles became a one-sided slaughter-fest, with Megas dominating the field. Even random matches became unplayable, as Megas skewed the favor in the direction of which team had a Mega (or which one had the least crappy one).
Problem after problem arose. The tiers were removed, making way for a total S#!)-storm of matches. Then a new gamemode was added, and, to encourage people to play it, was made into the PRIMARY gamemode, the one which granted the MOST AMOUNT OF POINTS, but only IF you won. This led to more than one occasion where any team starting off here or there, or only had this many of this type of bot, or had no teamwork at all, was completely destroyed, no matter how hard you fought, or how coordinated you were. It was a mess.
Eventually, I uninstalled this game. I was tired of watching a game with AMAZING potential get flushed down the $#!)er, all because the devs focused more on what a certain group of players wanted, or focused more on, you guessed it, MONEY.
In short: Please, for the love of your sanity and your Steam library, stay away from this game. It is not, I repeat, NOT worth playing anymore. All you will be doing is sitting there raging as your team and your bot are repeatedly decimated by over-powered and unbalanced bots, or put down and demeaned by 'premium' players who spend real-world cash to quickly build powerful bots, and use them to stomp your face into the ground.
You have my two cents. I have stated my reasons for leaving, and CHANGING my recommendation to a 'No'. If you feel that I, and many others, have not made it clear enough as to how bad this game is becoming, then I won't stop you from installing this game and trying it for yourself. Just know that you have be warned.
