This game carries on the legacy of the first Portal game by introducing new gameplay elements, mechanics and characters. Portal 2 is a masterpiece that is satisfying to play and makes once again stepping into the shoes (or rather, Long Fall Boots) of Chell a very fun experience. With a singleplayer and co-op campaign, the game is a huge improvement on the original and even puzzle and physics-based games as a whole. Having accidentely awakened GLaDOS after defeating her in the first game, Chell is given a new Portal Gun and begins testing once again under the watchful eye of GLaDOS. Along with a new Personality Core called Wheatley, the two travel through the test chambers, hoping to find an exit from the hell that is Aperture Science.
With new testing elements such as a tractor beam that can push and pull objects based on what direction it's going, blue gel that makes surfaces bouncy, and aerial faith plates which launch you into the air, Portal 2 makes coming back to Aperture Science a fun, refreshing experience. The puzzles in the first one were basic and limited to cubes, energy pellets and Turrets, but those were extremely fun and this game builds on the already great mechanics.
Storyline wise, it's basic, but it works! There's one particular plot twist in it that will catch you by surprise, and the characters and voice acting in this game are just amazing, in every sense of the word. I found GLaDOS to be an excellent villian that had a very good sense of passive-aggressiveness toward Chell, Wheatley to be a fun character that was delightful to see everytime (P.S. he reminds of an actually funny version of C-3PO), and frankly I just enjoyed what the game had to offer in terms of character development.
Overall, you most definitely should get this. Excellent in every way possible, though there's not a lot of replay value. That's ok, because you can make and play test chambers created by and other players for brand-new problem solving.

This is the equally innovative sequal to what could arguably be called one of the most innovative games of all time.   Being of such pedigree sets an extremely high standard for what one would expect from the game, and it still does not disappoint.
In addition to having just as fun puzzle-based gameplay as the orriginal it provides incredible atmosphere, with incredible backstory.   After playing Portal I would have never thought I could feel sorry for GLaDOS while still feeling angry at her, but this game proves me wrong.   The backstory of Aperature Science is as tragic as it is whimsical.  The major characters of Wheatly and GLaDOS are far more deeply developed than I could ever immagine.
The environments are beyond amazing, with each region having unique looks ranging from well built high-tech testing facuilties that "test subjects" are put through like lab rats, to aging abandoned industrial facuilaties.
The soundtrack is incredible and sets a the mood to scenes be it fear, curiousity, anger, whimsy, or downright insanity.
In addition to the one player and cooperative story modes there are time trials for added replayability.   This is a game perfectionists will love.
Furthermore, this game has continued to age gracefully since it's release, and looks good even by the latest standards.
I honestly can't say anything bad about this game, and almost anyone would like this game.   Even the 13 year old brat swearing like a sailor on X-Box live will find GLaDOS's attempts to belittle you and all the dark humor of Aperature Labs' history to be incredibly entertaining, so even they will likely enjoy the game so long as they get over the fact that you don't get to shoot deadly guns.

Update: August 11, 2017.
After the last few updates, Robocraft has once again become fun and playable.  There are still some minor balance issues here and there, but I'm rewriting my review to 'thumbs up'.
If you want to play high risk & high reward, then play a small bot w/a big gun.
If you want to play safer, then build a large brick with multiple redundant weapons.
Hover medics, Rail insects, Tesla assassin sleds, plasma bombers, Shotgun/Chaingun mechs, AA tanks, and good 'ole fashioned lazer cruisers, etc etc etc.  Lots of different combinations are available, and *viable* -- viable is the key here.
New players can play *anything* off the community robot factory, even if they don't have the parts for it.  This is a huge reason to play if you havn't tried it out before.  Try out a few different bots w/different play styles, and see if RC is for you.  Most free to plays require a lot of grinding before you can try out all the different weapons and movement types, no so with RC.
There is a lot to explore, and if you do like Robocraft, you can move on to building your own bots.  For most of us, that's the real fun and challange.
Enjoy :)

This game carries on the legacy of the first Portal game by introducing new gameplay elements, mechanics and characters. Portal 2 is a masterpiece that is satisfying to play and makes once again stepping into the shoes (or rather, Long Fall Boots) of Chell a very fun experience. With a singleplayer and co-op campaign, the game is a huge improvement on the original and even puzzle and physics-based games as a whole. Having accidentely awakened GLaDOS after defeating her in the first game, Chell is given a new Portal Gun and begins testing once again under the watchful eye of GLaDOS. Along with a new Personality Core called Wheatley, the two travel through the test chambers, hoping to find an exit from the hell that is Aperture Science.
With new testing elements such as a tractor beam that can push and pull objects based on what direction it's going, blue gel that makes surfaces bouncy, and aerial faith plates which launch you into the air, Portal 2 makes coming back to Aperture Science a fun, refreshing experience. The puzzles in the first one were basic and limited to cubes, energy pellets and Turrets, but those were extremely fun and this game builds on the already great mechanics.
Storyline wise, it's basic, but it works! There's one particular plot twist in it that will catch you by surprise, and the characters and voice acting in this game are just amazing, in every sense of the word. I found GLaDOS to be an excellent villian that had a very good sense of passive-aggressiveness toward Chell, Wheatley to be a fun character that was delightful to see everytime (P.S. he reminds of an actually funny version of C-3PO), and frankly I just enjoyed what the game had to offer in terms of character development.
Overall, you most definitely should get this. Excellent in every way possible, though there's not a lot of replay value. That's ok, because you can make and play test chambers created by and other players for brand-new problem solving.

Having played this game for a while now, I would say the game has it's overall pro's and con's, the former outweighing the latter. The creative aspect of the game is virtually unlimited and it's great fun to witness and learn from other people's creations whether they're in your team or fighting against you. It is also a relatively user friendly game and the basics can be picked up quickly by any newcomers. The game itself is also a very small download, considerably less than 1GB. However, there are a number of weak points in the game. One of these points is the purpose of using Galaxy Coins (blue coins, a variation of in-game currency). Aside from having to use them to specifically unlock more garage bays and exclusive shop robots, they dont really serve a purpose and add a pay-to-win aspect of the game that doesn't really work. By using real money to pay for in-game currency does not place you at an advantage to any of your peers, it just accelerates your process of unlocking more equipment and buying newer hardware, something that can just as easily (through patience and practice) be earned through the game using green coins. The use of CPU and Tier Systems is a good way of ensuring balance of equipment in the game, ensuring that everyone is at a level playing field, but they also negate the pay-to-win aspect of the game. Another flaw in the game is the ability to unlock weapons and equipment that do not rightfully belong in their respective Tier, by using Uber Tier Points (only unlocked by using blue coins bought for by real life money). Although this would negatively impact on either the players CPU usage or Tier banding, it can still be a minor nuisance. As a final note, the teamwork aspect of this game is somewhat lacking. The only way to communicate with other teammates is through typing, no options for speaking between team members, and although this is to reduce any unpleasant experiences with younger players, I feel this aspect leaves the teamwork element of the game on a weak note. That being said, I have enjoyed and still thoroughly enjoy this game and would recommend it to anyone who wants to apply their creativity and make a few friends along the way.

This is the equally innovative sequal to what could arguably be called one of the most innovative games of all time.   Being of such pedigree sets an extremely high standard for what one would expect from the game, and it still does not disappoint.
In addition to having just as fun puzzle-based gameplay as the orriginal it provides incredible atmosphere, with incredible backstory.   After playing Portal I would have never thought I could feel sorry for GLaDOS while still feeling angry at her, but this game proves me wrong.   The backstory of Aperature Science is as tragic as it is whimsical.  The major characters of Wheatly and GLaDOS are far more deeply developed than I could ever immagine.
The environments are beyond amazing, with each region having unique looks ranging from well built high-tech testing facuilties that "test subjects" are put through like lab rats, to aging abandoned industrial facuilaties.
The soundtrack is incredible and sets a the mood to scenes be it fear, curiousity, anger, whimsy, or downright insanity.
In addition to the one player and cooperative story modes there are time trials for added replayability.   This is a game perfectionists will love.
Furthermore, this game has continued to age gracefully since it's release, and looks good even by the latest standards.
I honestly can't say anything bad about this game, and almost anyone would like this game.   Even the 13 year old brat swearing like a sailor on X-Box live will find GLaDOS's attempts to belittle you and all the dark humor of Aperature Labs' history to be incredibly entertaining, so even they will likely enjoy the game so long as they get over the fact that you don't get to shoot deadly guns.

Well hello everybody.
I have to say I don't often write reviews but I feel I have no choice thanks to what has become of what was once my favourite game.
Once Upon A Time...
Robocraft was a brilliantly fun game that you could play with friendsa and have a good time. The matchmaking was balanced though the servers often didn't work. Bolt building was enjoyable and you were only limited by the blocks in game and your imagination. You had to work hard to progress and unlock better blocks which would increase your bots standing in a 10 tier system. Most importantly the game was free to play.
Eventually the devs started to move into another direction, they decided to make the game even more diverse and challenging. This was wonderfull and brought many more players to the game. The matchmaking was still balanced and had a variety of different modes. Though the game still felt the same, fun with the occasional server issue. And had a very active dev team in the community.
There were premium options in the game at this time however rather than making it PTW they were mereley an option to PTWFaster which kept matchmaking completely balanced and simply allowed you to move into a tier with more powerful bots and more experienced players. It could also simply be used to purchase cosmetic items.
This all sounds great so far right?
Well it all went downhill from there.
The progression system was completely revamped and essetially removed only relying on in game currency. The matchmaking was completely revamped and has become an incredibly unbalanced mess. Following this the game is simply no longer fun.
But wait!
It gets worse from here.
Cosmetic items that players have payed for were removed with no form of compensation. Bots that people have spent hours working on have been deleted and no blocks returned. And following this the whole premise of the game being FREE TO PLAY is a lie...
The game is now Pay to win with many items being exclusive to premium players. Having MIcrtransactions in order to get Functional blocks from crates like God dam COD. Players who are willing to spend large amounts on a supposedly free to play game get many advantages over everyone else fuelling an incredibly unbalanced matcmaking system.
And what makes it even worse is that for simple things such as colouring a bot free to play players only get 4 colours to choose from. This throws a large premise of the game out the window being player creativity.
I could spend hours writing a more detailed review, heck I could write a damn book. But this game is simply not worth it.
Thankyou  FreeJam for ruining one of the best games out there.

Portal 2 Review - Raymond KT
Portal 2 is a masterpiece, a work of art that you will love for its ingenious story pop-culture, references to logical puzzles and co-op multiplayer. Portal is perfect. Portal 2 is not. It's something better than that. It's human: hot-blooded, silly, poignant, irreverent, base, ingenious and loving. It's never less than a pure video game, but it's often more, and it will no doubt stand as one of the best entertainments in any medium. It's a masterpiece. Valve did an awesome job carrying on from where Portal 1 left off, the twists and turns in the story were as entertaining as they were unseen. I've yet to beat the single player campaign, but finished the whole co-op campaign in 6hrs. Honestly, I have no idea where people are pulling "It's just a 3hr game" from, because unless you're just rushing through everything without even caring about the storyline/graphic design/changes to the spaces there is just no freaking way you can beat the whole game (single player and campaign) in just 3hrs. And if you're seriously just buying this game to rush to the end, then you need to stop playing video games, because they are meant to be enjoyed.
This game is well worth the price tag if you enjoyed the first game, even more so if you're a fan of co-op games (which the portal 2 co-op experiences went way over what I was expecting it to be!)

Cool in theory, terrible in practice. I hate how this game encourages creativity, but only on the surface. In reality, creativity does not translate into victory at all. It's one of those pay to win games where you need to pump money into it in order to be competitive. Pieces used to make your robot are first unlocked using one kind of currency, then need to be bought with another kind of currency, then are equipped using yet another type of currency.
Wasting what little resources that trickle down; is made all the more frustrating when being wrecked by people who are dedicated enough to adhere to the rigid play styles that most consistently dominate. Strategy matters for nothing when faced with superior equipment. Obviously, this is the story of online gaming. But, I would not have expected that from a game about utilizing spacial qualities like shape and mobility.
While this game trips over the pitfalls of online gaming, it offers none of the better aspects of playing with other humans.    No coordination or communication within teams. If anyone ever uses the chat function it's to spam random letters. You are at risk from your teammates as much as any enemy. I cannot count how many times I've been basically immobilized by members of my own team.
Since there is no respawn, if you are disabled for any reason early in a match you're only choices are to leave the match, or watch your team and hope they win. Which is a huge waste of your time  if they don't. I have spent more time spectator than playing, and that would be fine if it was a choice that I had made. It is seriously bad design to punish non-pro players this much.
Do they seriously believe that if they punish us enough we'll pay in order to actually enjoy ourselves? I have a better Idea, don't play or don't pay. There are way more satisfying ways to waste time.

“Well done. Here are the test results: You are a horrible person. I’m serious, that’s what it says: “A horrible person.” We weren’t even testing for that. Don’t let that horrible-person thing discourage you. It’s just a data point. If it makes you feel any better, science has now validated your birth mother’s decision to abandon you on a doorstep.” – GLaDOS
In Portal 2, you (Chell) find yourself in a hotel room of sorts where you just woke up from hibernation. The story element and the humor from the characters you become involved with are truly what make the game great. I find the puzzle element to be simply a bonus.  I won’t give away what happens in Portal 2, you’ll have to find out for yourself. I will say however that GLaDOS does make a comeback and you are introduced to a humorous AI program named “Wheatley.”
The game is much, much longer than its predescesor…you’ll find yourself playing this game for at least a few hours. Some of the puzzles were tricky, especially the later ones that brought lasers and different kinds of slime into the mix. The new features and environments help keep the game fresh while the story unfolds to its final conclusion.
For those of you who enjoy teaming up with a friend, you’ll be happy to know that there is a Co-Op mode that allows two players to tackle puzzles together. The Co-Op mode was designed separately from the main game so the puzzles you and your partner will face are completely new and just as likely to leave you scratching your head. Each player gets a portal gun, meaning you can have up to four portals in the test chambers at once. Most puzzles are designed around this, making you both coordinate your portals and movements in order to advance to the next room.
Easy to recommend to anyone who enjoys puzzles and interacting with psychotic AIs.

Portal 2 Review - Raymond KT
Portal 2 is a masterpiece, a work of art that you will love for its ingenious story pop-culture, references to logical puzzles and co-op multiplayer. Portal is perfect. Portal 2 is not. It's something better than that. It's human: hot-blooded, silly, poignant, irreverent, base, ingenious and loving. It's never less than a pure video game, but it's often more, and it will no doubt stand as one of the best entertainments in any medium. It's a masterpiece. Valve did an awesome job carrying on from where Portal 1 left off, the twists and turns in the story were as entertaining as they were unseen. I've yet to beat the single player campaign, but finished the whole co-op campaign in 6hrs. Honestly, I have no idea where people are pulling "It's just a 3hr game" from, because unless you're just rushing through everything without even caring about the storyline/graphic design/changes to the spaces there is just no freaking way you can beat the whole game (single player and campaign) in just 3hrs. And if you're seriously just buying this game to rush to the end, then you need to stop playing video games, because they are meant to be enjoyed.
This game is well worth the price tag if you enjoyed the first game, even more so if you're a fan of co-op games (which the portal 2 co-op experiences went way over what I was expecting it to be!)
The best ever! Steam AND Valve, you have done a GREAT job!

Don't bother with this game in it's current state. If the concept interests you, wait to see if it ever comes out of Alpha.
The game currently seems to be getting worse with each update:
There are rather blatant balance issues (an overwhelming majority of players will agree that SMGs have been overpowered for six months, and Railguns keep getting even worse after each patch). The fixes that are released to try to adress supposed balance problems are blunders at best, nerfing seemingly random types of vehicles and with extremely arbitrary implementations that result in things like only one type of gun mattering at all in boss fights. Old players also get a massive advantage in versus matches against new players, which will torment you during the entire grind to tier 10.
It's very often that an update completely breaks the game. Even after hotfixes, it's obvious that the developers are very inexperienced and lack any sort of quality control or testing, for example, accidentally moving the killfeed to cover the minimap (and the following admission from the responsible developer that nobody had actually even bothered to try the change in-game!), apparent lack of pre-constructed bots to test their changes (they claimed they didn't realize wing mechanic changes could affect bomber planes...), and serious netcode issues.
But what makes me worry about the future of this game the most is the fact that the developers seem to completely avoid player feedback. The subforum specifically dedicated to gameplay feedback is completely barren of developer insight, nearly all threads go without an official response and when there is one, it's never positive or willing to change anything about the game. The only topic that seems to bait the dev team out of hiding is monetization. You also might as well forget about cheater reports...
EDIT: Now this is just rich. As of the latest update they are charging money for essential bot building information such a speedometer. Not only they have not fixed ANY of the game's problems ever since this review was published, they have actually managed to limit your creativity even more if you're a non-paying player. If this game wasn't pay-to-win before, it is now.

Don't get me wrong. Robocraft is a perfectly good game and all, but I do not recommend playing it. I will address why towards the end of the review. For now, let me address the critical aspects of Robocraft as a whole.
The Gameplay ranges from average to great - solely depending on how serious your teamates are about winning. The game consists of you and your team building whatever vehicles you want and setting about demolishing the other team. As of the date this review was made, you can have access to 5 different ways to blow the enemy sky high: SMGs, Plasma Cannons, Railguns, Tesla blades and a Nano-beamer which can restore allies vehicles. You can stack Tesla blades with other guns, but you can't have an SMG with a Railgun. The problem is that these are not very well balanced: Railguns are far worse than Plasma cannons, just as an example. Remember how I said that the battles can range up to great depending on your teammates? If you are using a railgun, you are literally dependant on your allies protecting you while it is recharging. And it takes a long time to do so, during which you are more vulnerable than a snowflake in a volcano, for lack of a better analogy. And since blowing up enemy vehicles is a part of the game, you can blow up individual parts of the enemy vehicles - in the time in takes for you to read this review up to here, you can now fire your railgun again, except you can't because someone has blown it up. Now you have to wait for someone else to come across and restore your guns so you can defend yourself. And now you are dead because your healing ally is busy polishing someone else's vehicle. And this happens more often than not. I should mention that the tier system in place for research (yes, research requires you to acquire Tech Points in varying tiers, and unless you pay real money, there is no way to cross-tier your Tech Points) is not that great - more than once have I seen Nano-beamers (which are acquired at Tier 7, minimum) used in a Tier 2 or 3 match, I have once had the pleasure of seeing an enemy using a Tier 10 Plasma in Tier 4 - Ouch is a massive understatement. At least now you have boss fights where a lot of T4s can fight a big, bulky, one-shotting T10. But this happens so rarely it might as well not have been implemented.
There are items you can acquire to help you stealth your way around the map, such as Radar Jammers, but then the enemy can just spot you by pressing Q - which makes you very obvious to every enemy on the map - so there isn't a point. Also, only two parts of your vehicle - the pilot seat and the block it is sitting on - determine life or death.
In order to acquire better stuff, you either pay endlessly (It takes at least $20 and a lot of grind to unlock everything in one sitting), you have to not only acquire Tech Points, but also Robo Points which are used for purchasing stuff once you have it available. Up until recently, dying yielded you a lot less points, even if you wiped out more than half the enemy team - the emphasis is on surviving rather than killing. Ironically, killing is the only way to acquire more points to pore into your vehicles. And that is pretty much all I need to say about the Gameplay.
The Aesthetics are not exactly what I would call good, but it isn't terrible either. Robocraft is one of those games where you can literally build anything you want and it would be the way your vehicle is. Wait a minute, "build anything you want"? Isn't this somewhat vaguely familiar? As in overdone by this point? Not that this game does it poorly, but I think I have seen enough ugly vehicles, that are ugly on purpose, but I have seen some rather... rude... looking vehicles. There is very little moderation in terms of vehicle aesthetics. Otherwise, some of the maps are very good and are pleasing to look at, but then you build a flying vehicle and seen the endless plains outside the map. If it were me, I would have just used a skybox - they already implemented a force field to prevent you from leaving in a flying vehicle. At least a high-res Skybox would have been acceptable, and would yield less complaints, and would have been a lot more processor friendly. And that is all I have to say about Aesthetics - they are only graphics and are only responsible for maybe 20% of a game's value.
The soundtrack, even when the music volume is on full, can be rather quiet at times. I get it, it is supposed to create tension when I do rarely hear it, but if anything it annoyed me. Maybe that is because I prefer the soundtrack in any game to fit what the game is about - I do not associate the need for stealth with a game that is clearly about blowing the pilot seat out of a heavily armoured vehicle, and where stealth does little more than get you killed quicker if you try. I ended up turning off the music and listened to the Tyrian OST - which was much more suitable, but  I just happen to be listening to another game's OST while playing this one. So yeah, go figure.
I understand most people would not recommend a game because of its developers. This happened to Paranautical Activity, the developers said some rather nasty stuff to their fans and to Valve, and as a result they had their game kicked out. But the Developers for Robocraft are not like that at all. They regularly add new patches to their game to make it more fun - recently, a "Hero Bonus" was added to compensate those people that die wiping out more than half the enemy team. And they make newspaper articles to hint at new features being developed. They also take some feedback on the odd occassion, albeit more of an acknowledgement than anything. For a team of 10 people, what they have achieved is pretty good so far. I encourage them to make a game that you have to pay money to play, as opposed to "Pay to win", which is what Robocraft is rather sadly.
Ok people. I said that I don't reccommend this game and here is the reason. Now, I'm not a hacker, and as someone who will eventually get into game development, I fully understand the concerns that developers have for their games to ensure that people don't cheat to win. But there are far better ways of doing this than using EasyAntiCheat (also called EAC, Robocraft refers to its system as Roboshield). In case you don't know why anti-virus software has such a big problem with EAC, it is because EAC literally acts like spyware. When you play Robocraft, you are giving permission for the guys at EAC to monitor your personnal details. They can rename it however they like, it doesn't change what they are doing. Having access to your data is basically giving up your privacy for security, an area that is already being heavily debated in the Information Technology industry (remember the PAPA framework anyone? If you don't, I suggest you Google "Mason, PAPA Framework"). In anycase, they tell us that EAC is using the data being data-mined to detect hackers and such, but that is a lot of processing power being used, and I have trouble believing that it is all for 'verification' of the game's validicity. True, this is EASY Anti Cheat that FreeJam are using, but nothing is ever labelled as EASY unless there are ways around it. You may have noticed that less than 50% of Robocraft players are hanging around, and even that number is ever decreasing due to EAC. A far better and more person friendly approach would have been to use Valve's Anti Cheat (also called VAC). For one, VAC doesn't act like spyware, it is server side only (which is another advantage, you can't have your users decompile your EAC on their client to find exploits and whatnot) and uses less processing power which can free up more servers. And while yes, VAC is open-source, this is actually an advantage.
And that is the review. DO NOT PLAY until they use VAC instead of EAC. Hopefully, they will correct that mistake soon.

The game itself was amazing, the puzzles were challenging and the whole game is a thrill to get through. It is a great continuation from the first game for those veterans and amazing for first-timers. The start really got me into it, waking up after being in stasis for God knows how long with some "Minor/serious" brain problems (as told by your new companion, Weatley) and seeing how much the facility has changed. After going through some familiar test chambers, you meet up with Weatley again to try and get the single portal gun.
A few more test chambers, and some time just carrying Weatley, GLaDOS is seen now dilapidated and deactivated. Then comes to show how stupid Weatley is by accidentily activating GLaDOS. The aniamtions for GLaDOS is a nice change from how she is when you first fight her in Portal 1 with which she's pretty much stationary for the most part.
Even after that, there's many twists and turns that are, at first, hard to wrap my head around until I thought long enough like the Prophet Turret's quotes which would actually make sense much, much later. The game just blew my mind by how well done it is as it makes want to play this game again and again. Heck, I might get the expansion, Conversion, and try it out as well.

Absolutely brilliant! Valve takes their smash hit game from 2007, and completely expands upon every single detail. Everything from the single-player story mode, to co-op, to level design and music... every single detail possible was attended to. "Oh, we could add more challenges to puzzles." "Let's expand upon Aperture Science." On top of that, the co-op is very enjoyable and you'll spend countless hours with your friend/ girlfriend trying to figure out how to get that Companion Cube over to the other side. The story is great and expands upon the science powerhouse that is Aperture Science. Longer that the original and bigger in scope than Half-Life 2, the story is truly a treat for everyone. Of course, not every little detail is perfect, as their are some issues that I do have with the game. But they aren't anything major that detracts from the overall gaming experience, just little nitpicks here and there. Overall, this game deserves a solid 9/10!

Robocraft is a fun game to play!

An excellent customizable vehicle combat experience. Building a vehicle that works takes patience and multiple test runs, like in Kerbal Space Program, but the reward is getting to show off your toy on the battlefield. Fun, dynamic battles and music that gets your blood flowing combine into a great multiplayer sandbox arena. The game is freemium, but not overwhelmingly so. You can still have a great time as a free user.
My only complaint is the significant limitation of what you *can* build versus what you *should* build. For instance, I built a strong, normal-looking tank and it stood up to competition quite well, but wasn't really that creative. I then built a giant Cheshire cat grin that flew into the battlefield and shot lasers from its mouth, but it was often blown up by the normal-looking tanks before I got a chance to show it off.
Many of your creations might be cool to look at, but they won't stand up under enemy fire. While the realism of this is understandable, I would like to see a little more reward for creativity and ingenuity in the game's mechanics. How about racing, or obstacle courses, or even just a community showcase? The goal of a game like this should not only be to have fun, dynamic battles where bullets chip away at your constructions and ultimately leave you with just a couple of wheels and a chair, but also to show off the fun creations that the players build.

It's hard to think of the proper way to review this game.  I'll start out by saying that if I had to rate the game, it would be a 9.5/10.  It's really that good (and, if I'm being honest with myself, that .5 deduction is hardly something that will bother most people).
Gameplay:
The gameplay is a step up from the original Portal in every way.  From the storyline to the physics and controls, this game has upgraded all of it.  While the story in Portal was pretty short, this one is long and immersive, both in the single player campaign and the multiplayer campaign.  The voice acting is superb (and very often hilarious) and the level design is incredible (you'll notice throwback levels if you played the original).
Replayability:
Out of every game I own, this game retains the most replay value thanks to a built in level creator and steam workshop support.  You can build all of your own levels and map designs with in a super easy to use point and click editor.  It's literally as simple as connect the dots.  This includes both single player and multi player levels.  When you want to play new levels you just subscribe in the workshop and there it is.
This is where my .5 deduction lies.  If you want to create some of the elements you see in the single player campaign, you'll have to use the hammer world editor to do so, rather than the in game editor.  Most of these are purely aesthetic in nature (certain themes found in game such as overgrowth), but there are some mechanical designs I wish were available in the basic editor.  These include things like porous metal walls that you can shoot portals through (and stand on, etc) that are useful to create some more clever designs, the ability to trigger animations, etc.  Like I said, it's not like you can't make them if you really wanted to, it's just much more complex to pull off.
TLDR:  Buy this game and you might get cake.

Well here we are Portal 2 the masterful puzzle game that gripped me till the very end.
This game is incredible, building on the success of Portal the sequel originally named Portal 2 (*clap**clap**clap*) adds better designed chambers, incredible story telling, great voice acting, freaking comedy and the amazing "Now I only want you gone" at the end of the game (sorry "still alive" this one is just so much better).
The game has a 8 hour long Single Player Campaign a slightly shorter Co-Op Campaign and also a Map editor so therefore millions of community created chambers WOW that is a lot of content for a puzzle game.
The puzzles can be shockingly easy and very difficult at times but the hilarious characters GLADOS, Wheatley and Cave Johnson will have you laughing out loud many times and this will encourage you to not give up on the puzzles. I have to say the satisfaaction after you complete a chamber is incredible.
The gripping story is well enough but also the backstory of Aperture and it's CEO Cave Johnson is amazing we also get to find out who GLADOS really is and the new gameplay mechanics are really fun to play with a great example of this is the gels in Portal 2 there is a jumpy gel a speed gel and a portal surface gel these can be extremely fun and a great distraction form the constant amount of puzzles thrown your way.
In the end is recommending Portal 2 really a question I didn't think so.
Final Verdict: Portal 2 9/10

Portal 2 is the amazingly imersive and fun sequel to the amazingly imersive and fun videogame known as portal. It isn't however one of those sequels where they give you the same product with prettier graphics and do nothing to improve on it; the game contains many great new innovations. At its core, portal is a puzzle platformer game, and this aspect is combined with the story in a way that forces you to think of outside-the-box solutions. The characters are all compelling; even the silent protagonist gets some characterization during the game. She's smart, good at jumping, and is able to jump over both emotional and physical obstacles with ease. When things get tough, and she has a murderous AI tryng to kill her at every turn, she just keeps testing.
The game has essentially three modes. There's the story, co-op, and community made maps. The community for this game  is amazing. They take all the resources Valve has lent them, and they make games barely recognizable as part of portal. It could also go in the opposite direction, and you get a game that feels like it should be a part of the main story. One major downside is that you cann't play co-op, or in  community maps, if you lack an internet connection. There are many great maps that make you think and analyze the tools you're given in different ways; It's a shame that you can't just download and play one of them while on the go.
If you're not into puzzle platforming, in-depth and imersive storytelling doesn't impress you, and you don't like any of your friends enough to play this with them without committing murder, this isn't the game for you.

The only real suggestions i can make to the devs are as follows:
1. Boss battles sometimes spawn your vehicle right in line of sight of the boss.  It is no fun to be gunned down with one powerful blast within 2 seconds of the match. I would recommend changing player spawn points behind map obstacles to prevent this.  I realize that it may have been done intentionally as a way to give an early edge to the Boss, but it could be taken as sloppy consideration by many (and is no fun for the guy on the receiving end of a 1 hit kill pulse blast).
2. Ally icons on the mini map need to specify the type of weapon that the player has equipped to their vehicle. For example, a circle with the letter "P" would be sufficient for pulse cannon. This would encourage team play through increased awareness of what each team member possesses in their arsenal. I might decide to follow a particular ally who is equipped with a healing nano tech cannon if i new he had one. as it stands, im relegated to visually observing each ally i pass by on my way to whichever route i choose to follow.  This becomes a less likely method for identifying your allies capabilities if you are in a flying vehicle since you will typically be far above them and will likely outpace them.
Overall, I feel this game is headed in the right direction and i would recommend it to any fellow gamer.

Robocraft what was once a decent game got broken down in bits.
"Everything" has been simplified...
Back in the day you had tiers, which meant a noob would never face off an expierence user at the get go. Which also allowed expierence users to build bots with just enough points to play in sudden tiers. So you could face off smaller bots with your own small bot while now that isn't posible. Ofcourse you can run with a small bot but now you will face off bots of 2000CP...
Now there is only 2 tiers, bellow 2000 and above 2000 which are custom games entirely.
Instead we get now loot boxes at the end of a round xx if u won xx if u lost.
All the blocks have been removed and we got only normal or the light blocks left.
I won't say that the tallent system was good but this is even worse.
Catch up system being broken, while you have the entire match 3 points active.
The enemy team can destroy a crystal and win with 1 point active while we have 2 afterwards.
What the f-ck ?!? its like having 90% and they have 30% yet they can still win with the crystal.
I understand that you want a catch up system but I've never seen it this bad.
I didn't write this review because I hate the game.
The opposite is true I just wish they never simplified the game like this.

Ah, there is so much to say about Portal 2 that I don't know where to begin. First off, if you are deciding to buy Portal or Portal 2, go for the bundle when it's on sale. The bundle will save you money, and if it's on sale, it's a steal! Now to the actual game. The controls are exactly the same in singleplayer, and it is much longer than the original game, so it is worth the buy. If you loved Portal but wished for a more story driven game, Portal 2 is for you. Watch Aperture Labs unfold before your very eyes and witness the glory of GLaDOS, the new cores such as Wheatley and the Space Core, and even the new robots Atlas and P-Body. For $20, I believe it is worth it. For $5, which I got it for on sale, how could you pass up the offer! Also, the game has a great workshop feature were you can download community made maps and make your own for the community to try! Overall, the only reason I could not reccomend it is if you don't have the hardware space, but if you do, do yourself a favor and install it as soon as possible!

Used to be good, but the client-server protocol is not encrypted and cheating was possible. Their solution to this problem was terrible. Rather than fix the protocol, they wrapped the software in an 'Easy Anti-Cheat' application. This application is variously reported as a trojan or spyware. by many antivirus applications and with good reason. There is no privacy policy listed anywhere for the software.
Tech errata:
EAC monitors all incoming and outgoing traffic, hooks into system processes, and reads all keyboard and mouse input. This behavior is not limited to the game client; It attempts to inject a dll into every process that utilizes directx -- which includes Internet Explorer, Chrome, and Firefox. The application is capable of taking screenshots, recording keyboard and mouse input, and launching executables remotely. In effect, it is a command and control bot client running on your computer and the only assurance it won't wake up and steal all your personal data is... well, there isn't an assurance. In fact, the company expressly disclaims any liability or responsibility, and will not comment on what it does do. Even World of Warcraft's "Warden" software is not as invasive. Worse, all that is necessary to defeat it is to run the packet sniffer from within a VM. VMware in 'NAT' mode uses raw sockets, which EAS does not hook into, instead of winsocks5, which it does. You can still use the exact same cheats as before to give yourself unlimited resources; It just requires a different tool than the one that has been on demo at YouTube. And no, I won't tell you which one; This is a game review, not a howto on cheating.
Bottom line: They screwed the pooch. Don't buy it. Don't even play it. It is not worth the risk of someone hacking their servers and turning every computer this game is installed on into their own playground. If the company doesn't trust its own products enough to assume liability, you shouldn't either.

Basically Minecraft meets Space Engineers meets Team Fortress 2.
Build and construct robots, fight in battles, get Robo Points (in game currency) buy better weapons, armor, cosmetics, and utilies, rinse and repeat. If you don't mind grinding some Robo Points to get to the next tier, and if you don't mind being occasionally instakilled, and if you don't mind a few glitches and bugs, this game is for you.
There is no real tutorial and you are going to have to figure out some of the game mechanics on your own or by reading the wiki.
The graphics are average. They look fine from a distance but when you zoom in they seem rather ugly, but what did you expect from an early access F2P game that's not from a major game company.
The great things about this game is that your robot is completely up to you. There is no real standards or presets, and there is 4 different types of guns. SMGs, the fast-firing laser that you have to start out with, Plasma Cannons, which you unlock at T3 and are basically rocket launchers that fire slowly, railguns which are basically snipers which fire extremely slowly, and Nano Disruptors, which can heal your teammates (but not yourself!)
Also, it's up to you whether your robot will be land-based, hovering, aerial, or a crawler.
Once you have finished your robot you can choose 1 of 3 gamemodes: Practice (figting and killing AIs and not earning any points) Battle (fighting real players that are the same tier as you) or Boss (Available at T8 and above, play as a boss against robots of much weaker tiers.)
Overall, I would give this game a 7/10 for the creativity and the different gamemodes.

I can't believe I forgot to write a review of this game! Well, let us just say that Portal 2 is a game unlike any other. It combines the always interesting portal gun mechanic with hilarious humor and a deep, incredible storyline that is left in mystery. The graphics fit the game very well, and are a great example of the full capacity of the Source Engine. The puzzles are fun and each one is different. They vary in difficulty, but none are so difficult that they cause frustration. The soundtrack is truely awe inspiring. I still find myself listening to "Science is Fun," "Bombs for Throwing at You," and the ending song among other great parts of the soundtrack (I recommend listening to the entire soundtrack if you ever have to study for something! It makes it MUCH better!). The co-op is some of the most fun I have ever had with my friends in videogames. It is funny, challenging (but not too challenging), and a good chunk of game that will take you and a partner a good while to complete (depending on how often you play). The Perpetual Testing Initiative was also a great addition, and allows you to try puzzles of many difficulty levels. There are also some awesome custom co-op campaigns. The game also has some cool mods to try, and there are many other interesting ones coming out soon. The only problem with the game is that it has no sense of replayability, although I really don't see that as much of an issue. A really fun thing to try is to make a friend who has never played the game try it. Trust me, you won't be disappointed. Overall, Portal 2 is easily one of the greatest games I have ever played, and is probably one of the best games ever created. Despite its greatness though, I still retain the opinion that the original Portal is better. Play it first. The stories link together strongly, and the atmosphere and feel to the original is extremely well developed. Portal 1 is some (mostly) serious art. Portal 2 is art with a splash of fun. Bottom line is, you have to play Portal 2, but you also have to play Portal 1 first.

The ONLY problem I had with this game, seriously the only one, is that it becomes KIND OF like a Pay to Win game. You'll notice people flying around, or shooting giant guns and you'll say, "Hey! I want to do that, too! I'll build something like that after this match." Then after the match you look for how to get it and you need certain things a few tiers up. So you say, "OK, so I need to upgrade these star-things then. So how do I do that?" Then you pay the 'Galaxy Cash' needed to upgrade them, and then you never get any except for the 100 they give you at the beginning. And 100 is not much. The game is fun, and the robot construction is, too, but I would like the game a whole lot more if you got just a little Galaxy Cash after a match. I don't care even if you get 1 per round. Just SOME way other than paying real money for it.
Besides the one flaw this game has, its a great game. Its fun, unique (kinda) and feels good to play once you get the hang of it. Like most people (including myself), you'll make Robots that will flip upside down and render you useless, but then you find ways out of it. The whole game is experimentation, which I like. You try one thing, something about it didn't work, you change it, try it again, works a little better, change it again, not quite as good, change it a little bit more, works even better. I like things that work like this, you learn by playing the game. You don't have to sit there and listen to someone tell you how to right click and left click.
Overall, I give this game a 7/10. It has ALOT of potential to be one of those games that EVERYONE has heard about, played and enjoyed. I just feel that if they implement a way to get Galaxy Cash other than to pay for it, there would be so many people playing the game it would be crazy.

Portal 2 is a first person puzzle game with excellent physics challenges.
It is a second part of the story from the first Portal game.  The narrator
is dry and sarcastic, and very funny, and the story is well done; it helps
you propel through the game even when you are stumped by whatever puzzle
you may be working on.
The game performs smoothly, with will done level design.  The puzzles
are based off of manipulating the levels with a portal gun, as well as
using gravity and physics when necessary.  The difficulty and level design
progress in a balanced way, and does a great job of leading you in a linear
fashion, but leaving you to solve the puzzles on your own.  Awareness of
the details of the map is key.
For someone who likes puzzle games, this is an easy recommend.

Robocraft is basically Minecraft for robo-battle fans.
The number of possible robots you can make a virtually infinite, and every single one can serve a different purpose, although obviously some will be more useful than others.
It's a big test of creativity, strategy, and skill in PvP situations that is well balanced and addicting.
The levelling and accumulation of money is slow unless you have premium, but it's not obnoxious, and they give out free premium days so frequently you dont really even need to purchase premium.
All in all, well worth trying.
